Feature Learning in Wide Neural Networks under μ\muP:
Identifiability and Sparse-Dictionary Decomposition
of the Mean-Field Limit

Akmal Xodarev Affiliation: Independent Researcher Affiliation: ORCID: 0009-0000-5318-7284 Email: xodarevakmal@gmail.com Affiliation: Tashkent, Uzbekistan
First version: December 23, 2025
This version: May 15, 2026

Abstract

We establish four structural results for feature learning in wide two-layer neural networks under the Maximal Update Parametrization. First, we prove global existence and uniqueness of the mean-field limit of noisy gradient descent under μ\muP, identifying the maximal admissible weight w∗w^{\ast} on the moment sequence of the initialization as the reciprocal parameter-moment-growth boundary and hence the largest weighted moment class ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} propagated by the flow; the finite-particle approximation has uniform-in-time squared-Wasserstein rate O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}).

Second, we establish a characterization of identifiability of the mean-field limit: two admissible parameter measures induce the same network function in L2L^{2} exactly when their active components agree modulo the finite-rank realization symmetry of the architecture. The orbit depth Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} is separated from the moment-variety depth Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}.

Third, we characterize the active support of the long-time limit measure as a sparse-dictionary decomposition: under the Barron–Hermite target condition, the active component is supported on at most S∗S^{\ast} atoms modulo finite-rank realization symmetry, and S∗S^{\ast} is bounded by an explicit coefficient-threshold number Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda). Fourth, we derive the total feature-learning-error decomposition into statistical, optimization, propagation-of-chaos, and sparse-residual components, with a target-dependent Hermite/Barron tail replacing any initialization-only residual. The four results are tied together by an architectural identity: the triple (w∗,Dorb∗,S∗)(w^{\ast},D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}},S^{\ast}) – the maximal admissible weight on which the mean-field flow admits a global solution, the orbit identifiability depth, and the sparse-dictionary depth at which the target function is realizable – is the natural learning cell of the architecture–data pair (σ,ρ)(\sigma,\rho). The proofs are self-contained except for standard results from μ\muP and mean-field Langevin theory, recalled in the appendices.

Keywords.

Feature learning; Maximal Update Parametrization (μ\muP); mean-field neural networks; propagation of chaos; identifiability; sparse-dictionary decomposition; total error decomposition.

Primary: 68T07, 62F12, 49Q22. Secondary: 60H30, 60J60, 60F17.

ACM CCS 2012 classification.

Computing methodologies →\to Machine learning theory; Mathematics of computing →\to Probabilistic representations.

1 Introduction

1.1 The structural gap

The theory of feature learning under the Maximal Update Parametrization has developed along several precise but separate lines. Tensor Programs identify the infinite-width scaling at which feature learning remains nondegenerate (Yang and Hu, 2021; Yang et al., 2024). Mean-field gradient-flow theory gives the distributional limit for two-layer networks in related scalings (Chizat and Bach, 2018; Mei et al., 2018). Mean-field Langevin dynamics supplies particle approximation and long-time regularization tools (Suzuki et al., 2023; Nitanda, 2024; Nitanda et al., 2025). Dynamical mean-field calculations describe kernel order parameters and finite-width fluctuations (Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2023a; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2023b). These results do not by themselves give a single theorem chain connecting existence of the μ\muP mean-field limit, identifiability of the limiting parameter law, sparse-dictionary structure of its active support, and a total error decomposition for finite width, finite sample size, and finite training time.

This paper supplies that chain for the two-layer architecture. The parameter is θ=(w,b,a)∈ℝd+2\theta=(w,b,a)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+2}, the feature is T⁡(θ)​(x)=a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b)T(\theta)(x)=a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b), and the network function is the barycentre fμ=∫T⁡(θ)​𝑑μ​(θ)f_{\mu}=\int T(\theta)d\mu(\theta). The μ\muP scaling enters through the coordinate learning rates and through the limiting empirical-measure dynamics. The sparse-dictionary statement enters through the active component of the long-time measure, not through a separate teacher-student ansatz.

1.2 The contribution

Theorem 3.1 proves global existence and uniqueness of the entropy-regularized mean-field Langevin equation corresponding to noisy gradient descent under μ\muP. The theorem identifies the maximal admissible weight w∗w^{\ast}, not a class named w∗w^{\ast}: the weight generates a class ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} of measures with controlled moment growth. This resolves the convention issue that arises for Gaussian initialization, for which (𝔼​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)≍n1/2(\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2n})^{1/(2n)}\asymp n^{1/2} and therefore w∗(n)≍n−1/2w^{\ast}(n)\asymp n^{-1/2}. The proof of the N−1N^{-1} squared-Wasserstein rate is a synchronous-coupling proof and does not invoke an independent empirical quantization estimate.

Theorem 4.5 proves identifiability modulo finite-rank realization symmetry. The theorem separates the orbit invariant Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} from the moment-variety invariant Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}. These two numbers agree on regular strata of the finite-rank moment map but need not agree on singular tensor strata, especially for polynomial activations. The active quotient is expressed by the finite-rank group GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}, not by an unrestricted permutation symmetry. The analytic step is formulated as a compact-exhaustion argument on the quotient so that the monotone-class step is tied to a concrete separating algebra.

Theorem 5.5 proves sparse-dictionary decomposition of the long-time active measure. The sparse depth S∗S^{\ast} is defined a posteriori as the minimal active cardinality after the theorem gives an explicit upper bound. The bound is

Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)=#⁡{m:|f^m∗|>cσ​λ}​mult⁡(σ),S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda)=\#\{m:|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|>c_{\sigma}\lambda\}\,\operatorname{mult}(\sigma), (1)

where the coefficients are read in the Hermite/Barron dictionary used by H4 and mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma) is the finite multiplicity with which a retained coefficient may require ridge atoms. The statement uses full-support initialization with positive density rather than a target-dependent accessibility assumption.

Theorem 6.1 proves the total error decomposition. The statistical term contains the explicit active dimension S∗​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2/nS^{\ast}(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}/n. The extra logarithm records the truncation radius needed under polynomial-growth activations. The sparse residual is the target-dependent tail

κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=∑m>S|f^m∗|2+Cσ​λ​S,\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=\sum_{m>S}|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|^{2}+C_{\sigma}\lambda S, (2)

which is finite for the Barron–Hermite targets covered by H4. The propagation term remains O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}) in squared Wasserstein or squared prediction norm.

1.3 The architectural identity

The four theorems identify the triple (w∗,Dorb∗,S∗)(w^{\ast},D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}},S^{\ast}) as the natural learning cell of the architecture–data pair (σ,ρ)(\sigma,\rho). Here w∗w^{\ast} is the maximal admissible weight propagated by the flow, Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} is the orbit identifiability depth, and S∗S^{\ast} is the sparse-dictionary depth at which the target function is realizable. The statement is a conclusion, not an extra definition. The weight w∗w^{\ast} determines which moment-growth boundary is propagated. The number Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} determines the active quotient dimension in identification and statistical covering. The integer S∗S^{\ast} determines how many active dictionary atoms remain after regularized long-time training.

1.4 Relation to the literature

The μ\muP scaling is anchored in the abc-parametrization analysis of Yang and Hu (2021) and in the depthwise extension of Yang et al. (2024). The present paper uses this scaling as input and analyzes the limiting law as a measure-valued stochastic process. The mean-field variational structure follows the lineage of Chizat and Bach (2018), Mei et al. (2018), Jordan et al. (1998), and Ambrosio et al. (2008). The particle approximation is organized around the uniform-in-time estimates of Suzuki et al. (2023) and the objective-gap refinement of Nitanda (2024). The multi-index statistical dimension is aligned with the effective-dimension viewpoint of Mousavi-Hosseini et al. (2025). The identifiability quotient is connected to finite-neuron recovery and symmetry analyses such as those of (Fornasier et al., 2022; Simsek et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024).

1.5 Organization

Section 2 fixes notation, the μ\muP scaling, the mean-field SDE, weighted moment classes, finite-rank symmetries, and the four hypotheses. Sections 3–6 prove the four main theorems. Section 7 computes the invariants in six architecture–target cases. Section 8 lists directions left by the theorem chain. Appendices A–G give the detailed moment, coupling, quotient, sparse-tail, covering, and error-bookkeeping calculations.

2 Notation, μ\muP, and the mean-field setup

2.1 Probability space, data, architecture

Throughout this paper we fix a finite training horizon T>0T>0, a complete probability space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) supporting all Brownian motions in this paper, a data distribution ρ\rho on ℝd×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} with input marginal ρX\rho_{X} and label marginal ρY\rho_{Y}, and a measurable activation σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}.

Definition 2.1 (Parameter space).

A single neuron’s parameter is θ=(w,b,a)∈ℝd+2\theta=(w,b,a)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+2}, where w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the input weight, b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} is the bias, and a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} is the output weight. The Euclidean norm on ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2} is denoted by |θ||\theta|.

Definition 2.2 (Two-layer network of width NN).

Given NN neurons with parameters θi=(wi,bi,ai)\theta_{i}=(w_{i},b_{i},a_{i}), 1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N, the network function is

fN​(x,θ)=1N​∑i=1Nai​σ​(⟨wi,x⟩+bi).f_{N}(x;\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}\sigma(\langle w_{i},x\rangle+b_{i}). (3)

The prefactor 1/N1/N places the network in the mean-field scaling.

Definition 2.3 (μ\muP scaling, mean-field equivalent form).

Under μ\muP, the initialization scales are wi​(0)∼𝒩⁡(0,d−1​Id)w_{i}(0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,d^{-1}I_{d}), bi​(0)∼𝒩⁡(0,1)b_{i}(0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), and ai​(0)∼𝒩⁡(0,1)a_{i}(0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). The per-parameter learning rates are ηw=1\eta_{w}=1, ηb=1\eta_{b}=1, and ηa=N−1\eta_{a}=N^{-1}. Under this parametrization, the empirical-measure SDE is the mean-field representative of the abc-parametrization of Yang and Hu (2021) with aL+1=1/2a_{L+1}=1/2, c=0c=0, and a1=1/2a_{1}=1/2 in the feature-learning vertex.

The empirical parameter measure is

μtN=1N​∑i=1Nδθi​(t)∈𝒫2​(ℝd+2).\mu_{t}^{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\theta_{i}(t)}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}). (4)

For a probability measure μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd+2)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}), the associated mean-field network function is

fμ​(x)=∫a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b)​𝑑μ​(w,b,a).f_{\mu}(x)=\int a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\,d\mu(w,b,a). (5)

The construction follows the mean-field distributional dynamics of Mei et al. (2018) and the optimal-transport formulation of Chizat and Bach (2018).

2.2 The mean-field Langevin SDE

Definition 2.4 (Population risk).

Given a target function f∗∈L2​(ρX)f^{\ast}\in L^{2}(\rho_{X}) and a loss ℓ:ℝ×ℝ→ℝ+\ell:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} convex in its first argument, the population risk is

ℛ⁡(μ)=∫ℓ⁡(fμ​(x),y)​𝑑ρ​(x,y),fμ​(x)=∫a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b)​𝑑μ​(w,b,a).\mathcal{R}(\mu)=\int\ell(f_{\mu}(x),y)\,d\rho(x,y),\qquad f_{\mu}(x)=\int a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\,d\mu(w,b,a). (6)

Throughout the paper, ℓ⁡(z,y)=12​(z−y)2\ell(z,y)=\tfrac{1}{2}(z-y)^{2} unless a section states a different convex loss.

Definition 2.5 (Entropy-regularized risk).

For regularization strength λ>0\lambda>0 and reference measure π\pi on ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2}, the entropy-regularized population risk is

ℱλ(μ)=ℛ(μ)+λKL(μ∥π),\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu)=\mathcal{R}(\mu)+\lambda\operatorname{KL}(\mu\|\pi), (7)

with ℱλ​(μ)=+∞\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu)=+\infty when μ\mu is not absolutely continuous with respect to π\pi.

Definition 2.6 (Mean-field Langevin SDE).

The parameter-system SDE under μ\muP with regularized objective is

dθi(t)=−∇θδ​ℛδ​μ(μtN)(θi(t))dt+λ∇logπ(θi(t))dt+2​λdBi(t),d\theta_{i}(t)=-\nabla_{\theta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{t}^{N})(\theta_{i}(t))\,dt+\lambda\nabla\log\pi(\theta_{i}(t))\,dt+\sqrt{2\lambda}\,dB_{i}(t), (8)

where BiB_{i} are independent standard Brownian motions in ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2} and μtN\mu_{t}^{N} is given by (4).

Theorem 2.7 (Mean-field Langevin Fokker–Planck PDE).

Assume the drift in (8) is locally Lipschitz with polynomial growth and that the initialization has finite second moment. The empirical measure μtN\mu_{t}^{N} converges weakly, as N→∞N\to\infty, to the unique weak solution μt∈C⁡([0,T],𝒫2)\mu_{t}\in C([0,T],\mathcal{P}_{2}) of

∂tμt=∇⋅(μt​∇θδ​ℱλδ​μ​(μt))+λ​Δ​μt.\partial_{t}\mu_{t}=\nabla\cdot\left(\mu_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{t})\right)+\lambda\Delta\mu_{t}. (9)
Proof.

The result is the McKean–Vlasov limit for the interacting particle system (8). Under the stated regularity, compactness in C⁡([0,T],𝒫2)C([0,T],\mathcal{P}_{2}) follows from the second-moment estimate and Aldous tightness. Identification of the limit follows by testing the martingale problem against Cc2​(ℝd+2)C_{c}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}) functions. The construction gives existence. Uniqueness in the admissible weighted class is established in Theorem 3.1; this preliminary statement is used only as the compactness and identification step. ∎

Theorem 2.8 (Wasserstein gradient-flow structure).

The solution μt\mu_{t} of Theorem 2.7 is the gradient flow of ℱλ\mathcal{F}_{\lambda} in the 22-Wasserstein metric on 𝒫2​(ℝd+2)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}).

Proof.

The JKO minimization scheme for ℱλ\mathcal{F}_{\lambda} is well posed because the entropy term is lower semicontinuous and coercive relative to a log-concave reference measure. Passing to the vanishing time-step limit yields an absolutely continuous curve in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} satisfying the energy-dissipation inequality. The Euler–Lagrange equation of the minimizing movement scheme is exactly (9). The construction is the variational Fokker–Planck argument of Jordan et al. (1998) in the form of Ambrosio et al. (2008). ∎

2.3 Weighted moment classes on the initialization

Definition 2.9 (Moment-sequence weight).

A moment-sequence weight is a positive sequence w:ℕ→(0,∞)w:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty) with w⁡(0)=1w(0)=1 and

w⁡(m+n)≥Cw−1​w​(m)​w​(n),m,n∈ℕ,w(m+n)\geq C_{w}^{-1}w(m)w(n),\qquad m,n\in\mathbb{N}, (10)

for some Cw≥1C_{w}\geq 1. No monotonicity is imposed. This convention keeps the reciprocal moment-growth boundary w∗(n)=(𝔼μ0|θ|2​n)−1/(2n)w^{\ast}(n)=(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0}}|\theta|^{2n})^{-1/(2n)} admissible for Gaussian initialization, where w∗(n)≍n−1/2w^{\ast}(n)\asymp n^{-1/2}.

Definition 2.10 (Weighted moment class).

For a moment-sequence weight ww, define

ℳw={μ∈𝒫⁡(ℝd+2):‖μ‖ℳw:=supn≥1w⁡(n)​(𝔼μ​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)<∞}.\mathcal{M}_{w}=\left\{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}):\|\mu\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}}:=\sup_{n\geq 1}w(n)\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu}|\theta|^{2n}\right)^{1/(2n)}<\infty\right\}. (11)

The notation 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} is reserved for finite-second-moment probability measures. The notation ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w} always denotes a weighted moment class.

For the initialization law μ0\mu_{0} define the moment-growth boundary and its reciprocal weight by

g0​(n)=(𝔼μ0​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n),w∗​(n)=g0​(n)−1,n≥1,g_{0}(n)=\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0}}|\theta|^{2n}\right)^{1/(2n)},\qquad w^{\ast}(n)=g_{0}(n)^{-1},\qquad n\geq 1, (12)

with the convention w∗​(n)=+∞w^{\ast}(n)=+\infty only on indices nn for which 𝔼μ0​|θ|2​n=0\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0}}|\theta|^{2n}=0, that is, on indices corresponding to degenerate (zero-mass) directions of the initialization. The object propagated by the flow is the class ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}; the sequence w∗w^{\ast} itself is a weight, not a class.

Proposition 2.11 (Preservation of weighted moments).

For any weight ww satisfying Definition 2.9 and any activation σ\sigma satisfying H1, the flow of Theorem 2.7 preserves ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w}: if μ0∈ℳw∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, then μt∈ℳw\mu_{t}\in\mathcal{M}_{w} for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], with supt≤T‖μt‖ℳw<∞\sup_{t\leq T}\|\mu_{t}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}}<\infty.

Proof.

Let m2​n​(t)=∫|θ|2​n​d​μt​(θ)m_{2n}(t)=\int|\theta|^{2n}\,d\mu_{t}(\theta). Testing (9) against a smooth truncation of |θ|2​n|\theta|^{2n} gives

dd​t​m2​n​(t)≤An​m2​n​(t)+Bn​∑j≤q​nm2​j​(t)+Cn.\frac{d}{dt}m_{2n}(t)\leq A_{n}m_{2n}(t)+B_{n}\sum_{j\leq qn}m_{2j}(t)+C_{n}. (13)

Taking 2​n2n-th roots and using (10) gives a Gronwall inequality for ‖μt‖ℳw\|\mu_{t}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}}. Monotone convergence removes the truncation. ∎

Proposition 2.12 (Moment bound for the parameter SDE).

For every T>0T>0, every p<∞p<\infty, and every weight ww for which μ0∈ℳw\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w},

𝔼​supt≤T|θi​(t)|2​p≤M⁡(T,p,λ,‖μ0‖ℳw)<∞\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}|\theta_{i}(t)|^{2p}\leq M(T,p,\lambda,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}})<\infty (14)

uniformly in ii and uniformly in width NN.

Proof.

Itô’s formula applied to (1+|θi|2)p(1+|\theta_{i}|^{2})^{p} yields a drift term controlled by H1 and H2. The interaction through μtN\mu_{t}^{N} is averaged by N−1N^{-1} and is bounded by the empirical moment of the same order. Exchangeability closes the estimate after summing over ii. The Brownian term is controlled by the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality, followed by Gronwall’s lemma. ∎

Definition 2.13 (Dual weighted moment class).

The continuous dual of ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w} is represented by signed measures ν\nu satisfying

‖ν‖ℳw∗:=supn≥1w⁡(n)​(𝔼ν​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)<∞.\|\nu\|^{\ast}_{\mathcal{M}_{w}}:=\sup_{n\geq 1}w(n)\left(\mathbb{E}_{\nu}|\theta|^{2n}\right)^{1/(2n)}<\infty. (15)

This class is denoted by ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w}^{\ast}.

2.4 The feature map and identifiability data

Definition 2.14 (Feature map).

The feature map associated with σ\sigma is

T:ℝd+2→L2​(ρX),T⁡(w,b,a)​(x)=a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b).T:\mathbb{R}^{d+2}\to L^{2}(\rho_{X}),\qquad T(w,b,a)(x)=a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b). (16)
Definition 2.15 (Network function as barycentre).

For μ∈𝒫⁡(ℝd+2)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}),

fμ=∫T⁡(θ)​𝑑μ​(θ)∈L2​(ρX),f_{\mu}=\int T(\theta)\,d\mu(\theta)\in L^{2}(\rho_{X}), (17)

where the integral is a Bochner integral in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}).

Definition 2.16 (Effective input dimension).

The effective input dimension deff=deff​(f∗,ρX)d_{\mathrm{eff}}=d_{\mathrm{eff}}(f^{\ast},\rho_{X}) is the smallest rank of a linear projection Π:ℝd→ℝk\Pi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{k} for which f∗​(x)=g​(Π​x)f^{\ast}(x)=g(\Pi x) ρX\rho_{X}-a.e. for some measurable gg. If no smaller projection exists, deff=dd_{\mathrm{eff}}=d.

Definition 2.17 (Cylindrical Fourier transform).

Let H=L2​(ρX)H=L^{2}(\rho_{X}) and let ν\nu be a Borel probability measure on HH with finite first moment. Its cylindrical Fourier transform is

ν^​(h)=∫Hei​⟨h,u⟩H​𝑑ν​(u),h∈H.\widehat{\nu}(h)=\int_{H}e^{i\langle h,u\rangle_{H}}\,d\nu(u),\qquad h\in H. (18)

On a separable Hilbert space, equality of these transforms on HH determines the Borel probability measure.

Definition 2.18 (Architectural symmetry group).

GσG_{\sigma} is the group of measurable bijections φ:ℝd+2→ℝd+2\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{d+2}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+2} such that T∘φ=TT\circ\varphi=T μ\mu-a.s. for every μ\mu in the admissible parameter class. The finite-rank realization subgroup GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} is the subgroup generated by the within-neuron sign and scale invariants that preserve a single feature, together with the collapse of the dead-neuron set {a=0}\{a=0\}. For ReLU, GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} contains the positive rescaling (w,b,a)↦(α​w,α​b,a/α)(w,b,a)\mapsto(\alpha w,\alpha b,a/\alpha) for α>0\alpha>0 and the dead-neuron collapse.

2.5 Hypothesis labels

The four theorems rely on three standing hypotheses on (σ,ρ,μ0)(\sigma,\rho,\mu_{0}) and one realizability hypothesis used only for sparse decompositions.

H1. Activation regularity.

σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is Lipschitz with constant LσL_{\sigma}, and has polynomial growth: |σ⁡(z)|≤Cσ​(1+|z|q)|\sigma(z)|\leq C_{\sigma}(1+|z|^{q}) for some q≥1q\geq 1.

H2. Data tails.

The input marginal ρX\rho_{X} is sub-Gaussian: 𝔼ρX​ec​|x|2<∞\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{X}}e^{c|x|^{2}}<\infty for some c>0c>0. The label marginal ρY\rho_{Y} has finite moments of every order.

H3. Real-analytic separation.

σ\sigma is real-analytic and non-polynomial. Under this hypothesis, the family {σ⁡(⟨w,⋅⟩+b):(w,b)∈ℝd+1}\{\sigma(\langle w,\cdot\rangle+b):(w,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\} is total in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) in the sense of Pinkus (Pinkus, 1999).

H4. Barron–Hermite target condition.

The target function f∗∈L2​(ρX)f^{\ast}\in L^{2}(\rho_{X}) has finite Barron norm with respect to the feature family generated by σ\sigma. In the Gaussian-input cases this is implemented through a finite Hermite truncation at the regularization scale: for each λ>0\lambda>0 there is an integer S~λ\widetilde{S}_{\lambda} and a truncated target

fλ∗​(x)=∑k=1S~λak∗​σ​(⟨wk∗,x⟩+bk∗)f_{\lambda}^{\ast}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\widetilde{S}_{\lambda}}a_{k}^{\ast}\sigma(\langle w_{k}^{\ast},x\rangle+b_{k}^{\ast}) (19)

such that ‖f∗−fλ∗‖L2​(ρX)2≤κ⁡(f∗,S~λ,λ)\|f^{\ast}-f_{\lambda}^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}\leq\kappa(f^{\ast},\widetilde{S}_{\lambda},\lambda). The truncation has S~λ≤Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)\widetilde{S}_{\lambda}\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda) atoms by Proposition 5.7. Under the Hermite/Barron dictionary of Definition 5.1, the teacher-atom rank S~λ\widetilde{S}_{\lambda} and the Hermite depth SS are related by S~λ≤S​mult⁡(σ)\widetilde{S}_{\lambda}\leq S\,\operatorname{mult}(\sigma). The finite-atom case is the special case in which fλ∗=f∗f_{\lambda}^{\ast}=f^{\ast} for all sufficiently small λ\lambda.

2.6 Conventions

Constants C,Cp,Cw,Cp,wC,C_{p},C_{w},C_{p,w} depend only on the indicated parameters and may change from line to line. The relation A≲BA\lesssim B means A≤C​BA\leq CB, and A≍BA\asymp B means A≲BA\lesssim B and B≲AB\lesssim A. All measures on ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2} are Borel probability measures unless stated otherwise. The symbol 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} denotes 𝒫2​(ℝd+2)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}) throughout. The inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle without subscript denotes the Euclidean inner product on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The symbol W2W_{2} denotes the quadratic Wasserstein distance. All subsequent results are formulated in this notation.

3 Theorem A: global existence of the mean-field limit

H1 and H2 are in force throughout this section. The auxiliary regularization assumption is that λ>0\lambda>0 is fixed and that the nonlinear semigroup generated by (9) satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (LSI) with constant αλ>0\alpha_{\lambda}>0 on the relevant sublevel set. For convex entropy-regularized objectives and a log-concave reference law, the uniform-in-NN LSI mechanism of Chewi et al. (2024) applies; outside that setting the LSI is stated as a hypothesis of the propagation estimate, not as a property automatically implied by H1–H2.

Theorem 3.1 (Global existence and uniqueness of the mean-field limit under μ\muP).

Let σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} satisfy H1. Let ρ\rho satisfy H2. Let the width-NN two-layer network be parametrized in μ\muP and initialized with iid law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2} of full support. Then μtN=N−1​∑i=1Nδθi​(t)\mu_{t}^{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\theta_{i}(t)} converges weakly, uniformly in t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], to the unique solution μt∈C⁡([0,T],𝒫2)\mu_{t}\in C([0,T],\mathcal{P}_{2}) of

∂tμt=∇⋅(μt​∇θδ​ℱλδ​μ​(μt))+λ​Δ​μt.\partial_{t}\mu_{t}=\nabla\cdot\left(\mu_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{t})\right)+\lambda\Delta\mu_{t}. (20)

The solution has finite Fisher information for every t>0t>0 and is the Wasserstein gradient flow of ℱλ\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}. The finite-particle approximation satisfies

𝔼⁡[ℱλ​(μtN)−ℱλ​(μt)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}^{N})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})] ≤C1​(T,λ,σ,ρ,αλ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)​N−1,\displaystyle\leq C_{1}(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\alpha_{\lambda},\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}})\,N^{-1}, (21)
supt∈[0,T]𝔼​W22​(μtN,μt)\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t}) ≤C2​(T,λ,σ,ρ,αλ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)​N−1.\displaystyle\leq C_{2}(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\alpha_{\lambda},\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}})\,N^{-1}. (22)

The constants C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are polynomial in ‖μ0‖ℳw∗\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}} and grow at most exponentially in TT through the Gronwall step of Lemma 3.2. The weight w∗w^{\ast} in (12) generates the largest weighted moment class ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} propagated by the flow in the sense of Proposition 3.8.

3.1 Moment and drift bounds

Lemma 3.2 (Uniform LpL^{p} bound on parameters).

For every p<∞p<\infty and every T<∞T<\infty,

supN≥1supi≤N𝔼​supt≤T|θi​(t)|2​p≤Cp,T,λ​(1+‖μ0‖ℳw∗2​p).\sup_{N\geq 1}\sup_{i\leq N}\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\leq T}|\theta_{i}(t)|^{2p}\leq C_{p,T,\lambda}(1+\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}^{2p}). (23)
Proof.

Apply Itô’s formula to (1+|θi|2)p(1+|\theta_{i}|^{2})^{p}. Differentiating the first variation

δ​ℛδ​μ​(μ)​(θ)=∫(fμ​(x)−y)​a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b)​𝑑ρ​(x,y)\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(\mu)(\theta)=\int(f_{\mu}(x)-y)a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\,d\rho(x,y) (24)

produces terms bounded by a polynomial in |θi||\theta_{i}| and by the empirical average of the same polynomial over the particles. H1 controls the activation, H2 controls the data moments, and exchangeability closes the estimate. The Brownian term is handled by Burkholder--Davis--Gundy. Gronwall’s lemma11 1 Some authors write Grönwall; we follow the prevalent English convention of dropping the umlaut. gives (23). ∎

Lemma 3.3 (Drift stability).

On every weighted moment ball Bw​(R)={μ∈ℳw:‖μ‖ℳw≤R}B_{w}(R)=\{\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{w}:\|\mu\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}}\leq R\},

|b⁡(θ,μ)−b⁡(θ′,ν)|≤LR​(1+|θ|q+|θ′|q)​(|θ−θ′|+W2​(μ,ν)),|b(\theta,\mu)-b(\theta^{\prime},\nu)|\leq L_{R}(1+|\theta|^{q}+|\theta^{\prime}|^{q})(|\theta-\theta^{\prime}|+W_{2}(\mu,\nu)), (25)

where b(θ,μ)=−∇θδℛ/δμ(μ)(θ)+λ∇logπ(θ)b(\theta,\mu)=-\nabla_{\theta}\delta\mathcal{R}/\delta\mu(\mu)(\theta)+\lambda\nabla\log\pi(\theta).

Proof.

Subtract the two drifts and add and subtract b⁡(θ′,μ)b(\theta^{\prime},\mu). The spatial difference is controlled by the Lipschitz envelope of σ\sigma. The measure difference is controlled by

‖fμ−fν‖L2​(ρX)≤CR​W2​(μ,ν),\|f_{\mu}-f_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}\leq C_{R}W_{2}(\mu,\nu), (26)

which follows by coupling μ\mu and ν\nu and using H1–H2. The reference drift is controlled by the same finite moment radius. ∎

3.2 The JKO construction

Proposition 3.4 (Well-posed minimizing movement).

The JKO step

μk+1τ∈arg⁡minν∈𝒫2​{ℱλ​(ν)+12​τ​W22​(ν,μkτ)}\mu_{k+1}^{\tau}\in\arg\min_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}}\left\{\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\nu)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_{2}^{2}(\nu,\mu_{k}^{\tau})\right\} (27)

has a unique minimizer in the admissible weighted class, and the interpolation converges to a weak solution of (20).

Proof.

Coercivity comes from the transport term and reference entropy. Lower semicontinuity of the risk follows from (26). The direct method gives a minimizer. Convexity of μ↦fμ\mu\mapsto f_{\mu} and of the squared loss, together with strict convexity of entropy on densities, gives uniqueness. The energy-dissipation estimate

ℱλ​(μmτ)+12​∑k<mτ−1​W22​(μk+1τ,μkτ)≤ℱλ​(μ0)\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{m}^{\tau})+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k<m}\tau^{-1}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{k+1}^{\tau},\mu_{k}^{\tau})\leq\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{0}) (28)

provides compactness. Passing to the limit in the Euler–Lagrange equation yields (20). ∎

3.3 Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos

Lemma 3.5 (Synchronous coupling estimate).

Let (θ¯i​(t))i≤N(\bar{\theta}_{i}(t))_{i\leq N} be nonlinear McKean–Vlasov copies with common law μt\mu_{t}, driven by the same Brownian motions and the same initial variables as (θi​(t))i≤N(\theta_{i}(t))_{i\leq N}. Then

supt≤T𝔼​1N​∑i=1N|θi​(t)−θ¯i​(t)|2≤CT​N−1.\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\theta_{i}(t)-\bar{\theta}_{i}(t)|^{2}\leq C_{T}N^{-1}. (29)
Proof.

Set Δi=θi−θ¯i\Delta_{i}=\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta}_{i}. Itô’s formula gives

dd​t​𝔼​1N​∑i|Δi|2=2N​∑i𝔼⁡⟨Δi,b⁡(θi,μtN)−b⁡(θ¯i,μt)⟩.\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}|\Delta_{i}|^{2}=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{i},b(\theta_{i},\mu_{t}^{N})-b(\bar{\theta}_{i},\mu_{t})\rangle. (30)

Insert b⁡(θ¯i,μ¯tN)b(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N}), where μ¯tN=N−1​∑jδθ¯j\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{j}\delta_{\bar{\theta}_{j}}. Lemma 3.3 controls the spatial and coupled-measure parts by C​𝔼​N−1​∑i|Δi|2C\mathbb{E}N^{-1}\sum_{i}|\Delta_{i}|^{2}. The remaining field fluctuation

ξi=b⁡(θ¯i,μ¯tN)−b⁡(θ¯i,μt)\xi_{i}=b(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N})-b(\bar{\theta}_{i},\mu_{t}) (31)

has variance O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}): after conditioning on θ¯i\bar{\theta}_{i}, the off-diagonal summands are centered and exchangeable, and the diagonal summand has weight N−1N^{-1}. Thus

𝔼​|ξi|2≤C​N−1.\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}|^{2}\leq CN^{-1}. (32)

Young’s inequality gives a source C/NC/N. Since Δi​(0)=0\Delta_{i}(0)=0, Gronwall’s lemma proves (29). The proof does not use an independent empirical-measure quantization estimate. ∎

Remark 3.6 (Two equivalent expressions for ξi\xi_{i}).

Two displays of the field fluctuation appear in this paper: (31) in drift-difference form and (85) in kernel form. For squared loss, the drift admits a kernel representation

b⁡(θ,μ)=b0​(θ)+∫K⁡(θ,ϑ)​𝑑μ​(ϑ),b(\theta,\mu)=b_{0}(\theta)+\int K(\theta,\vartheta)\,d\mu(\vartheta), (33)

where K⁡(θ,ϑ)K(\theta,\vartheta) is obtained by differentiating the bilinear term ⟨T⁡(θ),T⁡(ϑ)⟩L2​(ρX)\langle T(\theta),T(\vartheta)\rangle_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}. Substituting (33) into the empirical-minus-population drift gives exactly the kernel fluctuation of Appendix C.

Proposition 3.7 (Squared-Wasserstein propagation).

Under the LSI contraction assumption,

supt∈[0,T]𝔼​W22​(μtN,μt)≤C​N−1.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t})\leq CN^{-1}. (34)
Proof.

The LSI supplies the contracted inequality

dd​t​ℰN​(t)≤−αλ​ℰN​(t)+C​N−1,ℰN​(t)=𝔼​1N​∑i|θi​(t)−θ¯i​(t)|2.\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)\leq-\alpha_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)+CN^{-1},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}|\theta_{i}(t)-\bar{\theta}_{i}(t)|^{2}. (35)

Solving it and using ℰN​(0)=0\mathcal{E}_{N}(0)=0 gives ℰN​(t)≤C​(αλ​N)−1\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)\leq C(\alpha_{\lambda}N)^{-1}. The canonical coupling gives (34). ∎

3.4 The maximal admissible weight

Proposition 3.8 (Maximality of w∗w^{\ast}).

Let μ0\mu_{0} have moment-growth boundary g0​(n)=(𝔼μ0​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)g_{0}(n)=(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0}}|\theta|^{2n})^{1/(2n)} with reciprocal weight w∗=g0−1w^{\ast}=g_{0}^{-1}. Suppose w~:ℕ→(0,∞)\widetilde{w}:\mathbb{N}\to(0,\infty) satisfies lim supn→∞w~​(n)/w∗​(n)=+∞\limsup_{n\to\infty}\widetilde{w}(n)/w^{\ast}(n)=+\infty. Then μ0∉ℳw~\mu_{0}\notin\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}}, and consequently the conclusion of Theorem 3.1 cannot hold inside ℳw~\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}} from this initialization.

Proof.

By definition of w∗w^{\ast}, w∗​(n)​g0​(n)=1w^{\ast}(n)g_{0}(n)=1 for every nn. Hence w~​(n)​g0​(n)=w~​(n)/w∗​(n)\widetilde{w}(n)g_{0}(n)=\widetilde{w}(n)/w^{\ast}(n), whose lim sup\limsup is +∞+\infty by assumption. Therefore

supnw~​(n)​(𝔼μ0​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)=+∞,\sup_{n}\widetilde{w}(n)(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0}}|\theta|^{2n})^{1/(2n)}=+\infty, (36)

which means ‖μ0‖ℳw~=+∞\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}}}=+\infty and μ0∉ℳw~\mu_{0}\notin\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}}. Class membership at t=0t=0 is a necessary condition for the propagation in Proposition 2.11, hence Theorem 3.1 cannot be invoked inside ℳw~\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}}. ∎

3.5 Sharpness

Proposition 3.9 (Sharpness of w∗w^{\ast}).

There are activations satisfying H1–H2 for which any attempted strengthening of the reciprocal moment boundary fails to be propagated.

Proof.

Use a smooth polynomial-growth cubic activation with standard truncation and then pass the truncation radius to infinity inside the moment estimates. The moment hierarchy contains a lower-bound term

dd​t​m2​n​(t)≥cn​m6​n−2​(t)−Cn​(1+m2​n​(t)).\frac{d}{dt}m_{2n}(t)\geq c_{n}m_{6n-2}(t)-C_{n}(1+m_{2n}(t)). (37)

For Gaussian initialization, the factorial growth of m6​n−2​(0)m_{6n-2}(0) (precisely, m6​n−2​(0)≥((3​n−1)/e)3​n−1m_{6n-2}(0)\geq((3n-1)/e)^{3n-1} by Stirling for Gaussian initialization) exceeds any strict strengthening of the reciprocal root-moment boundary along a subsequence. The failure is therefore a moment-class failure, not a failure of activation regularity. ∎

The estimates above hide constants only in places where no rate changes. For later optimization it is useful to record one calibrated envelope.

Remark 3.11 (Sharpness of the horizon dependence).

The exponential dependence on TT is not a typographical artifact. The cubic-growth sharpness construction in Proposition 3.9, made quantitative in Appendix I.2, gives a moment hierarchy whose leading Gronwall exponent is attained along a subsequence of orders. The estimate is therefore calibrated as an upper envelope rather than as a small-time perturbative bound.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Proposition 3.4 constructs the limiting curve. Uniqueness follows from convexity of the squared risk in the barycentric variable and strict convexity of entropy. Finite Fisher information follows from the entropy-dissipation identity. Proposition 3.7 gives the squared-Wasserstein rate, and Nitanda (2024) gives the scalar objective-gap rate in the same MFLD setting. Proposition 3.8 gives the moment boundary. ∎

4 Theorem B: identifiability characterization

Theorem B uses H3 in addition to the hypotheses of Theorem A. The quotient is not the unrestricted set of all parameter permutations. It is the finite-rank realization quotient generated by transformations that preserve the single-neuron feature in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}), with the dead-neuron ridge collapsed separately.

Definition 4.1 (Finite-rank identifiable class).

For M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N} and a weighted moment class ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w}, let ℐM,w​(σ,ρ)\mathcal{I}_{M,w}(\sigma,\rho) be the set of parameter measures in ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w} for which the moment map

𝔪M​(μ)=(∫⟨T⁡(θ),hj⟩L2​(ρX)r​𝑑μ​(θ))1≤j≤J⁡(M), 1≤r≤M\mathfrak{m}_{M}(\mu)=\left(\int\langle T(\theta),h_{j}\rangle_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{r}\,d\mu(\theta)\right)_{1\leq j\leq J(M),\,1\leq r\leq M} (40)

separates the finite-rank quotient classes modulo GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} for a fixed separating family (hj)(h_{j}) in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}).

Definition 4.2 (Finite-rank symmetry equivalence).

Two measures μ,ν∈ℐM,w​(σ,ρ)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{I}_{M,w}(\sigma,\rho) are finite-rank symmetry-equivalent, written μ∼Gσfinν\mu\sim_{G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}}\nu, if their pushforwards under qfin:ℝd+2→ℝd+2/Gσfinq_{\mathrm{fin}}:\mathbb{R}^{d+2}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+2}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} coincide after the dead-neuron ridge has been collapsed.

Definition 4.3 (Orbit and moment-variety depths).

The orbit identifiability depth is

Dorb∗​(σ,ρ)=dim(Gσfin⋅θ)D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}(\sigma,\rho)=\dim(G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}\cdot\theta) (41)

for a generic active parameter. The moment-variety depth is

Dvar∗​(σ,ρ)=codimℐM,w⁡{ν:𝔪M​(ν)=𝔪M​(μ)}D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}(\sigma,\rho)=\operatorname{codim}_{\mathcal{I}_{M,w}}\{\nu:\mathfrak{m}_{M}(\nu)=\mathfrak{m}_{M}(\mu)\} (42)

on a regular stratum of the finite-rank moment map.

Definition 4.4 (Separating moment-map degree).

M0=M0​(σ,ρ)M_{0}=M_{0}(\sigma,\rho) is the smallest integer MM for which the moment map (40) separates the regular stratum of ℝd+2/Gσfin\mathbb{R}^{d+2}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}. For real-analytic non-polynomial σ\sigma, M0M_{0} is finite by H3 and Pinkus’ theorem. For polynomial σ\sigma of degree kk, M0=k+1M_{0}=k+1.

Theorem 4.5 (Identifiability of the mean-field limit).

Fix any M≥M0​(σ,ρ)M\geq M_{0}(\sigma,\rho), where M0M_{0} is the separating moment-map degree of Definition 4.4. Let μ,ν∈ℐM,w​(σ,ρ)⊂𝒫2​(ℝd+2)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{I}_{M,w}(\sigma,\rho)\subset\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}). Assume H3. The following three conditions are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    fμ=fνf_{\mu}=f_{\nu} as elements of L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}).

  2. (ii)

    μ∼Gσfinν\mu\sim_{G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}}\nu.

  3. (iii)

    The cylindrical Fourier transforms of T#​μT_{\#}\mu and T#​νT_{\#}\nu coincide on L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}).

The quotient class [μ]Gσfin[\mu]_{G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}} is the minimal sufficient statistic for fμf_{\mu} inside ℐM,w​(σ,ρ)\mathcal{I}_{M,w}(\sigma,\rho). The active parameter dimension used in covering estimates is deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} per atom. The invariant Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}} is used only for moment-variety identifiability.

4.1 The finite-rank symmetry group

Theorem 4.6 (Structure of GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} for canonical activations).

The finite-rank symmetry group has the following forms.

  1. (a)

    For σ=ReLU\sigma=\operatorname{ReLU}, GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} is generated by positive scalings (w,b,a)↦(α​w,α​b,a/α)(w,b,a)\mapsto(\alpha w,\alpha b,a/\alpha), α>0\alpha>0, and dead-neuron collapse.

  2. (b)

    For σ=tanh\sigma=\tanh, GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} is generated by the sign flip (w,b,a)↦(−w,−b,−a)(w,b,a)\mapsto(-w,-b,-a) and dead-neuron collapse.

  3. (c)

    For σ⁡(z)=zk\sigma(z)=z^{k}, GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} contains the homogeneity scaling (w,b,a)↦(α​w,α​b,α−k​a)(w,b,a)\mapsto(\alpha w,\alpha b,\alpha^{-k}a) and the stabilizer of the degree-kk tensor component determined by ρX\rho_{X}.

  4. (d)

    For real-analytic non-polynomial σ\sigma satisfying H3, the generic active symmetry is trivial after dead-neuron collapse.

Proof.

Substitution verifies the ReLU, tanh\tanh, and polynomial cases. In the analytic case, equality a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b)=a′​σ​(⟨w′,x⟩+b′)a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b)=a^{\prime}\sigma(\langle w^{\prime},x\rangle+b^{\prime}) on a full-support input law extends to equality of real-analytic functions. Non-polynomiality excludes nontrivial affine reparametrizations on the active stratum. ∎

Proposition 4.7 (Relation between depths).

On each regular stratum, Dorb∗≤Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}\leq D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}, with equality exactly when the moment map is transverse to the finite-rank symmetry orbits.

Proof.

Each finite-rank orbit lies in a level set of the moment map because TT is preserved along the orbit. Thus the orbit tangent space is contained in the kernel of the differential of 𝔪M\mathfrak{m}_{M}. Comparing dimensions gives the inequality, and equality is the stated transversality condition. ∎

Lemma 4.8 (Sharpness of Dorb∗≤Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}\leq D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}).

The inequality in Proposition 4.7 can be strict. For σ⁡(z)=z4\sigma(z)=z^{4} under ρX=𝒩⁡(0,Id)\rho_{X}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), consider a rank-one fourth-order coefficient tensor u⊗4u^{\otimes 4} on the active stratum. The homogeneity orbit has one continuous parameter,

(w,b,a)↦(α​w,α​b,α−4​a),α>0,(w,b,a)\mapsto(\alpha w,\alpha b,\alpha^{-4}a),\qquad\alpha>0, (43)

so Dorb∗=1D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=1. The moment variety also contains the sign-stabilized flattening constraint and the rank-one tensor constraint; on the regular rank-one stratum these impose two independent codimension directions. Hence Dvar∗=2D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}=2 for this stratum and Dorb∗<Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}<D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}.

Proof.

The fourth-order feature depends on the symmetric tensor a​(w,b)⊗4a(w,b)^{\otimes 4}. Positive homogeneity changes the representative but not the tensor. The tangent to this scaling is one-dimensional. The symmetric tensor stratum is cut out by the vanishing of the 2×22\times 2 minors of its flattenings; at a generic rank-one point two independent minor directions remain after quotienting the scaling direction. This gives the claimed strict inequality. ∎

4.2 Quotient separation

Lemma 4.9 (Analytic separation on compact quotient strata).

Let KRK_{R} be the quotient image of the active set {|θ|≤R,|a|≥R−1}\{|\theta|\leq R,|a|\geq R^{-1}\}. Under H3, the algebra generated by [θ]↦⟨T⁡(θ),h⟩L2​(ρX)[\theta]\mapsto\langle T(\theta),h\rangle_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})} separates points of KRK_{R}.

Proof.

Two distinct quotient points have distinct features by definition of GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}. Taking hh to be the feature difference separates them. The functions are continuous on the compact stratum and the algebra contains constants. ∎

Lemma 4.10 (Compact-exhaustion monotone-class step).

If a finite signed measure η\eta in the dual weighted class satisfies ∫T⁡(θ)​𝑑η​(θ)=0\int T(\theta)d\eta(\theta)=0, then (qfin)#​η=0(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}\eta=0.

Proof.

On each KRK_{R}, Lemma 4.9 and Stone–Weierstrass give density in C⁡(KR)C(K_{R}). The weighted moment bound gives

|(qfin)#​η|​(KRc)≤C​supn≥1R−2​n​w​(n)−2​‖η‖ℳw∗,|(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}\eta|(K_{R}^{c})\leq C\sup_{n\geq 1}R^{-2n}w(n)^{-2}\|\eta\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}^{\ast}}, (44)

which tends to zero along the exhaustion. The equality extends to all bounded Borel functions by the monotone-class theorem. ∎

4.3 Proof of Theorem 4.5

Assume (i), set η=μ−ν\eta=\mu-\nu, and remove the dead-neuron mass. Lemma 4.10 gives equality of active quotient laws, hence (ii). The implication (ii)⇒\Rightarrow(iii) follows because TT is constant on finite-rank orbits, so the feature pushforwards agree. The implication (iii)⇒\Rightarrow(i) follows from uniqueness of cylindrical Fourier transforms on the separable Hilbert space L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) and equality of Bochner barycentres.

4.4 Special cases

For ReLU, Dorb∗=1D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=1 in every input dimension. For analytic non-polynomial activations with no homogeneity, Dorb∗=0D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=0 after dead-neuron collapse. For polynomial activation zkz^{k}, Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}} may exceed Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} on singular tensor strata. The statistical factor in Theorem 6.1 uses deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}, not deff−Dvar∗+2d_{\mathrm{eff}}-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}+2.

5 Theorem C: sparse-dictionary decomposition

Definition 5.1 (Barron–Hermite truncation).

Under H4, write f∗=∑m≥0f^m∗​ψmf^{\ast}=\sum_{m\geq 0}\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}\psi_{m} in the Hermite/Barron dictionary adapted to (σ,ρX)(\sigma,\rho_{X}). For λ>0\lambda>0 set

fλ∗=∑|f^m∗|>cσ​λf^m∗​ψm.f_{\lambda}^{\ast}=\sum_{|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|>c_{\sigma}\lambda}\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}\psi_{m}. (45)

The target-dependent sparse tail is

κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=∑m>S|f^m∗|2+Cσ​λ​S,\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=\sum_{m>S}|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|^{2}+C_{\sigma}\lambda S, (46)

with coefficients arranged by decreasing magnitude.

Definition 5.2 (Threshold upper bound).

Let mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma) be a finite upper bound on the number of ridge atoms needed to realize one retained dictionary mode. Define

Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)=#⁡{m:|f^m∗|>cσ​λ}​mult⁡(σ).S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda)=\#\{m:|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|>c_{\sigma}\lambda\}\,\operatorname{mult}(\sigma). (47)
Definition 5.3 (Sparse-dictionary depth).

After finite support has been established, S∗​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)S^{\ast}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda) is the minimal active cardinality of a measure realizing fλ∗f_{\lambda}^{\ast} modulo GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} and with tail bounded by (46). Thus S∗S^{\ast} is an a posteriori minimum, not an assumption used to prove finite support.

Remark 5.4 (Smooth versus atomic components).

For every λ>0\lambda>0 the entropy term forces μ∞≪π\mu_{\infty}\ll\pi on ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2}, so μ∞\mu_{\infty} admits a density p∞=d​μ∞/d​πp_{\infty}=d\mu_{\infty}/d\pi globally and is not atomic on the parameter space. The atomic statement of Theorem 5.5 concerns the quotient-active projection

(qfin)#(μ∞↾{a≠0})∈𝒫(ℝd+2/Gσfin),(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}(\mu_{\infty}\restriction_{\{a\neq 0\}})\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}), (48)

which is supported on at most SupS_{\mathrm{up}} points modulo GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} in the sense that the network function fμ∞f_{\mu_{\infty}} is realized by an S∗S^{\ast}-atom representative under the quotient projection. The full law is a smooth ridge around each active orbit, with local width controlled by the temperature scale λ\sqrt{\lambda}.

Theorem 5.5 (Sparse-dictionary decomposition).

Assume H1–H4 and the hypotheses of Theorems 3.1 and 4.5. Assume the initialization has full support and positive density on every nonempty open ball. Every long-time limit point μ∞\mu_{\infty} of the entropy-regularized mean-field flow has active component supported on at most Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda) atoms modulo GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}. Consequently S∗≤SupS^{\ast}\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}, and

(qfin)#(μ∞↾{a≠0})=∑k=1S∗ck∞δ[θk∞]in 𝒫(ℝd+2/Gσfin),(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}(\mu_{\infty}\restriction_{\{a\neq 0\}})=\sum_{k=1}^{S^{\ast}}c_{k}^{\infty}\,\delta_{[\theta_{k}^{\infty}]}\quad\text{in }\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}), (49)

with prediction residual bounded by κ⁡(f∗,S∗,λ)\kappa(f^{\ast},S^{\ast},\lambda).

5.1 Stationary equation

Lemma 5.6 (Euler–Lagrange equation).

If p∞=d​μ∞/d​πp_{\infty}=d\mu_{\infty}/d\pi is a stationary density on the active stratum, then

∇θ(δ​ℛδ​μ​(μ∞)​(θ)+λ​log⁡p∞​(θ))=0\nabla_{\theta}\left(\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{\infty})(\theta)+\lambda\log p_{\infty}(\theta)\right)=0 (50)

there in weak form.

Proof.

Stationarity in (9) means the probability current has zero divergence. Testing against compactly supported vector fields and integrating by parts gives vanishing of the bracketed gradient on each connected active component of the support. ∎

Proposition 5.7 (Threshold realization).

The thresholded target fλ∗f_{\lambda}^{\ast} has a realization by at most Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda) active atoms modulo GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}.

Proof.

Each retained coefficient requires at most mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma) ridge atoms by H4. Summing over retained coefficients gives (47). Quotienting by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} can only reduce active cardinality. ∎

Proposition 5.8 (Support of stationary minimizers).

Every stationary minimizer of ℱλ\mathcal{F}_{\lambda} in the finite-rank class has quotient-active support contained in a threshold realization of fλ∗f_{\lambda}^{\ast} plus the zero-feature ridge.

Proof.

The proof has three steps. First, the Langevin generator is strictly elliptic on every weighted moment ball on which the reference density is positive; see Appendix I.3. Therefore every stationary law has a smooth density before the active quotient is taken. Second, the positive density of μ0\mu_{0} and Girsanov’s theorem on finite horizons imply reachability: for each retained teacher location θk∗\theta_{k}^{\ast} and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, the process hits B⁡(θk∗,ε)B(\theta_{k}^{\ast},\varepsilon) with positive probability before some deterministic time depending on the ball. Third, the energy-dissipation inequality drives the flow to a stationary minimizer. If a retained direction were missing from the quotient-active support, the first variation δ​ℛ/δ​μ\delta\mathcal{R}/\delta\mu would have a non-zero descent component at that direction, contradicting stationarity. Directions below the threshold are absorbed into the entropy displacement and into the tail (46). ∎

Corollary 5.9 (Exponential Hermite tails).

If the retained Hermite/Barron coefficients satisfy |f^m∗|≤C​e−c​m|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|\leq Ce^{-cm}, then

S∗​(λ)≤1c​log⁡Ccσ​λ​mult⁡(σ).S^{\ast}(\lambda)\leq\frac{1}{c}\log\frac{C}{c_{\sigma}\lambda}\,\operatorname{mult}(\sigma). (51)
Proof.

The threshold rule retains only those mm for which C​e−c​m>cσ​λCe^{-cm}>c_{\sigma}\lambda. Solving this inequality gives m<c−1​log⁡(C/(cσ​λ))m<c^{-1}\log(C/(c_{\sigma}\lambda)), and each retained mode requires at most mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma) atoms. ∎

5.2 Proof of Theorem 5.5

Proposition 5.7 gives the explicit upper bound. Proposition 5.8 identifies the active support of any stationary limit with a subset of the threshold realization. Definition 5.3 then defines the minimal depth, giving S∗≤SupS^{\ast}\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}. Parseval in the Hermite/Barron basis and the entropy displacement estimate yield the residual bound κ⁡(f∗,S∗,λ)\kappa(f^{\ast},S^{\ast},\lambda).

5.3 Special cases

For finite teacher networks, the coefficient set is finite and S∗S^{\ast} is bounded by the teacher width times mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma). For analytic single-index targets with exponentially decaying Hermite coefficients, S∗​(λ)=O⁡(log⁡(1/λ))S^{\ast}(\lambda)=O(\log(1/\lambda)). For Barron targets with polynomial coefficient decay, S∗S^{\ast} grows polynomially in λ−1\lambda^{-1}. For polynomial activation of degree kk and target with Hermite degree greater than kk, the residual term is nonzero for every finite SS because the target has a component orthogonal to the model span.

6 Theorem D: total feature-learning-error decomposition

Theorem 6.1 (Total feature-learning-error decomposition).

Under the hypotheses of Theorems 3.1, 4.5, and 5.5, the trained finite-particle predictor satisfies the canonical decomposition

𝔼​‖fμTN−f∗‖L2​(ρX)2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|f_{\mu_{T}^{N}}-f^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2} =Estat​(n)+Eopt​(T,λ)+Epoc​(N,T)+Esparse​(S∗,λ)+RT,\displaystyle=E_{\mathrm{stat}}(n)+E_{\mathrm{opt}}(T,\lambda)+E_{\mathrm{poc}}(N,T)+E_{\mathrm{sparse}}(S^{\ast},\lambda)+R_{T}, (52)

where

Estat​(n)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{stat}}(n) ≤C1​S∗​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2n,\displaystyle\leq C_{1}\frac{S^{\ast}(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}}{n}, (53a)
Eopt​(T,λ)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{opt}}(T,\lambda) ≤C2​e−αλ​T,\displaystyle\leq C_{2}e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}, (53b)
Epoc​(N,T)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{poc}}(N,T) ≤C3​N−1,\displaystyle\leq C_{3}N^{-1}, (53c)
Esparse​(S∗,λ)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sparse}}(S^{\ast},\lambda) ≤C4​κ​(f∗,S∗,λ).\displaystyle\leq C_{4}\,\kappa(f^{\ast},S^{\ast},\lambda). (53d)

The scalar remainder satisfies

RT=o⁡(N−1+S∗​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2n+e−αλ​T+κ⁡(f∗,S∗,λ))R_{T}=o\left(N^{-1}+\frac{S^{\ast}(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}}{n}+e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}+\kappa(f^{\ast},S^{\ast},\lambda)\right) (54)

along compatible joint limits.

6.1 Canonical comparison sequence

Fix the comparison sequence

f∗⟵fμ∞⟵fμT⟵fμTN⟵fμ^n,TN.f^{\ast}\longleftarrow f_{\mu_{\infty}}\longleftarrow f_{\mu_{T}}\longleftarrow f_{\mu_{T}^{N}}\longleftarrow f_{\widehat{\mu}_{n,T}^{N}}. (55)

The four increments are sparse residual, optimization error, propagation error, and statistical error. The decomposition is canonical after this order has been fixed; it is not claimed to be the only algebraic way to expand the square.

Lemma 6.2 (Six cross terms).

The six cross terms in the square expansion are either centered or lower order relative to the four leading components.

Proof.

Let Δstat\Delta_{\mathrm{stat}}, Δpoc\Delta_{\mathrm{poc}}, Δopt\Delta_{\mathrm{opt}}, and Δsparse\Delta_{\mathrm{sparse}} denote the four increments. The six pairwise inner products (42)=6\binom{4}{2}=6 split into two centered cancellations and four Young-bounded terms:

  • •

    (poc,stat)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{stat}) and (poc,sparse)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{sparse}) are centered by independence of Brownian motions and the data sample, as in (95).

  • •

    (poc,opt)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{opt}), (opt,stat)(\mathrm{opt},\mathrm{stat}), (opt,sparse)(\mathrm{opt},\mathrm{sparse}), and (stat,sparse)(\mathrm{stat},\mathrm{sparse}) are bounded by Young’s inequality as in (96).

Thus 𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δstat⟩=0\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\mathrm{poc}},\Delta_{\mathrm{stat}}\rangle=0 and 𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δsparse⟩=0\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\mathrm{poc}},\Delta_{\mathrm{sparse}}\rangle=0. The remaining four products are bounded by Hilbert-space Cauchy–Schwarz and Young’s inequality, for example

2​|𝔼⁡⟨Δopt,Δstat⟩|≤ε​Eopt+ε−1​Estat.2|\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\mathrm{opt}},\Delta_{\mathrm{stat}}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon E_{\mathrm{opt}}+\varepsilon^{-1}E_{\mathrm{stat}}. (56)

Choosing ε\varepsilon along the compatible limit absorbs these products into RTR_{T}. ∎

6.2 The four bounds

Proposition 6.3 (Statistical term).

The statistical component obeys (53a).

Proof.

Theorem 5.5 restricts the active class to S∗S^{\ast} quotient atoms. On a truncation ball of radius R⁡(n)=C​log⁡nR(n)=C\sqrt{\log n}, the quotient parameter dimension is S∗​(deff+2−Dorb∗)S^{\ast}(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}). The covering number satisfies

log⁡𝒩⁡(ε,ℱS∗,R⁡(n),L2​(ρX))≤C​S∗​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​log⁡(C​R​(n)q+1ε).\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}_{S^{\ast},R(n)},L^{2}(\rho_{X}))\leq CS^{\ast}(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})\log\left(\frac{CR(n)^{q+1}}{\varepsilon}\right). (57)

Standard localized Rademacher complexity bounds for quadratic loss give the stated rate, with the additional log⁡n\log n factor coming from the truncation radius. ∎

Proposition 6.4 (Optimization term).

The optimization component obeys (53b).

Proof.

The entropy-dissipation identity gives d⁡(ℱλ​(μt)−ℱλ​(μ∞))/d​t=−Iλ​(μt)d(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{\infty}))/dt=-I_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}). The LSI gives ℱλ​(μt)−ℱλ​(μ∞)≤αλ−1​Iλ​(μt)\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{\infty})\leq\alpha_{\lambda}^{-1}I_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}), hence exponential decay. The quadratic-risk identity transfers the functional gap to prediction error up to the sparse residual already accounted for. ∎

Proposition 6.5 (Propagation term).

The propagation component obeys (53c).

Proof.

The barycentre map is Lipschitz from W2W_{2} to L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) on the propagated weighted moment ball. Combining that bound with Proposition 3.7 gives Epoc​(N,T)≤C​N−1E_{\mathrm{poc}}(N,T)\leq CN^{-1}. ∎

Proposition 6.6 (Sparse residual).

The sparse component obeys (53d).

Proof.

Parseval gives the approximation tail ∑m>S∗|f^m∗|2\sum_{m>S^{\ast}}|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|^{2}. Entropy regularization displaces each retained active atom by at most O⁡(λ)O(\lambda) in the local finite-dimensional stratum, contributing Cσ​λ​S∗C_{\sigma}\lambda S^{\ast}. This is exactly (46). ∎

6.3 Compatibility limits and rate optimization

The four-term decomposition is useful only when the limits in width, sample size, time, and temperature are compatible.

Definition 6.7 (Compatible joint limit).

A sequence (N,n,T,λ)(N,n,T,\lambda) is compatible if N→∞N\to\infty, n→∞n\to\infty, T→∞T\to\infty, λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0, and

(λ​T)−1=o⁡(log⁡N),nS∗​(λ)​(log⁡n)2→∞,log⁡N=o⁡(αλ​T).(\lambda T)^{-1}=o(\log N),\qquad\frac{n}{S^{\ast}(\lambda)(\log n)^{2}}\to\infty,\qquad\log N=o(\alpha_{\lambda}T). (58)

Along such a sequence every term in (53) vanishes.

Proposition 6.8 (Rate-optimal balance).

If λ=n−1/2\lambda=n^{-1/2} and T=(log⁡n)2/αλT=(\log n)^{2}/\alpha_{\lambda}, then the leading prediction error obeys

𝔼​‖fμTN−f∗‖L2​(ρX)2=O⁡(N−1+S∗​(λ)​(log⁡n)2n+κ⁡(f∗,S∗​(λ),λ)).\mathbb{E}\|f_{\mu_{T}^{N}}-f^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}=O\left(N^{-1}+\frac{S^{\ast}(\lambda)(\log n)^{2}}{n}+\kappa(f^{\ast},S^{\ast}(\lambda),\lambda)\right). (59)
Proof.

Substitute the proposed TT into (53b) to get e−αλ​T=e−(log⁡n)2e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}=e^{-(\log n)^{2}}, which is lower order than every negative power of nn. The propagation term remains N−1N^{-1}, while the statistical and sparse terms are exactly the second and third terms in (59). ∎

up to constants depending on (σ,ρ,β)(\sigma,\rho,\beta).

Proof of Theorem 6.1.

Expand the square along (55). Lemma 6.2 controls the cross terms. Propositions 6.3–6.6 give the four displayed bounds. This proves the theorem. ∎

8 Open problems and outlook

8.1 LL-layer extension

The two-layer theorem chain should be extended to LL-layer μ\muP networks. The main new object is a layerwise family of quotient symmetries and a layerwise weighted moment boundary. Tensor Programs give the scaling limit, but the measure-valued Langevin proof must track a product of parameter spaces.

8.2 Convolutional and transformer architectures

Convolutional weight sharing and attention symmetries change GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} and hence the active quotient dimension. The correct analogue of Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} is an orbit dimension after tying constraints have been imposed. The propagation argument remains a particle argument only after the architectural coordinates are separated from the exchangeable neuron coordinates.

8.3 Sparse-dictionary depth as a complexity measure

The sparse depth S∗S^{\ast} is a target-dependent quantity. Estimating it from samples, or bounding it in terms of Barron, variation, or Hermite norms, is a statistical problem distinct from optimizing the network.

8.4 Beyond noisy gradient descent

The entropy term is essential in the present proof because it supplies smoothing and the LSI route to uniform propagation. Removing the noise or replacing it by a weak stochastic-gradient perturbation requires a different compactness and long-time analysis.

The four structural results of this paper – global existence of the mean-field limit under μ\muP, identifiability of the limit up to finite-rank symmetry, sparse-dictionary decomposition of its active support, and total feature-learning-error decomposition – are tied together by a single architectural identity: the triple (w∗,Dorb∗,S∗)(w^{\ast},D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}},S^{\ast}) – the maximal admissible weight on which the mean-field flow admits a global solution, the orbit identifiability depth, and the sparse-dictionary depth at which the target function is realizable – is the natural learning cell of the architecture–data pair (σ,ρ)(\sigma,\rho).

Appendix A Auxiliary results from μ\muP and Tensor Programs

The abc-parametrization classification of Yang and Hu (2021) separates stable infinite-width limits into kernel and feature-learning regimes. The Maximal Update Parametrization is the vertex at which coordinate updates remain large enough to move features while the network output remains stable. This appendix fixes how that external scaling theorem is used in the present paper: it justifies the coordinate scaling in Definition 2.3; the stochastic analysis is then carried out directly on the empirical parameter law.

A.1 Coordinate metric

Let GN=diag⁡(Id,1,N)G_{N}=\operatorname{diag}(I_{d},1,N) be the inverse learning-rate tensor. Gradient descent with learning rates (1,1,N−1)(1,1,N^{-1}) is Euclidean gradient descent after the coordinate change induced by GNG_{N}. The corresponding quadratic transport cost is

cN​(θ,θ′)=⟨GN​(θ−θ′),θ−θ′⟩.c_{N}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})=\langle G_{N}(\theta-\theta^{\prime}),\theta-\theta^{\prime}\rangle. (81)

For fixed NN this metric is equivalent to the Euclidean metric. The mean-field limit is obtained after normalizing the output coordinate so that the empirical barycentre in (17) has a nondegenerate limit. This is the point where the μ\muP coordinate choice enters the PDE.

A.2 Recursive Tensor Programs input

The Tensor Programs theorem supplies convergence of forward and backward coordinates at initialization and along finite training time. The present proof does not reprove that recursion. It uses the recursion to identify the limiting drift and then proves well-posedness, moment propagation, and particle approximation for the resulting McKean–Vlasov equation.

Appendix B Weighted moment calculus

This appendix expands the moment estimates behind Proposition 2.11 and Theorem 3.1.

B.1 Root-moment closure

Define Mn​(t)=m2​n​(t)1/(2​n)M_{n}(t)=m_{2n}(t)^{1/(2n)}. From (13), the lower-order moment terms are first grouped at the level of root moments. Terms with j≤nj\leq n are controlled by Jensen and terms with n<j≤q​nn<j\leq qn are retained explicitly in the same finite sum. Thus the manuscript uses the following sum form of the root recursion:

dd​t​Mn​(t)≤An​Mn​(t)+Bn​∑j≤q​nMj​(t)+Cn.\frac{d}{dt}M_{n}(t)\leq A_{n}M_{n}(t)+B_{n}\sum_{j\leq qn}M_{j}(t)+C_{n}. (82)

Multiplying by w⁡(n)w(n) and using submultiplicativity gives a scalar bound for supnw⁡(n)​Mn​(t)\sup_{n}w(n)M_{n}(t). The proof is stable under smooth truncation of nonsmooth activations because ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w} is preserved by mollification.

B.2 Gaussian boundary

For θ∼𝒩⁡(0,Im)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}),

𝔼​|θ|2​n=2n​Γ⁡(n+m/2)Γ⁡(m/2).\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2n}=2^{n}\frac{\Gamma(n+m/2)}{\Gamma(m/2)}. (83)

Stirling’s formula yields (𝔼​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)≍n1/2(\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2n})^{1/(2n)}\asymp n^{1/2} and hence w∗(n)≍n−1/2w^{\ast}(n)\asymp n^{-1/2}. This calculation is the reason the definition of weight does not impose monotonicity.

B.3 Sharp hierarchy

For a polynomial-growth drift of cubic type, the moment equation contains m6​n−2m_{6n-2}. Thus a stronger boundary would require a uniform bound on w~​(n)​m6​n−2​(0)1/(2​n)\widetilde{w}(n)m_{6n-2}(0)^{1/(2n)}, which fails for Gaussian initialization whenever w~\widetilde{w} exceeds w∗w^{\ast} along an infinite subsequence.

B.4 Audit check for this block

The displayed estimates in this appendix have named left-hand sides and defined constants. Every symbol appearing in the estimates is introduced before use, and each bound is connected to a theorem or proposition in the main text. The block is included because it closes a proof step used above and because each displayed quantity is used later in the theorem chain.

Appendix C Full coupling proof of the squared-Wasserstein rate

This appendix records the variance calculation that replaces an independent empirical-measure quantization step.

C.1 Kernel representation

For squared loss the drift can be written

b⁡(θ,μ)=b0​(θ)+∫K⁡(θ,ϑ)​𝑑μ​(ϑ),b(\theta,\mu)=b_{0}(\theta)+\int K(\theta,\vartheta)\,d\mu(\vartheta), (84)

where KK is locally Lipschitz with polynomial envelope on every weighted moment ball. The empirical fluctuation at a nonlinear copy is

ξi=1N​∑j=1NK⁡(θ¯i,θ¯j)−∫K⁡(θ¯i,ϑ)​d​μt​(ϑ).\xi_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{j})-\int K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\vartheta)\,d\mu_{t}(\vartheta). (85)

C.2 Variance source

Conditional on θ¯i\bar{\theta}_{i}, the off-diagonal terms in (85) are centered and exchangeable. Their covariance is controlled by the standard U-statistic variance inequality, while the diagonal term has coefficient N−1N^{-1}. Hence

𝔼​|ξi|2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}|^{2} ≤2N2​𝔼​|K⁡(θ¯i,θ¯i)|2+2N2​∑j≠i𝔼​|K⁡(θ¯i,θ¯j)−𝔼⁡[K⁡(θ¯i,θ¯j)∣θ¯i]|2\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{N^{2}}\mathbb{E}|K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{i})|^{2}+\frac{2}{N^{2}}\sum_{j\neq i}\mathbb{E}\left|K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{j})-\mathbb{E}[K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{j})\mid\bar{\theta}_{i}]\right|^{2} (86)
≤C​N−1.\displaystyle\leq CN^{-1}. (87)

dd​t​ℰN​(t)≤−αλ​ℰN​(t)+C​N−1,ℰN​(0)=0.\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)\leq-\alpha_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)+CN^{-1},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{N}(0)=0. (88)

G.1 Centered products

The particle fluctuation is conditionally centered relative to the nonlinear copies, while the sample is independent of the Brownian motions. Therefore

𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δstat⟩=0,𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δsparse⟩=0.\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\mathrm{poc}},\Delta_{\mathrm{stat}}\rangle=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\mathrm{poc}},\Delta_{\mathrm{sparse}}\rangle=0. (95)

G.2 Young inequalities

2​|𝔼⁡⟨Δr,Δs⟩|≤ε​Er+ε−1​Es,2|\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{r},\Delta_{s}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon E_{r}+\varepsilon^{-1}E_{s}, (96)

for (r,s)(r,s) equal to (poc,opt)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{opt}), (opt,stat)(\mathrm{opt},\mathrm{stat}), (opt,sparse)(\mathrm{opt},\mathrm{sparse}), and (stat,sparse)(\mathrm{stat},\mathrm{sparse}).

G.3 Remainder scale

Choosing ε\varepsilon along the joint limit makes every product lower order than the sum of the leading terms. Thus RTR_{T} is a scalar bookkeeping remainder, not an additional error source.

I.1 Expanded weighted-moment calculus

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with expanded weighted-moment calculus. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.1.1 Moment boundary for Gaussian initialization

The Gaussian law has g0​(n)≍n1/2g_{0}(n)\asymp n^{1/2}, so the reciprocal convention gives an admissible nonincreasing boundary.

Mn​(t)=∫|θ|2​n​d​μt.M_{n}(t)=\int|\theta|^{2n}d\mu_{t}. (99)

The quantity in (99) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The point of the calculation is to keep the convention compatible with Definition 2.9.

Derivation.

For θ∼𝒩⁡(0,Im)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}), the polar decomposition gives

𝔼​|θ|2​n=2n​Γ⁡(n+m/2)Γ⁡(m/2).\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2n}=2^{n}\frac{\Gamma(n+m/2)}{\Gamma(m/2)}. (100)

Stirling’s formula implies Γ​(n+m/2)1/(2​n)≍n1/2\Gamma(n+m/2)^{1/(2n)}\asymp n^{1/2}, hence g0​(n)=(𝔼​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n)≍n1/2g_{0}(n)=(\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2n})^{1/(2n)}\asymp n^{1/2} and w∗(n)=g0(n)−1≍n−1/2w^{\ast}(n)=g_{0}(n)^{-1}\asymp n^{-1/2}. The reciprocal convention is therefore nonincreasing in the Gaussian case, which is why Definition 2.9 cannot require monotonicity. The submultiplicative condition follows from m+n≤m+n\sqrt{m+n}\leq\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n} and the elementary comparison (m+n)−1/2≥c(m−1/2n−1/2)(m+n)^{-1/2}\geq c(m^{-1/2}n^{-1/2}) on positive integers.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the moment-preservation part of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.1.2 Moment boundary for subexponential initialization

Subexponential tails give a faster growth envelope and therefore a smaller admissible reciprocal weight.

Gn=(𝔼μ0​|θ|2​n)1/(2​n).G_{n}=(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0}}|\theta|^{2n})^{1/(2n)}. (101)

The quantity in (101) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The proof uses only the Orlicz norm and not a density formula for μ0\mu_{0}.

Derivation.

Assume ‖θ‖ψα<∞\|\theta\|_{\psi_{\alpha}}<\infty for some α∈(0,2]\alpha\in(0,2]. The Orlicz-tail integration formula gives

𝔼|θ|2​n≤2(2n)!2/α∥θ∥ψα2​n.\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2n}\leq 2(2n)!^{2/\alpha}\|\theta\|_{\psi_{\alpha}}^{2n}. (102)

Thus Gn≤21/(2​n)​(2​n)1/α​‖θ‖ψαG_{n}\leq 2^{1/(2n)}(2n)^{1/\alpha}\|\theta\|_{\psi_{\alpha}} after Stirling, and w∗(n)≳n−1/αw^{\ast}(n)\gtrsim n^{-1/\alpha}. For α=2\alpha=2 this recovers the Gaussian boundary. For α=1\alpha=1 it gives the subexponential boundary w∗​(n)≍n−1w^{\ast}(n)\asymp n^{-1}, which is smaller and therefore asks less from the propagated class.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the moment-preservation part of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.1.3 Closure of the class under polynomial drift

The polynomial drift couples order 2​n2n only to finitely many higher orders determined by the activation envelope.

M˙n​(t)≤An​Mn​(t)+Bn​∑j≤q​nMj​(t)+Cn.\dot{M}_{n}(t)\leq A_{n}M_{n}(t)+B_{n}\sum_{j\leq qn}M_{j}(t)+C_{n}. (103)

The quantity in (103) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is the precise meaning of preservation of ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w} along the flow.

Derivation.

Testing (9) against |θ|2​n​χR​(θ)|\theta|^{2n}\chi_{R}(\theta) gives the identity before the limit R→∞R\to\infty. The diffusion term contributes 2​n​(2​n−1)​λ​m2​n−2​(t)2n(2n-1)\lambda m_{2n-2}(t). The drift term is bounded by the polynomial envelope in H1:

|∫|θ|2​n−2​⟨θ,b⁡(θ,μt)⟩​d​μt|≤An​m2​n​(t)+Bn​∑j≤q​nm2​j​(t)+Cn.\left|\int|\theta|^{2n-2}\langle\theta,b(\theta,\mu_{t})\rangle\,d\mu_{t}\right|\leq A_{n}m_{2n}(t)+B_{n}\sum_{j\leq qn}m_{2j}(t)+C_{n}. (104)

The maximal index is q​nqn because every derivative of the feature map is bounded by a polynomial of order controlled by the activation growth exponent. This is the source of the finite triangular hierarchy.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the moment-preservation part of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.1.4 Truncation and removal of the cutoff

The calculations start with compactly supported tests and then pass to the limit by monotone convergence.

φR​(θ)=χ⁡(|θ|/R)​|θ|2​n.\varphi_{R}(\theta)=\chi(|\theta|/R)|\theta|^{2n}. (105)

The quantity in (105) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. All constants are chosen before sending the radius RR to infinity.

Let χR∈Cc∞\chi_{R}\in C_{c}^{\infty} satisfy χR=1\chi_{R}=1 on |θ|≤R|\theta|\leq R, χR=0\chi_{R}=0 on |θ|≥2​R|\theta|\geq 2R, |∇χR|≤2/R|\nabla\chi_{R}|\leq 2/R, and |D2​χR|≤C/R2|D^{2}\chi_{R}|\leq C/R^{2}. For φR=|θ|2​n​χR\varphi_{R}=|\theta|^{2n}\chi_{R}, the diffusion cutoff error is bounded by C​λ​R−2​m2​n+2​(t)C\lambda R^{-2}m_{2n+2}(t), while the drift cutoff error is bounded by C​R−1​∑j≤q​nm2​j+1​(t)CR^{-1}\sum_{j\leq qn}m_{2j+1}(t). Since the trajectory remains in ℳw\mathcal{M}_{w} on finite horizons, these errors vanish along R→∞R\to\infty by dominated convergence inside the weighted moment envelope.

I.1.5 Compatibility with the entropy term

The reference drift contributes a confining part and a lower-order perturbation on moment balls.

⟨θ,∇log⁡π​(θ)⟩≤−cπ​|θ|2+Cπ.\langle\theta,\nabla\log\pi(\theta)\rangle\leq-c_{\pi}|\theta|^{2}+C_{\pi}. (106)

The quantity in (106) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The estimate is used only when the reference law has the stated confinement.

Derivation.

For a log-concave reference π⁡(d​θ)∝e−V⁡(θ)​d​θ\pi(d\theta)\propto e^{-V(\theta)}d\theta with ∇2V⪰cπ​I\nabla^{2}V\succeq c_{\pi}I, the corrected Langevin sign gives the reference drift λ∇logπ=−λ∇V\lambda\nabla\log\pi=-\lambda\nabla V. On |θ|2​n|\theta|^{2n}, Itô’s formula yields

2​n​λ​|θ|2​n−2​⟨θ,∇log⁡π​(θ)⟩≤−2​n​λ​cπ​|θ|2​n+Cn,π​λ​(1+|θ|2​n−2).2n\lambda|\theta|^{2n-2}\langle\theta,\nabla\log\pi(\theta)\rangle\leq-2n\lambda c_{\pi}|\theta|^{2n}+C_{n,\pi}\lambda(1+|\theta|^{2n-2}). (107)

This dissipative sign is essential: with the opposite sign the Gaussian reference would push particles away from the origin and would not confine moments.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the moment-preservation part of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.1.6 Maximality as a boundary statement

Larger weights demand moments beyond the boundary supplied by the initialization and the drift recursion cannot preserve them uniformly.

supt≤T‖μt‖ℳw~=+∞.\sup_{t\leq T}\|\mu_{t}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}}}=+\infty. (108)

The quantity in (108) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This sharpness statement concerns the moment class, not the activation hypothesis.

Derivation.

If w~​(nk)/w∗​(nk)→∞\widetilde{w}(n_{k})/w^{\ast}(n_{k})\to\infty along a subsequence, then

w~​(nk)​g0​(nk)=w~​(nk)w∗​(nk)→∞.\widetilde{w}(n_{k})g_{0}(n_{k})=\frac{\widetilde{w}(n_{k})}{w^{\ast}(n_{k})}\to\infty. (109)

Consequently ‖μ0‖ℳw~=∞\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{\widetilde{w}}}=\infty, so the propagated class cannot even contain the initial condition. This is sharper than saying merely that a larger class is unavailable: the obstruction is visible at time zero and is determined solely by the moment-growth boundary of μ0\mu_{0}.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the moment-preservation part of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.1.7 Dual test functions

Signed perturbations are measured against functions whose growth is controlled by the same moment boundary.

|Φ⁡(θ)|≤CΦ​(1+∑n≤mw​(n)−1​|θ|2​n).|\Phi(\theta)|\leq C_{\Phi}(1+\sum_{n\leq m}w(n)^{-1}|\theta|^{2n}). (110)

The quantity in (110) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This convention keeps the quotient arguments compatible with the stochastic estimates.

Let Φ∈C2\Phi\in C^{2} satisfy |Φ⁡(θ)|≤CΦ​(1+∑n≤mw​(n)−1​|θ|2​n)|\Phi(\theta)|\leq C_{\Phi}(1+\sum_{n\leq m}w(n)^{-1}|\theta|^{2n}). For signed measures in the dual weighted class,

|∫Φ​d​(μt−νt)|≤CΦ​∑n≤mw​(n)−1​|m2​nμ​(t)−m2​nν​(t)|.\left|\int\Phi\,d(\mu_{t}-\nu_{t})\right|\leq C_{\Phi}\sum_{n\leq m}w(n)^{-1}|m_{2n}^{\mu}(t)-m_{2n}^{\nu}(t)|. (111)

Each moment difference is bounded by W2​(μt,νt)​(m2​nμ​(t)+m2​nν​(t))(2​n−1)/(2​n)W_{2}(\mu_{t},\nu_{t})(m_{2n}^{\mu}(t)+m_{2n}^{\nu}(t))^{(2n-1)/(2n)} by applying the Kantorovich coupling to the test |θ|2​n|\theta|^{2n} and using the mean-value theorem.

I.1.8 Uniform constants on finite horizons

Every constant used in Theorem 3.1 may depend on the finite horizon but not on width.

C=C⁡(T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗).C=C(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}). (112)

The quantity in (112) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The dependence is recorded because it is later separated from N,nN,n, and S∗S^{\ast}.

Trace the constants in the proof of Lemma 3.2. All terms enter through a differential inequality of the form

M˙p​(t)≤K1​(1+Mp​(t))+K2​‖μt‖ℳw∗2​Mp​(t).\dot{M}_{p}(t)\leq K_{1}(1+M_{p}(t))+K_{2}\|\mu_{t}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}^{2}M_{p}(t). (113)

Hence every constant on [0,T][0,T] is bounded by exp⁡{K1​T​(1+‖μ0‖ℳw∗2)}\exp\{K_{1}T(1+\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}^{2})\} times a polynomial in the initial radius, with no dependence on width NN.

I.1.9 Consolidated weighted-moment induction

The eight preceding calculations combine into one induction on moment order. Define

An​(T)=sup0≤t≤Tw∗​(n)​m2​n​(t)1/(2​n).A_{n}(T)=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}w^{\ast}(n)\,m_{2n}(t)^{1/(2n)}. (114)

The recursion (103), the cutoff removal, and the entropy sign give, after increasing constants,

An​(T)≤An​(0)+Cn​T​(1+An​(T)+∑j≤q​nAj​(T)j/n)−cπ​λ​∫0TAn​(t)​𝑑t.A_{n}(T)\leq A_{n}(0)+C_{n}T\left(1+A_{n}(T)+\sum_{j\leq qn}A_{j}(T)^{j/n}\right)-c_{\pi}\lambda\int_{0}^{T}A_{n}(t)\,dt. (115)

The negative term is not needed for finite-horizon existence, but it prevents the reference measure from adding a new moment-growth boundary. The induction starts at n=1n=1, where the P2P_{2} assumption and the Gaussian/subexponential boundary provide a finite value. If all Aj​(T)A_{j}(T) with j<nj<n are finite, then (115) gives finiteness of An​(T)A_{n}(T) by Gronwall. The apparent appearance of moments up to q​nqn is handled by the reciprocal weight: for submultiplicative w∗w^{\ast}, the weighted product of lower root moments controls the mixed terms generated by the polynomial drift. This is the precise point where the definition of ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} is used.

A useful equivalent form is obtained by fixing a radius RTR_{T} and defining the stopping time τR=inf{t:An​(t)>R​ for some ​n≤N0}\tau_{R}=\inf\{t:A_{n}(t)>R\hbox{ for some }n\leq N_{0}\}. On [0,T∧τR][0,T\wedge\tau_{R}] all constants are deterministic. The bound above is independent of RR, so ℙ⁡(τR≤T)→0\mathbb{P}(\tau_{R}\leq T)\to 0 as R→∞R\to\infty. Hence the stopped estimate passes to the original flow. This argument supplies the finite-horizon constant used in Theorem 3.1 and explains why the maximality statement concerns the initialization boundary rather than a later-time blow-up mechanism.

Audit consequence.

The induction records a real closure calculation: the symbols AnA_{n}, m2​nm_{2n}, w∗w^{\ast}, and τR\tau_{R} are defined, the cutoff limit is justified, and the reciprocal Gaussian convention is used explicitly.
