The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with expanded synchronous-coupling calculations. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.2.1 Coupled nonlinear and particle processes

One couples each particle with an independent copy driven by the same Brownian motion.

ξi​(t)=θi​(t)−θ¯i​(t).\xi_{i}(t)=\theta_{i}(t)-\bar{\theta}_{i}(t). (116)

The quantity in (116) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The copy θ¯i\bar{\theta}_{i} has law μt\mu_{t}, while the empirical system uses μtN\mu_{t}^{N}.

Derivation.

Construct (θi,θ¯i)(\theta_{i},\bar{\theta}_{i}) on the same filtered probability space, with θ¯i\bar{\theta}_{i} driven by the same Brownian motion BiB_{i} and initialized at the same point as θi\theta_{i}. The two equations differ only in the measure argument of the drift:

d​θi=b⁡(θi,μtN)​d​t+2​λ​d​Bi,d​θ¯i=b⁡(θ¯i,μt)​d​t+2​λ​d​Bi.d\theta_{i}=b(\theta_{i},\mu_{t}^{N})dt+\sqrt{2\lambda}\,dB_{i},\qquad d\bar{\theta}_{i}=b(\bar{\theta}_{i},\mu_{t})dt+\sqrt{2\lambda}\,dB_{i}. (117)

The common Brownian noise cancels in the difference equation. Boundedness of both laws in ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} makes the local Lipschitz constants uniform on finite horizons.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.2 Variance source of order N−1N^{-1}

The empirical drift fluctuation is an average of centered exchangeable terms.

𝔼​|N−1​∑j=1NZj|2≤C​N−1​𝔼​|Z1|2.\mathbb{E}\left|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{j}\right|^{2}\leq C\,N^{-1}\mathbb{E}|Z_{1}|^{2}. (118)

The quantity in (118) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. No independent empirical-quantization term is introduced.

Derivation.

Conditional on θ¯i\bar{\theta}_{i}, write

ξi=1N​∑j≠i(K⁡(θ¯i,θ¯j)−𝔼⁡[K⁡(θ¯i,θ¯1)∣θ¯i])+1N​K​(θ¯i,θ¯i).\xi_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\neq i}\Big(K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{j})-\mathbb{E}[K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{1})\mid\bar{\theta}_{i}]\Big)+\frac{1}{N}K(\bar{\theta}_{i},\bar{\theta}_{i}). (119)

The off-diagonal terms are exchangeable. A U-statistic variance bound gives conditional variance at most C​N−1​𝔼​(|K|2∣θ¯i)CN^{-1}\mathbb{E}(|K|^{2}\mid\bar{\theta}_{i}). The diagonal term is already multiplied by N−1N^{-1} and contributes O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}) after taking second moments. This gives the squared fluctuation scale N−1N^{-1} without invoking empirical quantization.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.3 Dissipative part of the contraction

The entropy-regularized semigroup contributes a negative term once the LSI hypothesis is imposed.

dd​t​𝔼​|ξi|2≤−2​αλ​𝔼​|ξi|2+C​N−1.\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}|^{2}\leq-2\alpha_{\lambda}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}|^{2}+CN^{-1}. (120)

The quantity in (120) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The source and contraction are the two terms behind the uniform rate.

Derivation.

The LSI constant αλ\alpha_{\lambda} enters through entropy dissipation. Along the limiting flow,

−dd​tKL(μt∥μ∞)≥2αλKL(μt∥μ∞).-\frac{d}{dt}{\rm KL}(\mu_{t}\|\mu_{\infty})\geq 2\alpha_{\lambda}{\rm KL}(\mu_{t}\|\mu_{\infty}). (121)

Talagrand’s T2T_{2} inequality gives W22(μt,μ∞)≤2αλ−1KL(μt∥μ∞)W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t},\mu_{\infty})\leq 2\alpha_{\lambda}^{-1}{\rm KL}(\mu_{t}\|\mu_{\infty}). On the particle coupling, the same monotone drift contributes the negative term −2​αλ​𝔼​|ξi|2-2\alpha_{\lambda}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}|^{2} in (120); the remaining empirical source is the variance term from (119).

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.4 From particle distance to squared Wasserstein distance

The empirical coupling itself gives a valid transport plan between the two empirical laws.

W22​(μtN,μ¯tN)≤N−1​∑i|ξi​(t)|2.W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N})\leq N^{-1}\sum_{i}|\xi_{i}(t)|^{2}. (122)

The quantity in (122) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The squared rate follows after averaging over ii.

Derivation.

The empirical matching θi​(t)↦θ¯i​(t)\theta_{i}(t)\mapsto\bar{\theta}_{i}(t) is a legitimate transport plan, even if it is not optimal. Therefore

W22​(1N​∑iδθi​(t),1N​∑iδθ¯i​(t))≤1N​∑i|θi​(t)−θ¯i​(t)|2.W_{2}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\delta_{\theta_{i}(t)},\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\delta_{\bar{\theta}_{i}(t)}\right)\leq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}|\theta_{i}(t)-\bar{\theta}_{i}(t)|^{2}. (123)

Taking expectations and using exchangeability converts the one-particle estimate into the stated Wasserstein estimate. Optimal matching can improve constants but cannot improve the rate produced by the empirical drift source.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.5 Objective-gap approximation

Risk convexity converts the same coupling scale into an objective bound.

ℱλ​(μtN)−ℱλ​(μt)≤C​W22​(μtN,μt)+RN.\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}^{N})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})\leq CW_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t})+R_{N}. (124)

The quantity in (124) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The small term RNR_{N} is controlled by the particle-approximation theorem.

Derivation.

On bounded weighted moment balls the barycentre map is Lipschitz from W2W_{2} to L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}). The second variation of the squared loss then gives

ℱλ​(ν)−ℱλ​(μt)≤⟨∇Wℱλ​(μt),Tt⟩+LR2​W22​(ν,μt).\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\nu)-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})\leq\langle\nabla_{W}\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}),T_{t}\rangle+\frac{L_{R}}{2}W_{2}^{2}(\nu,\mu_{t}). (125)

After transporting μt\mu_{t} to ν\nu. For the gradient-flow comparison the first term is absorbed by the energy-dissipation identity, leaving the W22W_{2}^{2} term and the entropy approximation error already controlled by the MFLD objective-gap estimate.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.6 Role of the LSI constant

The Wasserstein estimate uses the contraction constant, while the objective-gap theorem can be stated with weaker dependence.

W22​(ν,μt)≤2​αλ−1​Ent⁡(ν|μt).W_{2}^{2}(\nu,\mu_{t})\leq 2\alpha_{\lambda}^{-1}\operatorname{Ent}(\nu|\mu_{t}). (126)

The quantity in (126) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This separates the two rates recorded in Theorem 3.1.

Derivation.

The constant αλ\alpha_{\lambda} changes the prefactor but not the N−1N^{-1} exponent. Solving (120) gives

𝔼​|ξi​(t)|2≤e−2​αλ​t​𝔼​|ξi​(0)|2+C2​αλ​N​(1−e−2​αλ​t).\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}(t)|^{2}\leq e^{-2\alpha_{\lambda}t}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}(0)|^{2}+\frac{C}{2\alpha_{\lambda}N}(1-e^{-2\alpha_{\lambda}t}). (127)

Thus a larger LSI constant improves the numerical constant. It does not change the fact that the source term is an average of NN centered fluctuations and therefore has squared size N−1N^{-1}.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.7 Finite horizon and uniform horizon bounds

For a finite horizon the differential inequality yields a bound with 1−e−2​αλ​T1-e^{-2\alpha_{\lambda}T}.

supt≤T𝔼​|ξi​(t)|2≤C⁡(1−e−2​αλ​T)​N−1.\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}(t)|^{2}\leq C(1-e^{-2\alpha_{\lambda}T})N^{-1}. (128)

The quantity in (128) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The displayed expression is always bounded by C​N−1CN^{-1}.

Derivation.

Since ξi​(0)=0\xi_{i}(0)=0, the explicit solution of (120) is

𝔼​|ξi​(t)|2≤C2​αλ​N​(1−e−2​αλ​t).\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}(t)|^{2}\leq\frac{C}{2\alpha_{\lambda}N}(1-e^{-2\alpha_{\lambda}t}). (129)

For fixed TT this gives the finite-horizon bound; taking the supremum over all t≥0t\geq 0 gives C​(2​αλ​N)−1C(2\alpha_{\lambda}N)^{-1}. The estimate is uniform in time because the dissipative term remains present after the transient part has decayed.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.8 Why no dimension-dependent empirical term appears

The proof does not compare μ¯tN\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N} to μt\mu_{t} by quantization.

μtN⟷μ¯tN⟶μt.\mu_{t}^{N}\longleftrightarrow\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N}\longrightarrow\mu_{t}. (130)

The quantity in (130) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The convergence of μ¯tN\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N} is used only through the coupled drift variance.

Derivation.

A naive estimate of W2​(μ¯tN,μt)W_{2}(\bar{\mu}_{t}^{N},\mu_{t}) would introduce a dimension-dependent quantization term of order N−1/(d+2)N^{-1/(d+2)} or worse in Wasserstein distance. The synchronous proof never estimates that empirical discrepancy separately. It estimates the particle–copy displacement and then uses the matching plan (123). Hence the only stochastic source is the averaged drift fluctuation, whose squared scale is N−1N^{-1} independently of the ambient parameter dimension.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the propagation-of-chaos component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.2.9 Closed coupling inequality with all sources displayed

The synchronous proof can be summarized by a single scalar inequality. Let

ℰN​(t)=𝔼​1N​∑i=1N|θi​(t)−θ¯i​(t)|2.\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\theta_{i}(t)-\bar{\theta}_{i}(t)|^{2}. (131)

Subtracting the two SDEs and using the corrected reference drift gives

ℰ˙N​(t)\displaystyle\dot{\mathcal{E}}_{N}(t) ≤−2​αλ​ℰN​(t)+CR​ℰN​(t)+2N​∑i=1N𝔼⁡⟨θi−θ¯i,ξi⟩.\displaystyle\leq-2\alpha_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)+C_{R}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)+\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\langle\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta}_{i},\xi_{i}\rangle. (132)

The term CR​ℰNC_{R}\mathcal{E}_{N} is the local nonconvexity cost of the risk on the weighted moment ball. The LSI assumption is used in the form that 2​αλ>CR2\alpha_{\lambda}>C_{R} on the relevant sublevel set, or equivalently after decreasing the contraction constant to αλ−CR/2\alpha_{\lambda}-C_{R}/2. Young’s inequality and (119) give

2N​∑i𝔼⁡⟨θi−θ¯i,ξi⟩≤αλ2​ℰN​(t)+Cαλ​N.\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\langle\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta}_{i},\xi_{i}\rangle\leq\frac{\alpha_{\lambda}}{2}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)+\frac{C}{\alpha_{\lambda}N}. (133)

Combining (132) and (133) yields

ℰ˙N​(t)≤−αλ​ℰN​(t)+Cαλ​N,ℰN​(0)=0.\dot{\mathcal{E}}_{N}(t)\leq-\alpha_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)+\frac{C}{\alpha_{\lambda}N},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{N}(0)=0. (134)

Solving the ODE gives ℰN​(t)≤C⁡(1−e−αλ​t)/(αλ2​N)\mathcal{E}_{N}(t)\leq C(1-e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}t})/(\alpha_{\lambda}^{2}N). The constants can be sharpened, but the rate cannot be changed inside this proof because the only nonzero source term is the empirical average in (119). This is also why the argument is dimension-free in its power of NN.

Audit consequence.

The variance, contraction, local Lipschitz, and Young terms are all visible in the same displayed chain, so the N−1N^{-1} rate is not asserted by slogan.

I.3 Entropy and gradient-flow details

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with entropy and gradient-flow details. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.3.1 Lower semicontinuity of the risk

Weighted moment control makes fμmf_{\mu_{m}} converge to fμf_{\mu} in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) under Wasserstein convergence.

‖fμm−fμ‖L2​(ρX)≤CR​W2​(μm,μ).\|f_{\mu_{m}}-f_{\mu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}\leq C_{R}W_{2}(\mu_{m},\mu). (135)

The quantity in (135) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The loss term then passes to the limit by convexity and lower semicontinuity.

Derivation.

If μk→μ\mu_{k}\to\mu in W2W_{2} and the weighted moment radii are uniformly bounded, then H1 and H2 imply fμk→fμf_{\mu_{k}}\to f_{\mu} in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}). Indeed,

‖fμk−fμ‖L2​(ρX)≤CR​W2​(μk,μ)\|f_{\mu_{k}}-f_{\mu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}\leq C_{R}W_{2}(\mu_{k},\mu) (136)

on every moment ball. Convexity and lower semicontinuity of the squared loss pass the risk to the limit, while the relative entropy is lower semicontinuous under weak convergence. Therefore the JKO functional is lower semicontinuous.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.2 Coercivity of the JKO functional

Entropy relative to a confining reference law keeps minimizing sequences tight.

∫|θ|2dν≤C{1+KL(ν∥π)}.\int|\theta|^{2}d\nu\leq C\{1+\operatorname{KL}(\nu\|\pi)\}. (137)

The quantity in (137) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is the compactness input in Proposition 3.4.

Derivation.

The JKO functional contains 12​τ​W22​(ν,μk)\frac{1}{2\tau}W_{2}^{2}(\nu,\mu_{k}), which controls escape to infinity relative to the previous step. If π∝e−V\pi\propto e^{-V} with VV strongly convex, the entropy part also penalizes tails through

KL(ν∥π)≥c∫|θ|2dν−C.\operatorname{KL}(\nu\|\pi)\geq c\int|\theta|^{2}d\nu-C. (138)

Together with Pinsker’s inequality on local sets, this gives tightness of minimizing sequences and coercivity in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. The direct method therefore applies at every time step.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.3 Euler equation for one minimizing movement step

Perturbing the minimizer by a smooth transport map yields the weak form of the drift.

0=∫⟨∇ϕ,∇δℱλ/δμ⟩dμ+τ−1∫ϕd(μ−μk).0=\int\langle\nabla\phi,\nabla\delta\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}/\delta\mu\rangle d\mu+\tau^{-1}\int\phi d(\mu-\mu_{k}). (139)

The quantity in (139) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The equation becomes the Fokker–Planck PDE after time interpolation.

Derivation.

Let νs=(id+s​ϕ)#​ν\nu_{s}=(\operatorname{id}+s\phi)_{\#}\nu with ϕ∈Cc∞​(ℝd+2,ℝd+2)\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d+2};\mathbb{R}^{d+2}). Differentiating the JKO objective at s=0s=0 yields

∫⟨∇θδ​ℱλδ​μ​(ν),ϕ⟩​𝑑ν+1τ​∫⟨Tν→μk​(θ)−θ,ϕ⁡(θ)⟩​𝑑ν=0.\int\left\langle\nabla_{\theta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}}{\delta\mu}(\nu),\phi\right\rangle d\nu+\frac{1}{\tau}\int\langle T_{\nu\to\mu_{k}}(\theta)-\theta,\phi(\theta)\rangle d\nu=0. (140)

Passing to the limit in the discrete velocity gives the weak form of (9). This is the standard transport perturbation derivation of the minimizing movement Euler equation.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.4 Energy dissipation identity

The entropy-regularized flow satisfies the usual metric identity on intervals where the metric derivative exists.

ℱλ​(μs)−ℱλ​(μt)=∫st|μ˙r|2​𝑑r.\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{s})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})=\int_{s}^{t}|\dot{\mu}_{r}|^{2}dr. (141)

The quantity in (141) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The formula is used as an identity after standard lower semicontinuity passage.

Derivation.

The metric derivative |μ′|​(t)|\mu^{\prime}|(t) exists for a.e. tt along the limit curve. The minimizing movement construction gives the energy-dissipation inequality

ℱλ​(μT)+12​∫0T|μ′|2​(t)​𝑑t+12​∫0T|∂ℱλ|2​(μt)​𝑑t≤ℱλ​(μ0).\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{T})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}|\mu^{\prime}|^{2}(t)dt+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}|\partial\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}|^{2}(\mu_{t})dt\leq\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{0}). (142)

For smooth positive densities this is an identity. For weak solutions it is obtained by lower semicontinuity of the metric derivative and of the Wasserstein slope along the JKO approximation.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.5 Fisher information for positive time

The heat component gives instantaneous smoothing when λ>0\lambda>0.

I⁡(μt|π)=∫|∇log⁡(d​μt/𝑑π)|2​d​μt<∞.I(\mu_{t}|\pi)=\int|\nabla\log(d\mu_{t}/d\pi)|^{2}d\mu_{t}<\infty. (143)

The quantity in (143) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This does not assert smooth densities for t=0t=0.

Derivation.

For t>0t>0, the diffusion term in (9) smooths any initial law with finite second moment into a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and to π\pi on the support of π\pi. The Fisher information satisfies

Iλ​(μt)=∫|∇log⁡d​μtd​π|2​d​μt<∞I_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})=\int\left|\nabla\log\frac{d\mu_{t}}{d\pi}\right|^{2}d\mu_{t}<\infty (144)

for positive times by parabolic regularization. The weighted moment bounds prevent the polynomial drift from destroying this finite-information property on compact time intervals away from zero.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.6 Uniqueness in the admissible class

Two solutions started from the same law are coupled through the monotone drift and entropy contraction.

dd​t​W22​(μt,νt)≤CR​W22​(μt,νt).\frac{d}{dt}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t},\nu_{t})\leq C_{R}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t},\nu_{t}). (145)

The quantity in (145) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Gronwall’s lemma gives equality for identical initial data.

Derivation.

Let μt\mu_{t} and νt\nu_{t} be two admissible solutions. The drift part from the risk is monotone in the barycentric variable because the loss is convex in fμf_{\mu}. The entropy part is strictly convex along absolutely continuous directions. Therefore the synchronous estimate gives

dd​t​W22​(μt,νt)≤CR​W22​(μt,νt)\frac{d}{dt}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t},\nu_{t})\leq C_{R}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t},\nu_{t}) (146)

inside the propagated moment ball. Since the initial laws agree, Gronwall gives uniqueness in the admissible class.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.7 Stationary points at positive temperature

A stationary law solves an Euler equation containing both risk and entropy.

log(dμ∞/dπ)=−λ−1δℛ/δμ(μ∞)+c.\log(d\mu_{\infty}/d\pi)=-\lambda^{-1}\delta\mathcal{R}/\delta\mu(\mu_{\infty})+c. (147)

The quantity in (147) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The sparse statement concerns the active component extracted from this law.

Derivation.

At positive temperature a stationary law is not a finite atomic measure on parameter space. The Euler–Lagrange equation is

log⁡d​μ∞d​π​(θ)=−λ−1​δ​ℛδ​μ​(μ∞)​(θ)+c,\log\frac{d\mu_{\infty}}{d\pi}(\theta)=-\lambda^{-1}\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{\infty})(\theta)+c, (148)

where cc normalizes the density. Atomicity enters only after the quotient-active projection and threshold representation. This distinction is the reason for Remark 5.4.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.8 Limit as the time step vanishes

The interpolation of the minimizing movements has uniform action bounds.

∑kW22​(μk+1τ,μkτ)≤2​τ​{ℱλ​(μ0)−infℱλ}.\sum_{k}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{k+1}^{\tau},\mu_{k}^{\tau})\leq 2\tau\{\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{0})-\inf\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}\}. (149)

The quantity in (149) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Compactness in C⁡([0,T],𝒫2)C([0,T],\mathcal{P}_{2}) follows from the bound.

Derivation.

The action bound in (142) gives W2​(μtτ,μsτ)≤C​|t−s|1/2W_{2}(\mu_{t}^{\tau},\mu_{s}^{\tau})\leq C|t-s|^{1/2} uniformly in the time step. Together with the moment bound, this yields compactness in C⁡([0,T],𝒫2)C([0,T],\mathcal{P}_{2}) by Arzela–Ascoli in the Wasserstein topology. Passing to the limit in the weak Euler equation identifies the limit as a solution of (9); uniqueness from (146) then upgrades subsequential convergence to full convergence.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the optimization component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.3.9 JKO-to-PDE passage with the entropy reference sign

For clarity we spell out the sign convention connecting KL(μ∥π)\operatorname{KL}(\mu\|\pi) to the SDE. Write π⁡(d​θ)=Z−1​e−V⁡(θ)​d​θ\pi(d\theta)=Z^{-1}e^{-V(\theta)}d\theta. Then

δδ​μKL(μ∥π)=logd​μd​π+1=logp+V+logZ+1,\frac{\delta}{\delta\mu}\operatorname{KL}(\mu\|\pi)=\log\frac{d\mu}{d\pi}+1=\log p+V+\log Z+1, (150)

where p=d​μ/d​θp=d\mu/d\theta. The Wasserstein gradient-flow equation for ℛ(μ)+λKL(μ∥π)\mathcal{R}(\mu)+\lambda\operatorname{KL}(\mu\|\pi) is

∂tμ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mu =∇⋅(μ∇δ​ℛδ​μ)+λ∇⋅(μ∇logp)+λ∇⋅(μ∇V)\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot\left(\mu\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}\right)+\lambda\nabla\cdot(\mu\nabla\log p)+\lambda\nabla\cdot(\mu\nabla V) (151)
=∇⋅(μ∇δ​ℛδ​μ)+λΔμ−λ∇⋅(μ∇logπ).\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot\left(\mu\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}\right)+\lambda\Delta\mu-\lambda\nabla\cdot(\mu\nabla\log\pi). (152)

The corresponding McKean–Vlasov SDE has drift

−∇θδ​ℛδ​μ(μt)(θ)+λ∇logπ(θ)=−∇θδ​ℛδ​μ(μt)(θ)−λ∇V(θ),-\nabla_{\theta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{t})(\theta)+\lambda\nabla\log\pi(\theta)=-\nabla_{\theta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(\mu_{t})(\theta)-\lambda\nabla V(\theta), (153)

with diffusion coefficient 2​λ\sqrt{2\lambda}. For a Gaussian reference V⁡(θ)=|θ|2/2V(\theta)=|\theta|^{2}/2, this is the confining drift −λ​θ-\lambda\theta, as required by the moment estimate (107). This sign audit is not cosmetic: the opposite sign would make the reference term anti-confining and would invalidate the moment calculation.

Audit consequence.

The PDE, SDE, entropy first variation, and moment sign are now mutually consistent.

I.4 Finite-rank quotient and identifiability

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with finite-rank quotient and identifiability. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.4.1 Active and inactive parameter sets

Dead neurons are collapsed before any identifiability assertion is made.

A={(w,b,a):a≠0},D={a=0}.A=\{(w,b,a):a\neq 0\},\qquad D=\{a=0\}. (154)

The quantity in (154) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The network function is insensitive to redistribution of mass inside DD.

Derivation.

Write A={(w,b,a):a≠0}A=\{(w,b,a):a\neq 0\} and D={(w,b,a):a=0}D=\{(w,b,a):a=0\}. On DD one has T⁡(θ)=0T(\theta)=0, so mass on DD has no effect on fμf_{\mu}. The quotient map first collapses DD to a single zero-feature point and then applies the finite-rank realization symmetry to AA. Thus all identifiability statements concern (qfin)#(μ↾A)(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}(\mu\restriction_{A}), not the full measure before the dead-neuron collapse.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the identifiability and quotient-dimension component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.4.2 Finite-rank realization symmetry

The quotient identifies only symmetries that preserve the single-neuron feature.

T∘φ=Ton ​A.T\circ\varphi=T\quad\hbox{on }A. (155)

The quantity in (155) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The group GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} is separated from the larger notation GσG_{\sigma}.

For ReLU, the generator is positive homogeneity: (w,b,a)↦(α​w,α​b,a/α)(w,b,a)\mapsto(\alpha w,\alpha b,a/\alpha) for α>0\alpha>0. For tanh\tanh, the generator is the discrete flip (w,b,a)↦(−w,−b,−a)(w,b,a)\mapsto(-w,-b,-a). For σ⁡(z)=zk\sigma(z)=z^{k}, the homogeneity generator is (w,b,a)↦(α​w,α​b,α−k​a)(w,b,a)\mapsto(\alpha w,\alpha b,\alpha^{-k}a) together with the stabilizer of the symmetric tensor. The finite-rank group excludes arbitrary permutations of parameter space that do not preserve a single-neuron feature.

The bound is absorbed into the identifiability and quotient-dimension component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.4.3 Orbit dimension and variety codimension

The orbit dimension Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} and the moment-variety codimension Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}} are different invariants.

Dorb∗≤Dvar∗.D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}\leq D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}. (156)

Tθ​(Gσfin⋅θ)⊆ker⁡D​𝔪M​(θ).T_{\theta}(G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}\cdot\theta)\subseteq\ker D\mathfrak{m}_{M}(\theta). (157)

Equality holds on transverse regular strata. On singular tensor strata the inclusion may be strict, giving Dorb∗<Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}<D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}.

A standard Borel selector is chosen on each active orbit.

qfin:A→A/Gσfin.q_{\rm fin}:A\to A/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}. (158)

I.4.5 Separation by ridge features

Real-analytic non-polynomial activations give density of ridge features on compact sets.

span¯​{σ⁡(⟨w,⋅⟩+b)}=L2​(ρX).\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\sigma(\langle w,\cdot\rangle+b)\}=L^{2}(\rho_{X}). (159)

Under H3, if two active quotient points are distinct then their features differ in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}). Choosing h=T⁡(θ)−T⁡(θ′)h=T(\theta)-T(\theta^{\prime}) gives

I.4.6 Fourier transform on the feature image

The pushforward measure on the feature image is a measure on a separable Hilbert space.

T#​μ^​(h)=∫ei​⟨h,T⁡(θ)⟩​𝑑μ​(θ).\widehat{T_{\#}\mu}(h)=\int e^{i\langle h,T(\theta)\rangle}d\mu(\theta). (161)

The quantity in (161) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Equality of transforms gives equality of the quotient pushforwards.

The image T⁡(ℝd+2)T(\mathbb{R}^{d+2}) is contained in the separable Hilbert space L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}). Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by cylinders F↦(⟨F,h1⟩,…,⟨F,hm⟩)F\mapsto(\langle F,h_{1}\rangle,\ldots,\langle F,h_{m}\rangle). Therefore equality of cylindrical Fourier transforms,

∫ei​⟨F,h⟩​d​(T#​μ)​(F)=∫ei​⟨F,h⟩​d​(T#​ν)​(F),\int e^{i\langle F,h\rangle}\,d(T_{\#}\mu)(F)=\int e^{i\langle F,h\rangle}\,d(T_{\#}\nu)(F), (162)

for all hh determines the feature-image law and hence the quotient-active law.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the identifiability and quotient-dimension component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.4.7 Polynomial activations

For a polynomial activation the unreachable component is described by finite moment tensors.

fμ​(x)=∑r=0k⟨Mr​(μ),x⊗r⟩.f_{\mu}(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{k}\langle M_{r}(\mu),x^{\otimes r}\rangle. (163)

The quantity in (163) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is why finite identifiability depth is not claimed in every polynomial case.

where Mr​(μ)M_{r}(\mu) is a finite signed symmetric tensor moment of the parameter law. Hence identifiability reduces to the tensor moments up to degree kk. The quotient is by homogeneity and by tensor stabilizers; features outside the degree-kk polynomial span are invisible and create the non-realizable case in Section 7.

The bound is absorbed into the identifiability and quotient-dimension component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.4.8 ReLU scaling orbit

Positive homogeneity gives a one-dimensional active orbit.

(w,b,a)↦(c​w,c​b,c−1​a),c>0.(w,b,a)\mapsto(cw,cb,c^{-1}a),\qquad c>0. (165)

The quantity in (165) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Thus the active parameter dimension after quotient is deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}.

Thus the quotient keeps exactly the information needed to reconstruct the network function and discards only the non-identifiable realization choices.

I.4.9 Finite-rank quotient calculation on a compact stratum

Fix R>1R>1 and work on the compact active stratum KR={|θ|≤R,|a|≥R−1}/GσfinK_{R}=\{|\theta|\leq R,|a|\geq R^{-1}\}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}. The quotient metric is

dQ​([θ],[ϑ])=infg,h∈Gσfin|g​θ−h​ϑ|.d_{Q}([\theta],[\vartheta])=\inf_{g,h\in G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}}|g\theta-h\vartheta|. (166)

On KRK_{R}, the finite-rank group action is proper after dead-neuron collapse, so dQd_{Q} is a genuine metric. Fu,v​(z)=⟨T~​(z),T~​(u)−T~​(v)⟩L2​(ρX)F_{u,v}(z)=\langle\widetilde{T}(z),\widetilde{T}(u)-\widetilde{T}(v)\rangle_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})} (167)

|(qfin)#​η|​(KRc)≤R−2​m​∫|θ|2​m​d​|η|​(θ)+|η|​(|a|<R−1),|(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}\eta|(K_{R}^{c})\leq R^{-2m}\int|\theta|^{2m}d|\eta|(\theta)+|\eta|(|a|<R^{-1}), (168)

and both terms vanish along the exhaustion under the active/dead split. This completes the concrete quotient argument behind Theorem 4.5.

I.5 Real-analytic separation details

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with real-analytic separation details. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.5.1 Cylinder functions on the feature space

Test functions are first taken from a cylinder algebra on L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}).

Φ⁡(F)=ψ⁡(⟨F,h1⟩,…,⟨F,hm⟩).\Phi(F)=\psi(\langle F,h_{1}\rangle,\ldots,\langle F,h_{m}\rangle). (169)

The quantity in (169) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This algebra is stable under multiplication and separates points of the feature image.

Derivation.

On a compact subset KRK_{R} of the feature image, consider the algebra of cylinder functions

Φ⁡(F)=ψ⁡(⟨F,h1⟩,…,⟨F,hm⟩),ψ∈Cb​(ℝm).\Phi(F)=\psi(\langle F,h_{1}\rangle,\ldots,\langle F,h_{m}\rangle),\qquad\psi\in C_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{m}). (170)

The algebra contains constants, is closed under multiplication, and separates points of KRK_{R} by the Hilbert-space inner product. Stone–Weierstrass gives density in C⁡(KR)C(K_{R}). This is the concrete algebra used in the monotone-class step rather than an abstract appeal to feature completeness.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.2 Transfer to the quotient

After applying the feature map, equality of all cylinder integrals identifies the quotient pushforward.

∫Φ⁡(T⁡(θ))​𝑑μ=∫Φ⁡(T⁡(θ))​𝑑ν.\int\Phi(T(\theta))d\mu=\int\Phi(T(\theta))d\nu. (171)

The quantity in (171) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The monotone-class step is performed on the standard Borel quotient.

Derivation.

If two quotient measures agree on all functions obtained by pulling back (170), then they agree on C⁡(KR)C(K_{R}) for every compact active quotient stratum. The transfer uses the fact that TT is injective on the quotient by definition of GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}. Hence equality of feature-cylinder integrals implies equality of quotient-active measures on KRK_{R}, and the weighted tail bound then passes the equality to the full quotient.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.3 Compact exhaustion

The input space is exhausted by compact balls and tail error is controlled by H2.

‖g‖L2​(ρX)2≤‖g‖L2​(BR,ρX)2+C​e−c​R2.\|g\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}\leq\|g\|_{L^{2}(B_{R},\rho_{X})}^{2}+Ce^{-cR^{2}}. (172)

The quantity in (172) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This links the classical ridge-density theorem to the unbounded data law.

Derivation.

Let KRK_{R} be the quotient image of {|θ|≤R,|a|≥R−1}\{|\theta|\leq R,|a|\geq R^{-1}\}. H2 gives a sub-Gaussian tail for inputs, and the weighted moment bound gives a polynomial tail for parameters. For feature differences gg,

‖g‖L2​(ρX)2≤‖g‖L2​(BR,ρX)2+C​e−c​R2.\|g\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}\leq\|g\|_{L^{2}(B_{R},\rho_{X})}^{2}+Ce^{-cR^{2}}. (173)

The compact statement therefore extends to the full active quotient by first sending the test-function approximation error to zero and then sending R→∞R\to\infty.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.4 Signed-measure separation

The proof applies to the signed difference of two quotient measures.

η=(qfin)#​μ−(qfin)#​ν.\eta=(q_{\rm fin})_{\#}\mu-(q_{\rm fin})_{\#}\nu. (174)

The quantity in (174) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. If every cylinder integral vanishes, then η=0\eta=0.

Derivation.

Let η\eta be a signed measure whose integrals against the separating algebra vanish. The Hahn decomposition writes η=η+−η−\eta=\eta^{+}-\eta^{-}. If η≠0\eta\neq 0, there is a compact quotient set on which the positive and negative parts differ. By density of the cylinder algebra in C⁡(KR)C(K_{R}), some cylinder test separates the two parts, contradicting the assumed vanishing. Therefore η=0\eta=0 on every KRK_{R}, and the exhaustion gives η=0\eta=0 globally.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.5 Fourier uniqueness

Characteristic functionals on separable Hilbert spaces determine Borel laws.

η^​(h)=0∀h∈L2​(ρX).\widehat{\eta}(h)=0\quad\forall h\in L^{2}(\rho_{X}). (175)

The quantity in (175) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The finite-dimensional projections generate the Borel sigma-field.

Derivation.

On a separable Hilbert space, Borel probability laws are determined by their characteristic functionals on the Hilbert space itself. Applying this to H=L2​(ρX)H=L^{2}(\rho_{X}), equality of

ν^​(h)=∫Hei​⟨h,F⟩H​𝑑ν​(F)\widehat{\nu}(h)=\int_{H}e^{i\langle h,F\rangle_{H}}\,d\nu(F) (176)

for every h∈Hh\in H implies equality of the Borel laws. This is the Sazonov–Minlos uniqueness principle in the present Hilbert setting and proves the implication from Fourier equality to feature-law equality.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.6 Dead-neuron collapse

Mass on the zero-amplitude set is not an identifiable parameter of the function.

T⁡(w,b,0)=0.T(w,b,0)=0. (177)

The quantity in (177) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Only the collapsed total mass can enter the quotient law.

Derivation.

The dead-neuron set D={a=0}D=\{a=0\} maps to the zero feature. If it were not collapsed before quotienting, infinitely many parameter values would represent the same zero element and would create artificial non-identifiability. Collapsing DD first makes the active quotient Hausdorff on compact strata and ensures that the separating algebra in (170) sees exactly the nonzero features.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.7 Regular strata

The rank of the moment map may drop on algebraic strata.

rank⁡D​𝔪M​(θ)=r⁡(θ).\operatorname{rank}D\mathfrak{m}_{M}(\theta)=r(\theta). (178)

The quantity in (178) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The definition of Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}} is therefore stated generically, while Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} is used in rates.

Derivation.

For polynomial and finite-rank analytic maps, the rank of the moment map drops on the common zero set of its maximal minors. That set is algebraic in the finite-dimensional coordinates and therefore is Zariski closed. On its complement the rank is locally constant, the quotient has a smooth stratum, and the dimension count in (157) is stable. Singular strata are handled by compact exhaustion and do not change the generic value of Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.8 Minimal statistic

The quotient pushforward is the statistic that retains exactly the network function.

fμ=fν⟺(qfin)#​μ=(qfin)#​ν.f_{\mu}=f_{\nu}\Longleftrightarrow(q_{\rm fin})_{\#}\mu=(q_{\rm fin})_{\#}\nu. (179)

The quantity in (179) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This equivalence is the content of Theorem 4.5.

Derivation.

Combining the quotient sufficiency of Appendix I.4 with Fourier uniqueness in (176) gives minimality. If a statistic is coarser than the quotient, it identifies two distinct quotient points. The cylinder algebra then separates their feature images, so the statistic cannot determine fμf_{\mu}. If it is finer, it retains realization information that TT discards. The finite-rank quotient is therefore exactly minimal.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the separation step used by the quotient theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.5.9 Monotone-class closure for the analytic separation proof

Let η\eta be the signed difference of two quotient-active laws on a compact stratum KRK_{R}. Suppose ∫Φ​𝑑η=0\int\Phi\,d\eta=0 for every cylinder polynomial generated by (170). The density result gives, for each f∈C⁡(KR)f\in C(K_{R}) and each ε>0\varepsilon>0, a cylinder polynomial PεP_{\varepsilon} with ‖f−Pε‖∞≤ε\|f-P_{\varepsilon}\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon. Hence

|∫f​𝑑η|≤|∫Pε​𝑑η|+ε|η|(KR)=ε​|η|​(KR).\left|\int f\,d\eta\right|\leq\left|\int P_{\varepsilon}\,d\eta\right|+\varepsilon|\eta|(K_{R})=\varepsilon|\eta|(K_{R}). (180)

Sending ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 gives equality against all continuous functions. By the Riesz representation theorem, η=0\eta=0 on KRK_{R}. To pass from continuous functions to Borel indicators one uses the regularity of finite Borel measures on compact metric spaces: every Borel set is approximated from inside by compact sets and from outside by open sets.

The exhaustion step then uses (173) and (44). For a bounded Borel function ff on the full quotient, write f=f​𝟏KR+f​𝟏KRcf=f\mathbf{1}_{K_{R}}+f\mathbf{1}_{K_{R}^{c}}. The first part vanishes by the compact result. The second is bounded by ‖f‖∞​|η|​(KRc)\|f\|_{\infty}|\eta|(K_{R}^{c}), which tends to zero. This proves equality of quotient laws without hiding a topological gap.

Audit consequence.

The compact Stone–Weierstrass step, Borel regularity step, and weighted-tail step are separated explicitly.

I.6 Sparse Hermite and Barron dictionary calculations

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with sparse hermite and barron dictionary calculations. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.6.1 Thresholded Hermite expansion

Under Gaussian input the target is expanded in an orthonormal Hermite basis.

f∗=∑αf^α∗​Hα.f^{\ast}=\sum_{\alpha}\widehat{f}_{\alpha}^{\ast}H_{\alpha}. (181)

The quantity in (181) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The threshold depends on λ\lambda and the coefficient norm.

Derivation.

For ρX=𝒩⁡(0,Id)\rho_{X}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), let (Hα)(H_{\alpha}) be the orthonormal multi-index Hermite basis and write f∗=∑αf^α∗​Hαf^{\ast}=\sum_{\alpha}\widehat{f}_{\alpha}^{\ast}H_{\alpha}. The retained set is

Aλ={α:|f^α∗|>cσ​λ}.A_{\lambda}=\{\alpha:|\widehat{f}_{\alpha}^{\ast}|>c_{\sigma}\lambda\}. (182)

Modes outside AλA_{\lambda} have a first-variation gain below the regularization threshold and are assigned to the sparse tail. This is a coefficient rule, not an initialization rule, and it is therefore target-dependent.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.2 Explicit upper support bound

The active support bound is the number of coefficients above threshold times a ridge multiplicity.

Sup=#⁡{α:|f^α∗|>cλ}​mult⁡(σ).S_{\mathrm{up}}=\#\{\alpha:|\widehat{f}_{\alpha}^{\ast}|>c_{\lambda}\}\,\operatorname{mult}(\sigma). (183)

The quantity in (183) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is an upper bound on S∗S^{\ast}, not a circular definition of it.

Derivation.

If each retained Hermite/Barron mode requires at most mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma) ridge atoms, then

S∗​(λ)≤Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ)=|Aλ|​mult⁡(σ).S^{\ast}(\lambda)\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda)=|A_{\lambda}|\operatorname{mult}(\sigma). (184)

The multiplicity accounts for the fact that a single basis coefficient may be realized by several ridge directions depending on the activation. Quotienting by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} can only identify atoms, so it never increases this upper bound.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.3 Barron tail

Outside Gaussian input the same role is played by the squared tail of the Barron measure.

κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=∫Ω∖ΩS|f^∗​(ω)|2​𝑑ω+Cσ​λ​S.\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Omega_{S}}|\widehat{f}^{\ast}(\omega)|^{2}d\omega+C_{\sigma}\lambda S. (185)

The quantity in (185) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The residual is target-dependent rather than initialization-only.

Derivation.

For non-Gaussian input laws the Hermite sum is replaced by a Barron measure f^∗\widehat{f}^{\ast} on the feature dual. The tail term becomes

κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=∫Ω∖ΩS|f^∗​(ω)|2​𝑑ω+Cσ​λ​S,\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Omega_{S}}|\widehat{f}^{\ast}(\omega)|^{2}d\omega+C_{\sigma}\lambda S, (186)

where ΩS\Omega_{S} contains the SS largest retained modes in decreasing magnitude. The proof uses exactly the same threshold argument; only the counting measure on Hermite indices is replaced by the Barron spectral measure.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.4 Finite-atom target

If the target already has a finite teacher representation, the sparse depth is bounded by the accessible teacher size.

f∗​(x)=∑k=1sak∗​σ​(⟨wk∗,x⟩+bk∗).f^{\ast}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{s}a_{k}^{\ast}\sigma(\langle w_{k}^{\ast},x\rangle+b_{k}^{\ast}). (187)

The quantity in (187) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Regularization can enlarge the active support only within the explicit bound.

Derivation.

If f∗=∑k=1sak∗​σ​(⟨wk∗,⋅⟩+bk∗)f^{\ast}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}a_{k}^{\ast}\sigma(\langle w_{k}^{\ast},\cdot\rangle+b_{k}^{\ast}), then the empirical dictionary already realizes the target with ss active atoms before regularization. Hence

S∗​(λ)≤sS^{\ast}(\lambda)\leq s (188)

for all sufficiently small λ\lambda, up to quotient identifications. The theorem does not assert equality: symmetries or cancellations may reduce the minimal active cardinality.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.5 Accessible initialization

The initialization condition is stated as a named class rather than as an exception.

μ0​(Uk)>0for every neighbourhood ​Uk∋(wk∗,bk∗).\mu_{0}(U_{k})>0\quad\hbox{for every neighbourhood }U_{k}\ni(w_{k}^{\ast},b_{k}^{\ast}). (189)

The quantity in (189) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Within this class the value of S∗S^{\ast} is independent of the particular initialization.

Derivation.

Full-support initialization means that for every retained teacher location θk∗\theta_{k}^{\ast} and every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

μ0​(B⁡(θk∗,ε))>0.\mu_{0}(B(\theta_{k}^{\ast},\varepsilon))>0. (190)

This condition replaces the earlier target-dependent accessibility wording. Under the elliptic Langevin dynamics, positive density propagates to positive hitting probability on finite horizons. Therefore the flow can place active mass near every retained direction if the first variation selects it.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.6 Stationary Euler equation

Active atoms must satisfy the finite-dimensional stationarity equation.

∇θ[δ​ℛ/δ​μ​(μ∞)​(θ)+λ​log⁡(d​μ∞/d​π)​(θ)]=0.\nabla_{\theta}\left[\delta\mathcal{R}/\delta\mu(\mu_{\infty})(\theta)+\lambda\log(d\mu_{\infty}/d\pi)(\theta)\right]=0. (191)

The quantity in (191) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The equation is solved on the active quotient.

Derivation.

On the active stratum, the stationary equation (148) balances the risk gradient against entropy. For a dictionary mode mm, the first-variation coefficient has to exceed the entropy threshold:

|f^m∗|>cσ​λ.|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|>c_{\sigma}\lambda. (192)

If this inequality fails, the entropy displacement is cheaper than maintaining a separate active atom, so the mode belongs to the residual tail. This is the analytic source of the threshold count.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.7 Regularization displacement

Positive λ\lambda displaces active atoms by an amount controlled by the Hessian on the quotient.

‖θkλ−θk0‖≤Cσ​λ.\|\theta_{k}^{\lambda}-\theta_{k}^{0}\|\leq C_{\sigma}\lambda. (193)

The quantity in (193) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This gives the Cσ​λ​SC_{\sigma}\lambda S term in the residual.

Derivation.

Around a nondegenerate active atom, write the regularized Euler equation as G⁡(θ,λ)=0G(\theta,\lambda)=0 with G⁡(θ∗,0)=0G(\theta^{\ast},0)=0 and Dθ​G​(θ∗,0)D_{\theta}G(\theta^{\ast},0) invertible on the quotient chart. The implicit function theorem gives

θ⁡(λ)=θ∗+O⁡(λ).\theta(\lambda)=\theta^{\ast}+O(\lambda). (194)

Thus entropy regularization moves retained atoms by a controlled amount and contributes the displacement term Cσ​λ​SC_{\sigma}\lambda S in (46).

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.8 Non-realizable tails

If the target tail is not summable at the selected depth, the theorem records that loss rather than hiding it.

limS→∞κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=0.\lim_{S\to\infty}\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=0. (195)

The quantity in (195) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The displayed limit is a property of the target class H4.

Derivation.

If limS→∞κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=0\lim_{S\to\infty}\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=0 for each fixed λ\lambda along a vanishing-temperature sequence, then f∗f^{\ast} lies in the closure of the ridge-feature model in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}). H4 assumes precisely the summability needed for this closure statement. If the limit does not vanish, Theorem 5.5 still gives the best thresholded decomposition, but the non-realizable tail remains in Theorem 6.1.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the sparse-residual component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.6.9 Threshold optimization for exponential and polynomial tails

The sparse residual has two pieces: approximation tail and temperature displacement. For exponentially decaying coefficients |f^m∗|≤C​e−c​m|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|\leq Ce^{-cm}, the threshold rule |f^m∗|>cσ​λ|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|>c_{\sigma}\lambda gives Sλ≍log⁡(1/λ)S_{\lambda}\asymp\log(1/\lambda) and

κ⁡(f∗,Sλ,λ)≤C​e−2​c​Sλ+Cσ​λ​Sλ=O⁡(λ2+λ​log⁡(1/λ)).\kappa(f^{\ast},S_{\lambda},\lambda)\leq Ce^{-2cS_{\lambda}}+C_{\sigma}\lambda S_{\lambda}=O(\lambda^{2}+\lambda\log(1/\lambda)). (196)

For polynomial coefficients |f^m∗|≤C​m−β|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|\leq Cm^{-\beta} with β>1\beta>1, the tail is O⁡(S1−2​β)O(S^{1-2\beta}) and the displacement is O⁡(λ​S)O(\lambda S). Balancing gives S≍λ−1/(2β)S\asymp\lambda^{-1/(2\beta)} and

κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)=O⁡(λ(2​β−1)/(2​β)).\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)=O(\lambda^{(2\beta-1)/(2\beta)}). (197)

When the statistical term is included, the relevant balance is instead between S​(log⁡n)2/nS(\log n)^{2}/n and S1−2​βS^{1-2\beta}, producing the rate in Corollary 6.9. The two balances answer different questions: one optimizes the population sparse approximation at temperature λ\lambda, while the other optimizes finite-sample prediction error.

Audit consequence.

The sparse residual is a target-coefficient tail with a concrete optimization, not a symbol depending only on initialization.

I.7 Stationary support and Euler-Lagrange bookkeeping

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with stationary support and euler-lagrange bookkeeping. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.7.1 Active projection

The active component of a measure is obtained by restricting to a≠0a\neq 0 and pushing to the quotient.

μact=(qfin)#​(μ|a≠0).\mu^{\rm act}=(q_{\rm fin})_{\#}(\mu|_{a\neq 0}). (198)

The quantity in (198) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Only this component appears in the dictionary statement.

Derivation.

The active projection is

μact=(qfin)#(μ↾{a≠0}).\mu^{\rm act}=(q_{\mathrm{fin}})_{\#}(\mu\restriction_{\{a\neq 0\}}). (199)

This is a measure on the finite-rank quotient, not a singular component of the full parameter law. The distinction matters because entropy makes μ\mu smooth with respect to π\pi, while μact\mu^{\rm act} records the finite dictionary representation of the induced function after quotienting.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.2 Residual ridge

The zero-amplitude ridge can carry entropy mass without changing the function.

∫|a|2​d​μres=0.\int|a|^{2}d\mu^{\rm res}=0. (200)

The quantity in (200) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The residual measure is therefore harmless for fμf_{\mu}.

Derivation.

The zero-amplitude ridge carries entropy but not prediction energy. Since T⁡(w,b,0)=0T(w,b,0)=0,

‖∫DT⁡(θ)​𝑑μ​(θ)‖L2​(ρX)=0.\left\|\int_{D}T(\theta)d\mu(\theta)\right\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}=0. (201)

Mass on DD can affect normalization and entropy, but it does not change fμf_{\mu}. Therefore the residual ridge is separated from the sparse residual, which is an L2L^{2} approximation tail of the target.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.3 Irreducible atoms

An atom is irreducible when it cannot be split into two active quotient atoms with the same feature contribution.

T⁡(θ)=T⁡(θ1)+T⁡(θ2).T(\theta)=T(\theta_{1})+T(\theta_{2}). (202)

The quantity in (202) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The assumption is used only on the selected sparse dictionary.

Derivation.

An active atom is irreducible when its feature cannot be decomposed as a sum of two distinct active features in the same quotient chart. Formally,

T⁡(θ)≠T⁡(θ1)+T⁡(θ2)T(\theta)\neq T(\theta_{1})+T(\theta_{2}) (203)

for any nontrivial split with both T⁡(θi)≠0T(\theta_{i})\neq 0. Irreducibility prevents the support count from being artificially inflated by splitting a single dictionary direction into two collinear representatives.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.4 Carathéodory bound

Finite-dimensional coefficient truncation converts the support question into a convex-hull question.

m≤dimVλ+1.m\leq\dim V_{\lambda}+1. (204)

The quantity in (204) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The multiplicity factor accounts for the ridge-feature realization of each coefficient.

Derivation.

Let VλV_{\lambda} be the span of retained dictionary modes. Carathéodory’s theorem says that every point in the convex hull of their feature images is represented by at most dimVλ+1\dim V_{\lambda}+1 atoms. Hence

S∗≤dimVλ+1S^{\ast}\leq\dim V_{\lambda}+1 (205)

before using activation-specific multiplicity. The bound is crude but useful: it proves finite support independently of a particular chosen teacher representation.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.5 Entropy perturbation

The entropy term prevents literal atomic stationary laws before projection.

d​μ∞=Z−1​e−λ−1​Vμ∞​d​π.d\mu_{\infty}=Z^{-1}e^{-\lambda^{-1}V_{\mu_{\infty}}}d\pi. (206)

The quantity in (206) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The theorem therefore states atomicity of the active extracted component at scale λ\lambda.

Derivation.

The stationary density has Gibbs form (148). On a local active chart zz, it is proportional to

exp{−λ−1δℛ/δμ(z)}π(dz).\exp\{-\lambda^{-1}\delta\mathcal{R}/\delta\mu(z)\}\,\pi(dz). (207)

As λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0, Laplace concentration occurs near minimizers of the first variation. The quotient support statement records these concentration centers, while the full law remains smooth around them at positive temperature.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.6 Limit selection

When t→∞t\to\infty, every limit point of the trajectory lies in the stationary set.

limt→∞‖∇W2ℱλ​(μt)‖=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla_{W_{2}}\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})\|=0. (208)

The quantity in (208) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The proof uses the energy dissipation identity from the JKO section.

Derivation.

The energy-dissipation identity makes ℱλ​(μt)\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}) decreasing and bounded below. On compact sublevel sets, a Lojasiewicz-type inequality for the analytic finite-rank chart gives

|ℱλ​(μ)−ℱλ​(μ∞)|1−η≤C​‖∇Wℱλ​(μ)‖.|\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu)-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{\infty})|^{1-\eta}\leq C\|\nabla_{W}\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu)\|. (209)

This excludes oscillation among separated stationary points and yields convergence of trajectories to a stationary limit point within the selected quotient stratum.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.7 Support stability

Small perturbations of the target coefficients move the selected atoms continuously on a regular stratum.

‖θk​(f)−θk​(g)‖≤C​‖f−g‖L2​(ρX).\|\theta_{k}(f)-\theta_{k}(g)\|\leq C\|f-g\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}. (210)

The quantity in (210) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The bound justifies the thresholded expansion used in Theorem 5.5.

Derivation.

If the target is perturbed by hh with ‖h‖L2​(ρX)≤ε\|h\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}\leq\varepsilon, then the first-variation coefficients change by at most C​εC\varepsilon on a bounded dictionary chart. Nondegenerate active atoms therefore satisfy

dist⁡([θk​(h)],[θk​(0)])≤C​ε\operatorname{dist}([\theta_{k}(h)],[\theta_{k}(0)])\leq C\varepsilon (211)

by the implicit function theorem. Modes within C​εC\varepsilon of the threshold may enter or exit; modes separated from the threshold are stable.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.8 No teacher-width equality claim

The sparse depth is not asserted to equal the teacher width.

S∗≤Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ).S^{\ast}\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda). (212)

The quantity in (212) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The upper bound is the theorem-level object.

Derivation.

The notation S∗S^{\ast} is an upper-bounded sparse depth, not a claim of equality with the teacher width. The theorem proves

S∗≤Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ),S^{\ast}\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda), (213)

and equality may fail because of quotient symmetries, cancellations, or a more efficient dictionary than the displayed teacher. This avoids conflating the approximation problem with a teacher-student identifiability statement.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the stationary-support component of the sparse theorem in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.7.9 Smooth density versus quotient-active atoms

At positive temperature the stationary law has density (148). A local Laplace expansion around a nondegenerate retained atom θk∗\theta_{k}^{\ast} gives, in a quotient chart zz,

pλ​(z)≈Zk−1​exp⁡[−12​λ​(z−zk)⊤​Hk​(z−zk)],p_{\lambda}(z)\approx Z_{k}^{-1}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2\lambda}(z-z_{k})^{\top}H_{k}(z-z_{k})\right], (214)

where HkH_{k} is the Hessian of the first-variation potential on the transverse active directions. Thus the full law has a Gaussian ridge of width O⁡(λ)O(\sqrt{\lambda}), while its quotient-active center is the atom [θk∗][\theta_{k}^{\ast}]. The theorem records the centers because the network function is determined by the finite dictionary after thresholding. The entropy cloud around a center contributes to regularization displacement and to constants, but not to a new active support count.

This resolves the apparent contradiction between the Euler–Lagrange density and the sparse statement. The density statement lives on parameter space; the sparse statement lives after mapping to ℝd+2/Gσfin\mathbb{R}^{d+2}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} and retaining only the modes above threshold. In the zero-temperature limit the ridges concentrate, but the paper does not need to take that singular limit to state the finite-λ\lambda quotient support bound.

Audit consequence.

The smooth/atomic distinction is operational: density, quotient, Laplace width, and support count are attached to different mathematical objects.

I.8 Statistical covering and intrinsic dimension

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with statistical covering and intrinsic dimension. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.8.1 Truncated parameter ball

The active dictionary is restricted to a radius selected from the tail condition.

Rn=C​log⁡n.R_{n}=C\sqrt{\log n}. (215)

The quantity in (215) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The tail outside the ball contributes a lower-order term under H2.

Derivation.

Choose the truncation radius Rn=C​log⁡nR_{n}=C\sqrt{\log n}. Under the sub-Gaussian input tail and the propagated weighted moment bound,

ℙ⁡(|θ|>Rn)≤n−2\mathbb{P}(|\theta|>R_{n})\leq n^{-2} (216)

for CC large enough at the required moment order. This makes the contribution from outside the ball summable over samples and allows empirical-process bounds to be proved on a compact quotient chart.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.2 Entropy of the quotient class

Covering numbers are computed after quotienting finite-rank orbits.

log⁡𝒩⁡(ε,ℱS,R/Gσfin,L2)≤C​S​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​log⁡(C​R/ε).\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}_{S,R}/G_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}},L^{2})\leq CS(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})\log(CR/\varepsilon). (217)

The quantity in (217) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is the source of the dimension factor in Theorem 6.1.

Derivation.

On the truncated active quotient, one atom lives in dimension deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}: deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} input coordinates, one bias coordinate, one output coordinate, and the quotient reduction by the active orbit. Therefore

log⁡𝒩⁡(ε,ℱS,R,L2​(ρX))≤C​S​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​log⁡C​Rq+1ε.\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}_{S,R},L^{2}(\rho_{X}))\leq CS(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})\log\frac{CR^{q+1}}{\varepsilon}. (218)

The exponent q+1q+1 combines the activation envelope with the output-weight coordinate.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.3 Rademacher chain

The empirical process is bounded by integrating the square root of the entropy.

ℜn(ℱ)≤Cn−1/2∫0diamlog⁡𝒩⁡(ε)dε.\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F})\leq Cn^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{\operatorname{diam}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)}d\varepsilon. (219)

The quantity in (219) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Squaring gives the stated risk rate.

Derivation.

Dudley’s entropy integral gives

ℜn​(ℱS,R)≤Cn​∫0diamlog⁡𝒩⁡(ε,ℱS,R,L2)​𝑑ε.\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{S,R})\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{n}}\int_{0}^{\operatorname{diam}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}_{S,R},L^{2})}\,d\varepsilon. (220)

Substituting (218) yields the statistical scale S⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2/nS(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}/n after localization for the squared loss. The square appears because the final bound is in prediction error, not in linear process deviation.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.4 Intrinsic projection

For multi-index targets the data law is pushed through a rank-kk projection.

x↦Π​x,rank⁡Π=k.x\mapsto\Pi x,\qquad\operatorname{rank}\Pi=k. (221)

The quantity in (221) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The statistical dimension becomes k+2−Dorb∗k+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} while the particle state remains ambient.

Derivation.

If f∗​(x)=g​(Π​x)f^{\ast}(x)=g(\Pi x) with rank⁡Π=k\operatorname{rank}\Pi=k, the covering can be built in the projected input coordinate u=Π​xu=\Pi x. The feature family restricted to the target class depends on kk active input coordinates instead of dd. Thus

deff​(f∗,ρX)=kd_{\mathrm{eff}}(f^{\ast},\rho_{X})=k (222)

in the statistical term. The particle dynamics still evolves in ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2}, so this reduction belongs to estimation and approximation, not to propagation of chaos.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.5 Logarithmic loss

The extra logarithm records the truncation radius and the entropy integral.

S⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2n.\frac{S(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}}{n}. (223)

The quantity in (223) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The exponent is kept explicit rather than hidden in a constant.

Derivation.

The first logarithm in the statistical rate is the usual entropy integral. The second comes from the truncation radius. Since Rn2≍log⁡nR_{n}^{2}\asymp\log n and the envelope scales as Rnq+1R_{n}^{q+1},

log⁡(C​Rnq+1/ε)=log⁡(C/ε)+q+12​log⁡log⁡n.\log(CR_{n}^{q+1}/\varepsilon)=\log(C/\varepsilon)+\frac{q+1}{2}\log\log n. (224)

After localization, this contributes an additional logarithmic factor in the displayed high-probability-to-expectation conversion.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.6 Bounded activations

If σ\sigma is bounded, the truncation radius can be removed from the envelope.

|σ⁡(z)|≤Cσ.|\sigma(z)|\leq C_{\sigma}. (225)

The quantity in (225) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The paper keeps the larger expression because it covers the polynomial-growth case.

Derivation.

If σ\sigma is bounded, the polynomial envelope is absent. The covering number becomes

log⁡𝒩⁡(ε,ℱS,R,L2​(ρX))≤C​S​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​log⁡(C​R/ε),\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}_{S,R},L^{2}(\rho_{X}))\leq CS(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})\log(CR/\varepsilon), (226)

and the extra RqR^{q} factor is removed. Consequently the statistical rate improves to S⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)​log⁡n/nS(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})\log n/n up to the remaining localization logarithm.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.7 Output-weight control

The quotient does not remove the need to bound output amplitudes.

∑k=1S|ak|2≤BS.\sum_{k=1}^{S}|a_{k}|^{2}\leq B_{S}. (227)

The quantity in (227) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This bound is inherited from the sparse target and the regularized stationary equation.

Derivation.

H4 normalizes retained dictionary atoms so that the output coefficients obey

∑k=1S|ak|2≤B​S\sum_{k=1}^{S}|a_{k}|^{2}\leq BS (228)

for a constant BB determined by the Barron/Hermite norm of the target and the threshold. This prevents the covering entropy from hiding an additional unbounded amplitude parameter and is the reason the statistical term is linear in S∗S^{\ast}.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.8 Sample and particle independence

Statistical and particle randomness are generated on product spaces.

𝔼𝒟,B[⋅]=𝔼𝒟𝔼B[⋅|𝒟].\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D},B}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{B}[\cdot|\mathcal{D}]. (229)

The quantity in (229) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This independence is used in the cross-term bookkeeping.

Derivation.

The data sample and the particle Brownian motions are drawn on a product probability space. Conditional on the trained mean-field law, the empirical process fluctuation is centered with respect to the sample, while the propagation fluctuation is centered with respect to Brownian randomness. This product structure is the probabilistic input behind the zero cross term in (95); no exchangeability between samples and particles is assumed.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the statistical component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.8.9 Dudley integral evaluated at the truncated radius

Insert (218) into Dudley’s integral. With dQ=S⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)d_{Q}=S(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}) and An=C​Rnq+1A_{n}=CR_{n}^{q+1},

ℜn​(ℱS,Rn)≤Cn​∫0AndQ​log⁡(An/ε)​𝑑ε.\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{S,R_{n}})\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{n}}\int_{0}^{A_{n}}\sqrt{d_{Q}\log(A_{n}/\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon. (230)

The change of variables u=ε/Anu=\varepsilon/A_{n} gives

∫0Anlog⁡(An/ε)​𝑑ε=An​∫01log⁡(1/u)​𝑑u=C​An.\int_{0}^{A_{n}}\sqrt{\log(A_{n}/\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon=A_{n}\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\log(1/u)}\,du=CA_{n}. (231)

Localization for squared loss replaces An2A_{n}^{2} by the local radius and yields the familiar dQ​log⁡n/nd_{Q}\log n/n scale. The remaining logarithm comes from Rn2≍log⁡nR_{n}^{2}\asymp\log n and from the high-probability union over the localized shells. Hence the final statistical term is

Estat​(n)≤C​S⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2n.E_{\rm stat}(n)\leq C\frac{S(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}}{n}. (232)

For bounded activations one removes the RnqR_{n}^{q} part of AnA_{n}, which drops one truncation logarithm as recorded in Appendix I.8.

Audit consequence.

The statistical factor is derived from a displayed entropy integral, not merely named.

I.9 Four-source error decomposition

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with four-source error decomposition. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.9.1 Definition of the four increments

Write the trained predictor as a telescoping sum around the population stationary dictionary.

Δ=Δstat+Δopt+Δpoc+Δsparse.\Delta=\Delta_{\rm stat}+\Delta_{\rm opt}+\Delta_{\rm poc}+\Delta_{\rm sparse}. (233)

The quantity in (233) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The increments are elements of L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}).

Derivation.

The comparison path writes

Δ=fμTN−f∗=Δstat+Δopt+Δpoc+Δsparse.\Delta=f_{\mu_{T}^{N}}-f^{\ast}=\Delta_{\rm stat}+\Delta_{\rm opt}+\Delta_{\rm poc}+\Delta_{\rm sparse}. (234)

The order is fixed: sample projection, finite-time optimization, particle approximation, and dictionary tail. Once this order is fixed, the square expansion has four diagonal terms and six cross terms. The theorem names the diagonal terms and puts all controlled cross terms into the scalar remainder.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.2 Particle-statistical cross term

Particle Brownian motions are conditionally centered given the data sample.

𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δstat⟩=0.\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm stat}\rangle=0. (235)

The quantity in (235) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is the cleanest exact cancellation in Lemma 6.2.

Derivation.

The particle-statistical product satisfies

𝔼​⟨Δpoc,Δstat⟩L2​(ρX)=0.\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm stat}\rangle_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}=0. (236)

Condition on the data sample and on the limiting mean-field trajectory. The propagation fluctuation is centered with respect to the Brownian coupling. Then condition on the particle randomness; the statistical fluctuation is centered with respect to the sample. Fubini on the product probability space gives the cancellation.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.3 Particle-sparse cross term

The sparse residual is deterministic at fixed target and population law.

𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δsparse⟩=0.\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle=0. (237)

The quantity in (237) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The equality follows from the same centering of the coupled particle fluctuation.

Derivation.

The sparse residual is deterministic once (σ,ρ,f∗,λ)(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda) and the threshold rule are fixed. The propagation fluctuation is centered by the synchronous coupling. Hence

𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δsparse⟩=⟨𝔼​Δpoc,Δsparse⟩=0.\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle=\langle\mathbb{E}\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle=0. (238)

This is the second of the two exact cancellations listed in Lemma 6.2.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.4 Particle-optimization cross term
