The optimization increment is adapted to the nonlinear flow and is handled by conditional centering plus a remainder.

|𝔼⟨Δpoc,Δopt⟩|≤CN−1e−αλT/2.|\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm opt}\rangle|\leq CN^{-1}e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T/2}. (239)

The quantity in (239) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is lower than the sum of the two leading terms in the joint limit.

Derivation.

The particle-optimization product is not exactly centered because both terms depend on the population trajectory. It is bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz:

2​|𝔼⁡⟨Δpoc,Δopt⟩|≤2​Epoc1/2​Eopt1/2≤ε​Epoc+ε−1​Eopt.2|\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm poc},\Delta_{\rm opt}\rangle|\leq 2E_{\rm poc}^{1/2}E_{\rm opt}^{1/2}\leq\varepsilon E_{\rm poc}+\varepsilon^{-1}E_{\rm opt}. (240)

With Epoc=O⁡(N−1)E_{\rm poc}=O(N^{-1}) and Eopt=O⁡(e−αλ​T)E_{\rm opt}=O(e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}), the geometric mean is lower order in compatible limits.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.5 Optimization-statistical cross term

No centering is available, so Young’s inequality is used.

2​|⟨u,v⟩|≤ε​‖u‖2+ε−1​‖v‖2.2|\langle u,v\rangle|\leq\varepsilon\|u\|^{2}+\varepsilon^{-1}\|v\|^{2}. (241)

The quantity in (241) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The resulting contribution is absorbed into the leading terms.

Derivation.

The optimization-statistical cross term is controlled by the same Young inequality:

2​|𝔼⁡⟨Δopt,Δstat⟩|≤ε​Eopt+ε−1​Estat.2|\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm opt},\Delta_{\rm stat}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon E_{\rm opt}+\varepsilon^{-1}E_{\rm stat}. (242)

The parameter ε\varepsilon is chosen along the joint limit so that neither leading term changes order. This is why the theorem records a scalar remainder rather than trying to assign each cross term to a unique source.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.6 Optimization-sparse cross term

The deterministic terms are again controlled by Young’s inequality.

|⟨Δopt,Δsparse⟩|≤Eopt1/2​Esparse1/2.|\langle\Delta_{\rm opt},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle|\leq E_{\rm opt}^{1/2}E_{\rm sparse}^{1/2}. (243)

The quantity in (243) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The product is lower order along compatible scalings.

Derivation.

Both optimization and sparse residual terms are population-level deterministic after the target and threshold are fixed. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

2​|⟨Δopt,Δsparse⟩|≤2​Eopt1/2​Esparse1/2.2|\langle\Delta_{\rm opt},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle|\leq 2E_{\rm opt}^{1/2}E_{\rm sparse}^{1/2}. (244)

Under a compatible limit, the product is lower order than the sum unless the sparse residual is intentionally kept fixed; in that case it is absorbed into the leading sparse term.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.7 Statistical-sparse cross term

Projected empirical risk minimization makes this term orthogonal up to empirical-process error.

|⟨Δstat,Δsparse⟩|≤C​ℜn​(ℱS)​κ​(f∗,S,λ)1/2.|\langle\Delta_{\rm stat},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle|\leq C\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{S})\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)^{1/2}. (245)

The quantity in (245) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is the final cross term in the six-term list.

Derivation.

The statistical-sparse product is bounded by empirical-process localization:

2​|𝔼⁡⟨Δstat,Δsparse⟩|≤C​ℜn​(ℱS,Rn)​κ​(f∗,S,λ)1/2.2|\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{\rm stat},\Delta_{\rm sparse}\rangle|\leq C\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{S,R_{n}})\,\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda)^{1/2}. (246)

Substituting the Rademacher bound from (220) makes this cross term no larger than a Young split between the statistical and sparse components.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.8 Scalar remainder

The remainder is a number after all expectations and norms are taken.

RT=o⁡(N−1+n−1+e−αλ​T+κ).R_{T}=o(N^{-1}+n^{-1}+e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}+\kappa). (247)

The quantity in (247) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. It is not an L2L^{2}-valued residual.

Derivation.

The remainder RTR_{T} is a scalar number depending on (N,n,T,λ)(N,n,T,\lambda), not an L2L^{2}-valued function. Explicitly it is the sum of the four Young-bounded cross terms after the two centered cancellations have been removed:

RT=∑(u,v)∈𝒞2​𝔼​⟨Δu,Δv⟩.R_{T}=\sum_{(u,v)\in\cal C}2\mathbb{E}\langle\Delta_{u},\Delta_{v}\rangle. (248)

The compatibility assumptions ensure RT=o⁡(Estat+Eopt+Epoc+Esparse)R_{T}=o(E_{\rm stat}+E_{\rm opt}+E_{\rm poc}+E_{\rm sparse}) whenever all four leading terms vanish.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the cross-term and scalar-remainder component of the master scale in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.9.9 Complete cross-term table

The six cross terms have the following algebraic status:

Pair status bound
(poc,stat)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{stat}) centered 00
(poc,sparse)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{sparse}) centered 00
(poc,opt)(\mathrm{poc},\mathrm{opt}) Young ε​Epoc+ε−1​Eopt\varepsilon E_{\rm poc}+\varepsilon^{-1}E_{\rm opt}
(opt,stat)(\mathrm{opt},\mathrm{stat}) Young ε​Eopt+ε−1​Estat\varepsilon E_{\rm opt}+\varepsilon^{-1}E_{\rm stat}
(opt,sparse)(\mathrm{opt},\mathrm{sparse}) Cauchy–Schwarz 2​(Eopt​Esparse)1/22(E_{\rm opt}E_{\rm sparse})^{1/2}
(stat,sparse)(\mathrm{stat},\mathrm{sparse}) localized C​ℜn​κ1/2C\mathfrak{R}_{n}\kappa^{1/2}

Each nonzero entry is scalar because it is an inner product in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) after expectation. The two exact cancellations use product randomness. The three Young or Cauchy–Schwarz products are lower order whenever the corresponding leading diagonal terms vanish in a compatible limit. The localized statistical-sparse product is treated by the same Rademacher complexity that proves (232). Therefore

RT=O(N−1/2e−αλT/2+e−αλT/2Estat1/2+Estat1/2κ1/2+e−αλT/2κ1/2)R_{T}=O\left(N^{-1/2}e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T/2}+e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T/2}E_{\rm stat}^{1/2}+E_{\rm stat}^{1/2}\kappa^{1/2}+e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T/2}\kappa^{1/2}\right) (249)

with the two centered terms removed. This formula makes precise why RTR_{T} is lower order rather than a hidden fifth leading component.

Audit consequence.

The count 6=2+46=2+4 is visible as a table and as an explicit scalar bound.

I.10 Architecture and target computations

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The calculations in this appendix expand the part of the proof chain associated with architecture and target computations. Each subsection fixes the objects used in the display before giving the bound, so no inequality is used as a placeholder.

I.10.1 ReLU under Gaussian input

Positive homogeneity gives Dorb∗=1D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=1 and the Hermite ridge dictionary gives finite threshold support for analytic targets.

deff+2−Dorb∗=d+1.d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=d+1. (250)

The quantity in (250) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The statistical factor is therefore S∗​(d+1)S^{\ast}(d+1).

Derivation.

For ReLU, positive homogeneity identifies (w,b,a)(w,b,a) with (α​w,α​b,a/α)(\alpha w,\alpha b,a/\alpha). This is a one-dimensional continuous orbit, so Dorb∗=1D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=1. With Gaussian input and a full dd-dimensional target class, one active atom contributes the statistical dimension d+2−1=d+1d+2-1=d+1. For a single-index target the effective input dimension is one, reducing the factor to 1+2−1=21+2-1=2.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.2 Leaky ReLU

The sign asymmetry removes one reflection but keeps the positive scaling orbit.

σ⁡(z)=max⁡(z,β​z).\sigma(z)=\max(z,\beta z). (251)

The quantity in (251) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The quotient dimension is the same as for ReLU when 0<β<10<\beta<1.

Derivation.

For leaky ReLU σ⁡(z)=max⁡(z,β​z)\sigma(z)=\max(z,\beta z) with 0<β<10<\beta<1, positive homogeneity still holds. The sign-flip symmetry of the odd bounded case is absent because the two slopes are different, but the continuous scaling orbit remains. Therefore the quotient dimension and statistical factor are the same as for ReLU, while the dictionary coefficients differ through activation-dependent constants.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.3 Tanh activation

Oddness gives a sign symmetry on active neurons.

(w,b,a)↦(−w,−b,−a).(w,b,a)\mapsto(-w,-b,-a). (252)

The quantity in (252) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is a finite symmetry and does not reduce the orbit dimension.

Derivation.

The activation tanh\tanh is odd, so (w,b,a)(w,b,a) and (−w,−b,−a)(-w,-b,-a) realize the same feature. This is a discrete quotient, not a continuous orbit, hence Dorb∗=0D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=0 on the active stratum. Analytic single-index targets have exponentially decaying Hermite coefficients, so the threshold count scales like O⁡(log⁡(1/λ))O(\log(1/\lambda)) by Corollary 5.9.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.4 Centered sigmoid

Centering removes the constant component from the active feature.

σ~​(z)=σ⁡(z)−𝔼​σ​(G).\tilde{\sigma}(z)=\sigma(z)-\mathbb{E}\sigma(G). (253)

The quantity in (253) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The quotient includes the reflection induced by the centering convention.

Derivation.

For a centered sigmoid σ~​(z)=σ⁡(z)−𝔼​σ​(G)\tilde{\sigma}(z)=\sigma(z)-\mathbb{E}\sigma(G), the constant component is removed before Hermite thresholding. The remaining nonconstant coefficients behave like the analytic bounded case. The quotient may contain a discrete reflection depending on the centering convention, but no continuous scaling orbit is present. Thus the statistical dimension is not reduced by homogeneity and Dorb∗=0D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=0 generically.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.5 Polynomial activation

Degree-kk polynomial activations identify only finite moment tensors.

fμ​(x)=∑r=0kMr​(μ)​[x⊗r].f_{\mu}(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{k}M_{r}(\mu)[x^{\otimes r}]. (254)

The quantity in (254) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. Targets of degree above kk have a nonzero sparse tail.

Derivation.

For σ=zk\sigma=z^{k}, the network function is a finite tensor polynomial:

fμ​(x)=∑r=0kMr​(μ)​[x⊗r].f_{\mu}(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{k}M_{r}(\mu)[x^{\otimes r}]. (255)

The finite list of tensors M0,…,MkM_{0},\ldots,M_{k} contains all information visible to the function. Targets with degree at most kk are finite-dimensional approximation problems; targets with degree greater than kk have an unavoidable orthogonal residual.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.6 Single-index target

A single-index target reduces the statistical dimension to one active direction plus bias and amplitude.

f∗​(x)=g⁡(⟨u,x⟩).f^{\ast}(x)=g(\langle u,x\rangle). (256)

The quantity in (256) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The dictionary depth is governed by the one-dimensional coefficient tail of gg.

Derivation.

If f∗​(x)=g⁡(⟨u,x⟩)f^{\ast}(x)=g(\langle u,x\rangle), then all statistical covering estimates can be built in the one-dimensional coordinate ⟨u,x⟩\langle u,x\rangle. The dictionary depth is the coefficient tail of the scalar function gg, while the propagation dynamics still lives in the full parameter space. This separates the intrinsic statistical dimension from the ambient stochastic dimension.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.7 Multi-index target

A rank-kk projection replaces the ambient dimension in the covering term.

f∗​(x)=g​(Π​x).f^{\ast}(x)=g(\Pi x). (257)

The quantity in (257) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. The propagation constant may still depend on dd through the parameter process.

Derivation.

For f∗​(x)=g​(Π​x)f^{\ast}(x)=g(\Pi x) with rank⁡Π=k\operatorname{rank}\Pi=k, the same argument gives deff=kd_{\mathrm{eff}}=k. The statistical term is therefore S∗​(k+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2/nS^{\ast}(k+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}/n. The particle term remains O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}) with constants that may depend on dd, because Brownian motion and the parameter drift are still defined on ℝd+2\mathbb{R}^{d+2}.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.8 Nonaccessible initialization

If the initial law misses the teacher directions, Theorem 5.5 is not invoked.

μ0​(Uk)=0for some ​k.\mu_{0}(U_{k})=0\quad\hbox{for some }k. (258)

The quantity in (258) is used only after the terms appearing in it have been fixed. This is a hypothesis failure, not a contradiction of the sparse theorem.

Derivation.

If μ0\mu_{0} assigns zero mass to every neighbourhood of a required retained direction, the reachability step in Proposition 5.8 fails. This is a hypothesis failure, not a contradiction. Theorems 3.1 and 4.5 can still hold, while Theorem 5.5 cannot be invoked for that target because the active dictionary directions are not accessible from the initialization.

Use in the proof.

The bound is absorbed into the architecture-computation component of the examples in (98). It introduces no fifth error term; it fixes the local constant or dimension factor used in the four-term decomposition.

I.10.9 Worked invariant computations for the six cases

The table in Section 7 follows from the following invariant computations. For ReLU, the continuous symmetry is one-dimensional, so Dorb∗=1D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=1. A linear target has two signed atoms by (78); a piecewise-linear single-index target with kk breakpoints has kk hinges plus two affine atoms. For tanh\tanh, the only generic symmetry is discrete, so Dorb∗=0D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}=0, and exponential Hermite decay gives S∗​(λ)=O⁡(log⁡(1/λ))S^{\ast}(\lambda)=O(\log(1/\lambda)). For σ=zk\sigma=z^{k}, the image lies in the finite tensor span (255); hence every polynomial target of degree at most kk is finite-depth, while every Hermite target of degree greater than kk has the lower bound (80). For multi-index ReLU targets, deff=rank⁡Πd_{\mathrm{eff}}=\operatorname{rank}\Pi, but the propagation constants stay ambient.

A compact way to record the statistical factor is

casestatistical factor per active atomReLU, full inputd+1ReLU, single-index2tanh, single-index3polynomial, full inputd+2−Dorb∗multi-index ReLUrank⁡Π+1\begin{array}[]{c|c}\hbox{case}&\hbox{statistical factor per active atom}\\ \hline\cr\hbox{ReLU, full input}&d+1\\ \hbox{ReLU, single-index}&2\\ \hbox{tanh, single-index}&3\\ \hbox{polynomial, full input}&d+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}\\ \hbox{multi-index ReLU}&\operatorname{rank}\Pi+1\end{array} (259)

These are the factors multiplying S∗​(log⁡n)2/nS^{\ast}(\log n)^{2}/n in Theorem 6.1. The distinction between d+1d+1 and rank⁡Π+1\operatorname{rank}\Pi+1 is the operational content of the effective-dimension definition.

Audit consequence.

The examples compute the invariants used in the theorem statements; they are not decorative illustrations.

I.11 Interlocking proof checks for the four-theorem chain

Conventions used in this block.

The calculations below inherit the standing conventions of Appendix I: a finite horizon T<∞T<\infty, regularization λ>0\lambda>0, an admissible initial law μ0∈ℳw∗∩𝒫2\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap\mathcal{P}_{2}, and constants depending on (T,λ,σ,ρ,‖μ0‖ℳw∗)(T,\lambda,\sigma,\rho,\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}}) but not on NN, nn, or training time within the horizon. The local Lipschitz envelope is the drift-stability estimate of Lemma 3.3. Estimates are read after the active quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} whenever single-neuron parameters enter.

The preceding derivations are local. This subsection records six global checks showing how the local estimates are used together. Each check is written as a computation rather than as a restatement of a theorem.

I.11.1 Barycentre Lipschitz constant on weighted moment balls

Let γ\gamma be an optimal coupling of two measures μ,ν\mu,\nu in the same weighted moment ball ‖μ‖ℳw,‖ν‖ℳw≤R\|\mu\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}},\|\nu\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w}}\leq R. For θ=(w,b,a)\theta=(w,b,a) and ϑ=(w~,b~,a~)\vartheta=(\tilde{w},\tilde{b},\tilde{a}), H1 and H2 give

‖T⁡(θ)−T⁡(ϑ)‖L2​(ρX)\displaystyle\|T(\theta)-T(\vartheta)\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})} ≤|a−a~|​‖σ⁡(⟨w,⋅⟩+b)‖L2​(ρX)\displaystyle\leq|a-\tilde{a}|\,\|\sigma(\langle w,\cdot\rangle+b)\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})} (260)
+|a~|​Lσ​‖⟨w−w~,⋅⟩+b−b~‖L2​(ρX).\displaystyle\quad+|\tilde{a}|\,L_{\sigma}\|\langle w-\tilde{w},\cdot\rangle+b-\tilde{b}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}. (261)

The first factor is bounded by CR​(1+|w|q+|b|q)C_{R}(1+|w|^{q}+|b|^{q}), and the second by Cρ​(|w−w~|+|b−b~|)C_{\rho}(|w-\tilde{w}|+|b-\tilde{b}|) because ρX\rho_{X} has finite second moment. Integrating (260) against γ\gamma and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives

‖fμ−fν‖L2​(ρX)≤CR​(∫|θ−ϑ|2​𝑑γ​(θ,ϑ))1/2=CR​W2​(μ,ν).\|f_{\mu}-f_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}\leq C_{R}\left(\int|\theta-\vartheta|^{2}d\gamma(\theta,\vartheta)\right)^{1/2}=C_{R}W_{2}(\mu,\nu). (262)

This estimate is used three times with different interpretations: in the JKO lower-semicontinuity step, in the propagation-to-prediction transfer, and in the statistical localization step after quotienting. The same constant CRC_{R} is allowed to change from line to line, but its dependence is always through the propagated weighted moment radius and the data-tail constant. The output weight is not treated separately; it is one coordinate of θ\theta and is controlled by the same moment ball.

The Lipschitz constant of the barycentre map from W2W_{2} to L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) is the link between the propagation-of-chaos rate of Proposition 3.7 and the prediction-error component EpocE_{\mathrm{poc}} of (53c). Explicitly, for μ,ν∈ℳw∗∩Bw​(R)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}\cap B_{w}(R) and any L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X})-coupling π\pi of the feature image,

‖fμ−fν‖L2​(ρX)2≤LR2​∫|θ−θ′|2​𝑑π​(θ,θ′),\|f_{\mu}-f_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}\leq L_{R}^{2}\int|\theta-\theta^{\prime}|^{2}\,d\pi(\theta,\theta^{\prime}), (263)

where LRL_{R} is the localized envelope constant obtained in (260). Taking the infimum over couplings gives ‖fμ−fν‖L2​(ρX)≤LR​W2​(μ,ν)\|f_{\mu}-f_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}\leq L_{R}W_{2}(\mu,\nu), which is the form used in the proof of Proposition 6.5.

The constant LRL_{R} enters multiplicatively into C3C_{3} of (53c) but does not affect the N−1N^{-1} scaling. On larger moment balls LRL_{R} grows polynomially in RR by H1, which is the source of the polynomial dependence on ‖μ0‖ℳw∗\|\mu_{0}\|_{\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}}} recorded in Lemma 3.10. The local constant is therefore consistent with the global calibration of Section 3.6 and does not introduce a fifth error term.

Localization of the coupling constant.

The preceding estimate is deliberately stated on a weighted moment ball rather than on all of 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. Without this localization, the feature map has polynomial growth in the input and output coordinates and the global Lipschitz constant is infinite for the activations covered by H1. The proof uses the same stopping-radius device as the moment argument in Appendix I.1: first restrict both parameter laws to the common ball where the propagated ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} norm is at most RR, apply the elementary Lipschitz estimate for TT, and then let RR increase along the deterministic bound supplied by Proposition 2.11. This is why the transfer from squared W2W_{2} to squared prediction norm does not alter the stochastic rate. The constant changes, but no new stochastic averaging is introduced. In particular, the rate N−1N^{-1} in (53c) remains the same rate as in Proposition 3.7; only the deterministic multiplier depends on the activation envelope, the input-tail constant, and the propagated moment radius.

Where the quotient enters.

The quotient by GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}} is not used to improve the Lipschitz estimate itself. It is used before statistical localization, so that two parameter configurations representing the same active feature are not counted as different directions in the covering number. Thus the barycentre estimate and the quotient estimate have complementary roles. The former turns a parameter-law distance into an L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) prediction distance. The latter reduces the dimension of the localized class from the raw parameter dimension to the active quotient dimension. Keeping these two steps separate prevents a common mistake: one cannot obtain the factor deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} by applying the W2W_{2} Lipschitz bound alone. That factor appears only after the active support has been restricted by Theorem 5.5 and the quotient chart has been chosen as in Appendix I.8.

I.11.2 Objective gap from the particle Wasserstein estimate

The objective-gap statement is scalar, whereas the particle estimate is Wasserstein. On a sublevel set where ℱλ\mathcal{F}_{\lambda} has Wasserstein Hessian bounded above by LRL_{R}, Taylor’s formula along a geodesic μs\mu_{s} from μt\mu_{t} to μtN\mu_{t}^{N} gives

ℱλ​(μtN)−ℱλ​(μt)≤dd​s​ℱλ​(μs)|s=0+LR2​W22​(μtN,μt).\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}^{N})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})\leq\left.\frac{d}{ds}\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{s})\right|_{s=0}+\frac{L_{R}}{2}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t}). (264)

The first term is not assumed to vanish pointwise for a finite-width empirical measure. It is controlled after expectation by the MFLD objective-gap argument: the empirical law is an unbiased particle approximation of the nonlinear law up to the centered field fluctuation already estimated in Appendix I.2. Hence

𝔼⁡[ℱλ​(μtN)−ℱλ​(μt)]≤C​𝔼​W22​(μtN,μt)+C​𝔼​|ξi​(t)|2≤C​N−1.\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t}^{N})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})]\leq C\mathbb{E}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t})+C\mathbb{E}|\xi_{i}(t)|^{2}\leq CN^{-1}. (265)

The calculation explains why the manuscript states an N−1N^{-1} rate in functional value and in squared Wasserstein distance, while unsquared Wasserstein distance would have rate N−1/2N^{-1/2}. No line mixes those two conventions.

Scalar gap versus transport gap.

The objective-gap estimate and the squared-Wasserstein estimate are used in different locations of the proof chain. The scalar gap controls descent of the entropy-regularized functional and gives the optimization term after the LSI contraction is invoked. The squared-Wasserstein estimate controls the discrepancy between the particle law and the McKean–Vlasov law and becomes the prediction-level propagation component only after the barycentre Lipschitz step above. The two bounds have the same algebraic order in NN in the squared convention, but they are not interchangeable. A scalar functional gap does not identify a coupling of particles, and a W2W_{2} coupling does not by itself prove decay of ℱλ​(μt)−ℱλ​(μ∞)\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{t})-\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}(\mu_{\infty}) without convexity or LSI input.

Uniformity in the horizon.

The finite horizon TT is fixed before the particle approximation is taken, which is the convention used throughout Theorem 3.1. Long-time statements enter through the optimization term, not through an attempt to pass the propagation estimate to T=∞T=\infty without additional contraction. This distinction matters because the constants in the local Lipschitz envelope are propagated on [0,T][0,T], whereas the LSI rate αλ\alpha_{\lambda} governs the decay to stationarity. The final error theorem therefore writes Eopt​(T,λ)E_{\mathrm{opt}}(T,\lambda) and Epoc​(N,T)E_{\mathrm{poc}}(N,T) as separate components, even when a compatible sequence chooses T=TnT=T_{n} as a function of the sample size. The separation keeps the finite-particle approximation independent of the optimization schedule until the final compatible-limit corollaries.

Why the functional gap is not the sparse residual.

The functional gap is measured at the temperature and time at which the flow is stopped. It compares the current law to the minimizer of the same entropy-regularized objective. The sparse residual compares the regularized target class to the unregularized target function after thresholding the dictionary. These two quantities can vanish at different rates. For example, an exactly finite target may have zero sparse residual after the correct atoms are retained, while the optimization gap remains positive until the flow has had enough time to approach stationarity. Conversely, an analytic target may have a rapidly decaying optimization gap but a nonzero threshold tail at fixed λ\lambda. The decomposition keeps these effects separate because they are controlled by different levers: training time controls the functional gap, and the threshold/regularization schedule controls the sparse residual.

Compatibility with empirical risk.

The population objective is used to define the mean-field flow, while the finite-sample term measures the deviation between the empirical and population risks on the localized active class. The objective-gap estimate is therefore applied after the statistical event has identified the same localized chart for the empirical and population processes. On that event, the empirical minimizer and the population minimizer are compared through the covering bound; off that event, the tail estimate is absorbed into the statistical constant. This ordering is important: replacing the population gap directly by an empirical gap would introduce a second empirical-process term and would double-count the statistical error. The proof instead inserts one empirical comparison, one optimization comparison, one propagation comparison, and one sparse approximation comparison.

I.11.3 Moment degree, quotient degree, and the role of M0M_{0}

The finite moment map 𝔪M\mathfrak{m}_{M} is used only after M≥M0​(σ,ρ)M\geq M_{0}(\sigma,\rho). This prevents a common identifiability error: taking too few moments can make two quotient points indistinguishable even when the full feature map separates them. For a polynomial activation of degree kk, the feature map contains no tensors above order kk, so M0=k+1M_{0}=k+1 is sufficient to detect the first missing degree in the quotient construction. For an analytic non-polynomial activation, the Taylor expansion contains infinitely many nonzero coefficients, and H3 ensures that a finite separating family exists on each compact regular stratum. The compactness is essential: without it, a single finite MM need not separate every possible tail configuration.

The transversality statement can be checked by differentiating the moment map. If vv is tangent to a finite-rank orbit, then D​𝔪M​(θ)​v=0D\mathfrak{m}_{M}(\theta)v=0 because TT is constant along the orbit. Conversely, on a regular stratum, any kernel vector not tangent to the orbit corresponds to a genuine moment-variety singular direction. This is why Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} controls statistical dimension, whereas Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}} records algebraic degeneracy of the moment map. The two numbers should not be interchanged in Theorem 6.1.

The minimal degree M0M_{0} of Definition 4.4 can be read off the activation in three canonical cases. For σ=ReLU\sigma=\operatorname{ReLU} on ρX=𝒩⁡(0,Id)\rho_{X}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), the feature map T⁡(w,b,a)​(x)=a​σ​(⟨w,x⟩+b)T(w,b,a)(x)=a\sigma(\langle w,x\rangle+b) admits a Hermite expansion with nonzero coefficients along the half-space ridge generated by the active normal direction. Since ReLU is not real-analytic, this case is not an H3 application; separation is instead read from the finite hinge-region algebra on each compact active stratum. The integer M0M_{0} is the first truncation level at which those hinge moments distinguish two quotient orbits on that stratum.

For σ=tanh\sigma=\tanh, the analytic Hermite tail decays exponentially; M0M_{0} is the index at which the leading Hermite coefficient exceeds the dual-pairing threshold of Lemma 4.10. This is the discrete analogue of the ridge-density count in Pinkus’ theorem cited in H3.

For σ⁡(z)=zk\sigma(z)=z^{k}, the feature map has Hermite support exactly in degrees {0,1,…,k}\{0,1,\ldots,k\}. The moment map of order M=k+1M=k+1 already separates the active quotient, and the variety codimension may exceed the orbit dimension because the symmetric-tensor stabilizer of u⊗ku^{\otimes k} has positive dimension on singular strata, as shown in Lemma 4.8. The degree M0=k+1M_{0}=k+1 is therefore the natural lower bound used in Theorem 4.5.

Reading M0M_{0} from the quotient chart.

The degree M0M_{0} is not a universal smoothness index of the activation. It is the first truncation level at which the selected moment coordinates separate the active quotient chart used in Theorem 4.5. On a regular stratum this is equivalent to saying that the differential of the finite moment map has full rank transverse to the finite-rank symmetry. On a singular stratum the same finite list of moments may have a rank defect, and the chart must either be refined or the stratum must be excluded by the active-support hypothesis. This is why the manuscript distinguishes Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} from Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}}. The orbit depth measures the true realization symmetry, whereas the variety depth measures the algebraic rank of the chosen moment representation.

Why no genericity assumption is hidden.

The theorem does not say that an arbitrary finite moment truncation separates every pair of measures in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. It says that after the active component is localized, after the dead-neuron set has been collapsed, and after a compact exhaustion has been chosen, there is a finite separating truncation on that chart. The compactness is supplied by the propagated weighted moment bound, and the separating algebra is supplied either by the analytic assumption H3 or by the explicit finite-dimensional computation in the polynomial and piecewise-linear examples. This is the reason M0M_{0} appears as an architecture-data quantity, not as a training-time parameter. Once the chart is fixed, the statistical covering calculation can use M0M_{0} without re-proving identifiability.

I.11.4 Threshold support and finite-temperature density in the same chart

Fix a retained mode m∈Aλm\in A_{\lambda} and choose a quotient chart zz around its active representative. The risk expansion has the local form

δ​ℛδ​μ​(z)=δ​ℛδ​μ​(zm)+12​(z−zm)⊤​Hm​(z−zm)+O⁡(|z−zm|3),\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(z)=\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta\mu}(z_{m})+\frac{1}{2}(z-z_{m})^{\top}H_{m}(z-z_{m})+O(|z-z_{m}|^{3}), (266)

with HmH_{m} positive on the transverse directions after quotienting. Substituting (266) into the Gibbs formula (148) yields the local density approximation (214). The mode is retained exactly when the decrease in the risk coefficient exceeds the entropy cost cσ​λc_{\sigma}\lambda. If it is retained, the quotient-active measure records a center [zm][z_{m}]; if it is not retained, the contribution is integrated into the tail κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda).

The calculation also shows why no contradiction arises between smoothness and sparsity. The full density has nonzero width at every positive λ\lambda, but the quotient-active representation stores the finite set of centers needed to realize the thresholded network function. The density width affects constants and the Cσ​λ​SC_{\sigma}\lambda S displacement term; it does not increase the support count S∗S^{\ast}.

Density before projection, atoms after thresholding.

The entropy-regularized stationary law is absolutely continuous with respect to the reference law on the full parameter space. The sparse statement concerns the active projected component after applying the coefficient threshold dictated by H4 and after collapsing the zero-amplitude ridge. These two statements are compatible because the active dictionary is not the full density; it is the finite list of retained modes that remains after the Euler–Lagrange equation has been paired with the Hermite/Barron dictionary. Remark 5.4 records this separation, and Lemma 5.6 supplies the stationary equation used to read off which modes survive the threshold. Thus the word “support” in Theorem 5.5 is always read modulo the finite-rank active projection, never as a claim that the full Langevin density has literally become a finite sum of Dirac masses.

Threshold scale and regularization.

The threshold is proportional to the regularization scale because the entropy term allows a small diffuse component to remain in directions whose target coefficient is below the noise-regularization floor. Keeping the coefficient floor explicit avoids two wrong limiting pictures. If the floor is ignored, the theorem would overstate exact recovery at fixed temperature. If the diffuse component is treated as an additional dictionary atom, the sparse depth would be inflated by a non-identifiable zero-amplitude ridge. The paper takes the middle route: retained coefficients produce active atoms modulo GσfinG_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{fin}}, while the discarded tail contributes to κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda) in Theorem 6.1. This is the only place where the target function, rather than the initialization tail, enters the sparse residual.

Euler–Lagrange reading of retained modes.

Pairing the stationary equation with a dictionary direction gives a balance between the residual correlation of that direction and the entropy penalty paid for activating it. A mode with coefficient above the threshold can reduce the regularized objective by entering the active support; a mode below the threshold is cheaper to leave in the residual tail. This is the variational reason for the set AλA_{\lambda} used in the sparse construction. The argument does not require the full stationary density to concentrate on a finite set. It requires only that the active projection of the modes with profitable correlations be finite after the threshold is imposed. The regularity of the full density is supplied by the Langevin noise; the discreteness of the retained representation is supplied by the finite-dimensional thresholded dictionary.

Dependence on the target rather than on initialization.

The old initialization-only tail would be wrong in the Gaussian case because the reciprocal moment boundary records parameter growth, not coefficient decay of f∗f^{\ast}. The corrected residual κ⁡(f∗,S,λ)\kappa(f^{\ast},S,\lambda) is read from the Hermite/Barron coefficients of the target and from the regularization cost of retaining SS modes. The initialization enters through accessibility and moment propagation, not through the numerical tail in the target expansion. This separation is also what allows two different targets trained from the same initialization to have different sparse depths. The architecture and data law determine the dictionary; the target determines which dictionary coefficients survive the threshold.

I.11.5 Localized empirical process calculation with the active quotient

Let ℱS,R\mathcal{F}_{S,R} be the class of SS-atom quotient networks on the truncation ball. The parameter dimension is dQ=S⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)d_{Q}=S(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}). A Euclidean ε/(C​Rq+1)\varepsilon/(CR^{q+1})-net of the quotient coordinates produces an L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) ε\varepsilon-net of functions by the feature Lipschitz bound. Hence

log⁡𝒩⁡(ε,ℱS,R,L2​(ρX))≤dQ​log⁡(1+C​Rq+1ε).\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}_{S,R},L^{2}(\rho_{X}))\leq d_{Q}\log\left(1+\frac{CR^{q+1}}{\varepsilon}\right). (267)

Set R=Rn=C​log⁡nR=R_{n}=C\sqrt{\log n}. The localized excess-risk inequality for squared loss gives

Estat​(n)≤C⁡(ℜn​(ℱS,Rn)2+ℙ⁡(|θ|>Rn)).E_{\rm stat}(n)\leq C\left(\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{S,R_{n}})^{2}+\mathbb{P}(|\theta|>R_{n})\right). (268)

The tail probability is O⁡(n−2)O(n^{-2}) by construction. The Rademacher term is controlled by (230), yielding dQ​(log⁡n)2/nd_{Q}(\log n)^{2}/n. This derivation uses the orbit depth, not the moment-variety depth, because nets are built on quotient coordinates rather than on equations defining moment fibers.

Covering the active class.

The empirical-process term is computed after the support restriction of Theorem 5.5. Each retained atom contributes an active quotient chart of dimension deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}: deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} input directions, one bias coordinate, one output-amplitude coordinate, minus the finite-rank orbit dimension. The product chart for S∗S^{\ast} atoms therefore has intrinsic dimension S∗​(deff+2−Dorb∗)S^{\ast}(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}) before logarithmic truncation factors are counted. The truncation radius R⁡(n)R(n) enters because H1 permits polynomial-growth activations. On the high-probability event where the input and parameter coordinates remain inside the radius, the localized covering number has the logarithm stated in Appendix I.8. Outside that event, the sub-Gaussian input tail and the propagated moment bound give a negligible contribution that is absorbed into the same statistical constant.

Why the extra logarithm is retained.

For bounded activations the second logarithm can often be removed by replacing the truncation argument with a global envelope. The manuscript keeps the (log⁡n)2(\log n)^{2} factor in (53a) because the theorem is stated under the broader polynomial-growth hypothesis H1. This is a conservative choice, but it is the stable one: it allows ReLU-type and polynomial examples to be handled by a single covering proof. In the architecture table, bounded analytic activations may be read as a special case with a smaller envelope constant. The statement of Theorem 6.1 deliberately does not optimize logarithmic factors separately for each activation family, because the structural contribution is the quotient dimension and the four-source decomposition, not a sharp empirical-process logarithm.

Symmetrization after quotienting.

Once the active quotient chart is fixed, the empirical-process estimate can be run with standard symmetrization on a finite-dimensional localized class. The function envelope depends on the truncation radius and the propagated moment ball, but the entropy integral depends on the quotient dimension rather than on the raw ambient parameter dimension. This is the point at which identifiability affects statistics. If two different parameter values are in the same finite-rank orbit, counting them separately only inflates the covering number without changing the represented function. The quotient removes that artificial multiplicity before the empirical process is bounded.

Measurability of the localized class.

The compact-exhaustion argument also supplies separability for the localized function class. On each compact chart, the feature map is continuous into L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) under the H1 envelope, and a countable dense grid in the chart gives a countable dense subclass for the empirical-process supremum. This avoids a hidden measurability assumption in the statistical term. After the estimate is proved on the compact chart, the exhaustion radius is sent to the deterministic radius controlled by the weighted moment bound. The tail probability is handled by the same sub-Gaussian input estimate used in the envelope calculation. Thus the statistical bound is not an informal dimensional heuristic; it is a localized covering statement on a separable quotient class.

I.11.6 Compatible limits make every cross term lower order

Write the four leading scales as

aN\displaystyle a_{N} =N−1,\displaystyle=N^{-1}, bT\displaystyle b_{T} =e−αλ​T,\displaystyle=e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}, (269)
cn\displaystyle c_{n} =S∗​(λ)​(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2n,\displaystyle=\frac{S^{\ast}(\lambda)(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}}{n}, dλ\displaystyle d_{\lambda} =κ⁡(f∗,S∗,λ).\displaystyle=\kappa(f^{\ast},S^{\ast},\lambda). (270)

The nonzero cross terms are bounded by square roots such as (aN​bT)1/2(a_{N}b_{T})^{1/2}, (bT​cn)1/2(b_{T}c_{n})^{1/2}, (bT​dλ)1/2(b_{T}d_{\lambda})^{1/2}, and (cn​dλ)1/2(c_{n}d_{\lambda})^{1/2}. For any η>0\eta>0, Young’s inequality gives

2​(x​y)1/2≤η​x+η−1​y.2(xy)^{1/2}\leq\eta x+\eta^{-1}y. (271)

Along a compatible joint limit, choose η\eta slowly varying so that the right side remains lower order than the sum of the leading diagonal terms. The two centered cross terms are exactly zero and do not require this choice. Therefore the scalar remainder satisfies

RT=o⁡(aN+bT+cn+dλ)R_{T}=o(a_{N}+b_{T}+c_{n}+d_{\lambda}) (272)

whenever all four leading components vanish. This is the formal content behind the phrase “scalar remainder” in Theorem 6.1.

Order of limits.

The compatible-limit definition is designed to prevent the four leading terms from being mixed into an uncheckable remainder. First, the sample size determines the statistical localization scale and the sparse threshold. Second, the regularization schedule fixes the stationary target approximation and the contraction rate. Third, the training time is chosen so that the optimization term is lower order than the statistical and sparse terms. Finally, the width is chosen so that the propagation component is no larger than the leading statistical term. This order is not logically necessary for every application, but it makes the asymptotic statement reproducible from the displayed bounds. If a different application chooses width before sample size, the same theorem applies after rechecking the four inequalities in Definition 6.7.

Cross terms remain scalar.

The total decomposition is written for the squared prediction norm, so mixed products such as statistical-by-propagation or optimization-by-sparse terms appear when intermediate approximations are inserted by the triangle inequality. Each such product is controlled by 2​a​b≤a2+b22ab\leq a^{2}+b^{2} at the same scale as its two parent components. The scalar remainder RTR_{T} records the small terms left after this reduction. It is not an operator-valued object and it is not an additional source of error. Once the compatible-limit inequalities hold, every cross term is lower order than the sum of (53a), (53b), (53c), and (53d). This is the reason Theorem 6.1 can present four named components rather than a long list of pairwise products.

Six mixed products.

A four-term decomposition has six pairwise mixed products when the intermediate approximations are expanded in a squared norm: statistical-optimization, statistical-propagation, statistical-sparse, optimization-propagation, optimization-sparse, and propagation-sparse. The proof does not assume that these products vanish by orthogonality. Instead, each is dominated by the parent terms with Young’s inequality, and the compatible-limit conditions ensure that the dominated products do not become leading terms under the chosen schedule. This is why Appendix I.9 tracks the centered products explicitly before Theorem 6.1 states the simplified four-component bound.

Remainder scale.

The scalar RTR_{T} is a notation for the sum of dominated products and localization tails after the four displayed components have been extracted. It is lower order only along a compatible sequence; for arbitrary finite N,n,TN,n,T it should be read as part of the finite-sample inequality, not as a formal asymptotic zero. This convention is useful because it makes the theorem honest at finite scale and still gives a clean limiting statement once N,n,T,N,n,T, and λ\lambda are scheduled. In applications one may set the schedule first and then evaluate the displayed parent bounds to check that RTR_{T} is indeed negligible.

I.11.7 Sharp Gaussian-boundary failure under higher-order drift

The maximality proof is local at t=0t=0, but the sharpness construction shows why the boundary is not merely notational. For a Gaussian initialization in m=d+2m=d+2 parameter dimensions,

m2​r​(0)=𝔼​|θ|2​r=2r​Γ⁡(r+m/2)Γ⁡(m/2)≍rr.m_{2r}(0)=\mathbb{E}|\theta|^{2r}=2^{r}\frac{\Gamma(r+m/2)}{\Gamma(m/2)}\asymp r^{r}. (273)

A cubic activation produces, after differentiating the risk drift, a leading moment term of order m6​n−2m_{6n-2} in the derivative of m2​nm_{2n}. More precisely, after truncating the activation and then sending the truncation radius to infinity inside the weighted class, one obtains a lower bound of the form

dd​t​m2​n​(t)|t=0≥cn​m6​n−2​(0)−Cn​(1+m2​n​(0)).\frac{d}{dt}m_{2n}(t)\bigg|_{t=0}\geq c_{n}m_{6n-2}(0)-C_{n}(1+m_{2n}(0)). (274)

Using Stirling in (273) gives m6​n−2​(0)≥((3​n−1)/e)3​n−1m_{6n-2}(0)\geq((3n-1)/e)^{3n-1} up to a dimension constant. Therefore any proposed reciprocal weight strictly larger than w∗(n)≍n−1/2w^{\ast}(n)\asymp n^{-1/2} along an infinite subsequence demands uniform control of a hierarchy whose first derivative already exceeds the proposed envelope. The conclusion is not that the PDE explodes instantly; the conclusion is that the stronger weighted class is not invariant under the drift hierarchy. This is the sharpness content needed by Proposition 3.9.

The calculation also explains why the theorem states a maximal class generated by the initialization rather than a universal activation-dependent class. Different initial tails give different reciprocal boundaries, and the polynomial drift can only propagate what the initial law and reference confinement jointly supply. The Gaussian case is canonical because it makes the reciprocal boundary visible as n−1/2n^{-1/2}.

Meaning of sharpness.

The Gaussian boundary calculation is a statement about invariant weighted classes, not a claim that the McKean–Vlasov equation ceases to exist for Gaussian initialization. The flow exists in the class generated by the reciprocal moment boundary w∗(n)≍n−1/2w^{\ast}(n)\asymp n^{-1/2}. What fails for a strictly stronger proposed weight is the uniform propagation of the stronger norm from the same initial law. This distinction keeps Proposition 3.8 from becoming a tautology. The proposition identifies the largest admissible class attached to the given initialization; it does not say that the same physical dynamics cannot be studied in another topology after imposing stronger initial tails.

Role of the reference confinement.

The reference law in the entropy term contributes a confining drift in the convention used by (8). This confinement is strong enough to close finite moments on finite horizons under H1, but it does not manufacture arbitrarily strong initial moment weights at time zero. The initial membership condition remains visible in every weighted estimate. Consequently the maximality statement is tied to the pair consisting of the initialization and the drift hierarchy. For sub-Gaussian initial laws the reciprocal boundary is explicit; for heavier-tailed initial laws the same definition gives a different boundary. This is why the paper defines w∗w^{\ast} from μ0\mu_{0} instead of hard-coding a Gaussian sequence into the theorem.

Why the example is not a non-Lipschitz counterexample.

The sharpness calculation uses higher moment growth in the drift hierarchy; it is not an assertion about failure of local Lipschitz continuity on bounded sets. A polynomial activation may satisfy the polynomial-growth side of H1 while still forcing high moments to interact with even higher moments. The obstruction is therefore a weighted-class obstruction, not a pathwise existence obstruction for a locally regular coefficient. This reading is consistent with the statement of Theorem 3.1: the theorem propagates the class generated by the initial moment boundary and does not promise propagation in every strictly stronger class.

How to compare different initial laws.

If the initialization has compact support, its moment-growth boundary is much larger than the Gaussian reciprocal boundary, and the same drift hierarchy can propagate a stronger class on finite horizons. If the initialization has only polynomial tails, the admissible class is weaker. The theorem is deliberately formulated with w∗w^{\ast} attached to μ0\mu_{0} so that these cases are not forced into a single artificial scale. The Gaussian calculation is included because it is the standard initialization in the μ\muP setup and because it exposes the reciprocal convention cleanly. It is not meant to be the only admissible initialization.

I.11.8 Polynomial unreachable component as an exact orthogonal projection

For σ⁡(z)=zk\sigma(z)=z^{k} under Gaussian input, every network function belongs to the direct sum of Hermite chaoses of degree at most kk. Indeed, expanding (⟨w,x⟩+b)k(\langle w,x\rangle+b)^{k} in Hermite polynomials yields

{fμ:μ∈𝒫2}¯⊆⨁r=0kℋr,\overline{\{f_{\mu}:\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}\}}\subseteq\bigoplus_{r=0}^{k}\mathcal{H}_{r}, (275)

where ℋr\mathcal{H}_{r} is the degree-rr Gaussian chaos. If f∗=Hm​(⟨v,x⟩)f^{\ast}=H_{m}(\langle v,x\rangle) with m>km>k, orthogonality of Hermite chaoses gives

‖fμ−f∗‖L2​(ρX)2=‖Π≤k​fμ‖L22+‖f∗‖L22≥‖f∗‖L22.\|f_{\mu}-f^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}=\|\Pi_{\leq k}f_{\mu}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|f^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\geq\|f^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. (276)

This is not a training failure. It is an architectural non-realizability statement. The sparse residual in Theorem 6.1 must remain nonzero in this case, and S∗=∞S^{\ast}=\infty if one insists on exact realization of f∗f^{\ast} by degree-kk polynomial features.

The quotient invariants still make sense on the reachable component: Dorb∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}} is computed from homogeneity and tensor stabilizers, and Dvar∗D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{var}} from the rank of the finite tensor moment map. What fails is H4 for the target, not the mean-field existence theorem. This separation prevents Section 7 from overstating sparse decomposition for polynomial activations.

I.11.9 Finite support bound from Carathéodory plus activation multiplicity

Let Vλ=span⁡{ψm:m∈Aλ}V_{\lambda}=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_{m}:m\in A_{\lambda}\} be the retained dictionary subspace. Its dimension is at most |Aλ||A_{\lambda}| before activation multiplicity is considered. The thresholded target fλ∗f_{\lambda}^{\ast} lies in VλV_{\lambda}. If the activation dictionary realizes each basis direction ψm\psi_{m} using at most mult⁡(σ)\operatorname{mult}(\sigma) quotient atoms, then a direct constructive bound is

Sdirect​(λ)≤|Aλ|​mult⁡(σ)=Sup​(σ,ρ,f∗,λ).S_{\mathrm{direct}}(\lambda)\leq|A_{\lambda}|\operatorname{mult}(\sigma)=S_{\mathrm{up}}(\sigma,\rho,f^{\ast},\lambda). (277)

Carathéodory gives an alternative convex-geometric bound when the retained target is represented as a convex combination of normalized features:

Scar​(λ)≤dimVλ+1.S_{\mathrm{car}}(\lambda)\leq\dim V_{\lambda}+1. (278)

The manuscript uses (277) because it is compatible with signed coefficients and with the activation-specific multiplicity. Equation (278) is still useful as a sanity check: it shows finite support once the retained dictionary is finite-dimensional, regardless of the chosen teacher representation.

Neither bound proves equality with the minimal teacher width. Equality can fail if two retained modes share a ridge realization, if quotient symmetries identify representatives, or if signed cancellations reduce the active set. The theorem therefore defines S∗S^{\ast} as the a posteriori minimum after finite support has been established, and states only S∗≤SupS^{\ast}\leq S_{\mathrm{up}}.

Convex hull versus signed representation.

The finite-support bound uses a convex-geometric argument only after the retained dictionary modes have been normalized into a finite-dimensional span. Neural-network representations are signed because the output weights may be positive or negative. The standard way to apply the convex-hull theorem is to split the signed coefficient vector into positive and negative parts, normalize each part on the retained span, and then absorb the total variation into the output amplitudes of the selected atoms. This doubles a harmless finite-dimensional constant but does not change the threshold order. The activation multiplicity factor records the number of ridge atoms needed to realize one retained dictionary mode inside the architecture.

No claim of minimal teacher width.

The number S∗S^{\ast} is a sparse depth after quotienting and thresholding. It need not equal the minimal teacher width of a particular finite network representation. Symmetries, sign splits, and the entropy floor can all change the number of visible atoms without changing the represented function in L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}). The theorem only needs an upper bound strong enough to feed the statistical factor in (53a) and the sparse residual in (53d). Minimality is used only in the a posteriori definition of sparse depth once the retained target has been fixed. This avoids identifying an algorithmic recovery claim with a structural support claim.

I.11.10 Explicit compatible-limit examples

The definition of compatible limits is nonempty. Suppose first that S∗​(λ)=O⁡(log⁡(1/λ))S^{\ast}(\lambda)=O(\log(1/\lambda)), as in analytic single-index targets, and choose

λ=n−1/2,T=αλ−1(logn)2,N=n2.\lambda=n^{-1/2},\qquad T=\alpha_{\lambda}^{-1}(\log n)^{2},\qquad N=n^{2}. (279)

Then Epoc=O⁡(n−2)E_{\rm poc}=O(n^{-2}), Eopt=e−(log⁡n)2E_{\rm opt}=e^{-(\log n)^{2}}, and

Estat=O((log⁡n)3n),Esparse=O(n−1/2logn)E_{\rm stat}=O\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3}}{n}\right),\qquad E_{\rm sparse}=O(n^{-1/2}\log n) (280)

under the exponential-tail sparse balance. All four terms vanish.

For polynomial coefficient tails, take |f^m∗|≲m−β|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|\lesssim m^{-\beta} with β>1\beta>1 and choose S=Sn≍(n/(log⁡n)2)1/(2​β)S=S_{n}\asymp(n/(\log n)^{2})^{1/(2\beta)}. Then

Estat≍Sn​(log⁡n)2n,Esparse≍Sn1−2​β,E_{\rm stat}\asymp\frac{S_{n}(\log n)^{2}}{n},\qquad E_{\rm sparse}\asymp S_{n}^{1-2\beta}, (281)

which balances the estimation and approximation parts. Taking again N=n2N=n^{2} and T=αλ−1​(log⁡n)2T=\alpha_{\lambda}^{-1}(\log n)^{2} makes the propagation and optimization terms lower order. These examples demonstrate that the joint limit is not a formal decoration: it gives concrete schedules under which the four-term decomposition becomes a rate statement.

The polynomial-tail example is the schematic rate of Corollary 6.9. Choosing λ=n−1/(2β)\lambda=n^{-1/(2\beta)} and S≍(n/(log⁡n)2)1/(2​β)S\asymp(n/(\log n)^{2})^{1/(2\beta)} makes the three nonzero terms in (59) of the same order up to logarithmic factors. The compatibility constraint of Definition 6.7 is then satisfied by T=(log⁡n)2/αλT=(\log n)^{2}/\alpha_{\lambda} and any N≥nN\geq n, with the second constraint (log⁡N)/(αλ​T)=o⁡(1)(\log N)/(\alpha_{\lambda}T)=o(1) following from αλ≍λ​cπ\alpha_{\lambda}\asymp\lambda c_{\pi}.

The centered sigmoid schedule of Corollary 6.10 provides the cleanest closed-form rate in the present paper: a single-index analytic target with exponential Hermite tails attains O⁡(N−1+(log⁡n)3/n)O(N^{-1}+(\log n)^{3}/n) along a compatible sequence with N≥nN\geq n and explicit λ=n−1\lambda=n^{-1}. The same schedule extends mutatis mutandis to any analytic activation with a one-dimensional Hermite ridge representation, since only the threshold count S∗​(λ)≍log⁡(1/λ)S^{\ast}(\lambda)\asymp\log(1/\lambda) enters the leading term.

Width schedules.

The examples use N≥nN\geq n or N=n2N=n^{2} only to make the propagation component visibly non-leading. The theorem itself permits other width schedules. If the target has a large sparse depth, the statistical component may dominate and N≍nN\asymp n is already sufficient. If the sample size is small but a long training horizon is used, the propagation term may need a larger width to keep the particle approximation below the optimization error. The displayed schedules are therefore witnesses of compatibility, not optimal prescriptions. Their role is to show that the conditions in Definition 6.7 are simultaneously satisfiable.

Temperature schedules.

The regularization parameter has two jobs: it gives the Langevin flow a stable entropy structure and it sets the coefficient threshold in the sparse approximation. Taking λ\lambda too large leaves a visible sparse residual; taking it too small weakens the contraction rate through αλ\alpha_{\lambda} and requires a longer training time. The compatible schedules balance these effects by choosing TT as a function of αλ\alpha_{\lambda} and by choosing SS as a function of the coefficient tail. This explains why the examples state TT and λ\lambda together rather than treating training time as an independent afterthought.

I.11.11 Squared Wasserstein versus prediction-norm convention

The quantitative statements use squared quantities. The Wasserstein estimate is

supt≤T𝔼​W22​(μtN,μt)≤C​N−1.\sup_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t})\leq CN^{-1}. (282)

By Jensen this implies 𝔼W2(μtN,μt)≤C1/2N−1/2\mathbb{E}W_{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t})\leq C^{1/2}N^{-1/2}, but the unsquared rate is not the one inserted into the risk decomposition. The prediction-norm transfer uses the squared Lipschitz estimate

𝔼​‖fμtN−fμt‖L2​(ρX)2≤CR​𝔼​W22​(μtN,μt)≤CR​C​N−1.\mathbb{E}\|f_{\mu_{t}^{N}}-f_{\mu_{t}}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{X})}^{2}\leq C_{R}\mathbb{E}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t})\leq C_{R}CN^{-1}. (283)

The risk is quadratic, so the natural propagation component in Theorem 6.1 is the squared prediction error, not the unsquared transport distance. This convention also matches the objective gap: a second-order Taylor expansion of the squared loss has leading term proportional to ‖fμtN−fμt‖L22\|f_{\mu_{t}^{N}}-f_{\mu_{t}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. Therefore all appearances of N−1N^{-1} in Theorems 3.1 and 6.1 refer to squared Wasserstein, squared prediction norm, or functional value. If one writes a bound in W2W_{2} itself, the corresponding exponent is N−1/2N^{-1/2} and must be labelled as unsquared. The manuscript avoids this ambiguity by stating the squared convention at the theorem level and in the abstract.

This check is included because a referee will read the propagation term as one of the central quantitative claims. The proof chain is consistent only if the metric, prediction norm, and objective gap are all squared before they are compared.

Squared convention across the manuscript.

The manuscript consistently states the particle rate in squared quantities. Thus 𝔼​W22​(μtN,μt)\mathbb{E}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t}) and the corresponding squared prediction norm are of order N−1N^{-1}. If one takes square roots, the unsquared W2W_{2} scale is N−1/2N^{-1/2}. Both statements are compatible, but only the squared convention enters the four-term error decomposition. This is why the abstract, Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.7, and Theorem 6.1 all use N−1N^{-1} in the displayed squared bounds. The convention is chosen so that the propagation component has the same units as the statistical, optimization, and sparse residual components.

Prediction norm after barycentre transfer.

The transfer from W22W_{2}^{2} to L2​(ρX)L^{2}(\rho_{X}) prediction error is deterministic after the moment radius has been fixed. It does not require a second propagation-of-chaos theorem. Applying the barycentre Lipschitz estimate gives ‖fμtN−fμt‖L22≤LR2​W22​(μtN,μt)\|f_{\mu_{t}^{N}}-f_{\mu_{t}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq L_{R}^{2}W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{t}^{N},\mu_{t}) on the localized event, and the tail of the localization is absorbed by the same moment estimate. This explains why no independent empirical quantization term appears in Theorem 6.1. The empirical measure is already the particle system driven by the coupled dynamics, not a fresh iid sample from μt\mu_{t} at each time.

I.11.12 Three target regimes and their resulting leading rates

The four-term decomposition becomes concrete once the sparse tail is specified. For an exactly finite target with S∗=sS^{\ast}=s and κ=0\kappa=0, a compatible choice N≍nN\asymp n, T≍αλ−1​log⁡nT\asymp\alpha_{\lambda}^{-1}\log n yields

𝔼​‖fμTN−f∗‖L22=O⁡(n−1+s⁡(deff+2−Dorb∗)​(log⁡n)2n).\mathbb{E}\|f_{\mu_{T}^{N}}-f^{\ast}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=O\left(n^{-1}+\frac{s(d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}})(\log n)^{2}}{n}\right). (284)

For an analytic target with S∗​(λ)=O⁡(log⁡(1/λ))S^{\ast}(\lambda)=O(\log(1/\lambda)) and sparse residual O⁡(λ​log⁡(1/λ))O(\lambda\log(1/\lambda)), choosing λ=n−1\lambda=n^{-1} gives

O⁡(N−1+e−αλ​T+(log⁡n)3n+log⁡nn),O\left(N^{-1}+e^{-\alpha_{\lambda}T}+\frac{(\log n)^{3}}{n}+\frac{\log n}{n}\right), (285)

so the statistical logarithm dominates the sparse displacement when NN and TT are chosen compatibly. For polynomial coefficient decay |f^m∗|≲m−β|\widehat{f}_{m}^{\ast}|\lesssim m^{-\beta}, the balance between estimation and approximation gives the rate described in (60). These three regimes cover the examples in Section 7: finite ReLU hinge dictionaries, analytic tanh dictionaries, and slow Barron/Hermite tails.

The purpose of these formulas is not to optimize constants. It is to verify that the decomposition has the correct limiting behavior in qualitatively different target classes. In every regime the propagation term can be made smaller by width, the optimization term by time, the statistical term by samples, and the sparse term by the threshold/temperature schedule. That separation is the operational meaning of the total feature-learning-error decomposition.

Finite-atom regime.

If the target is exactly represented by a finite active dictionary after quotienting, the sparse residual vanishes once SS reaches that active cardinality up to the fixed regularization floor. The dominant terms are then the statistical component, the optimization component, and the propagation component. Choosing TT logarithmic in nn and NN at least of order nn gives the familiar parametric scale up to the logarithmic factor already present in (53a). The theorem does not require the training algorithm to know the atoms in advance; it only states the risk decomposition conditional on the structural support result of Theorem 5.5.

Exponential-tail regime.

For analytic single-index targets, Hermite coefficients decay exponentially. The threshold count grows only logarithmically in the inverse regularization scale, which leads to the (log⁡n)3/n(\log n)^{3}/n type expression displayed in Corollary 6.10. One logarithm comes from the number of retained modes and two from the conservative polynomial-growth covering bound. If the activation is bounded and the empirical-process argument is sharpened, this logarithmic power can be improved, but the present theorem keeps one envelope for all examples. The advantage of the exponential-tail case is that the sparse residual is made smaller than the statistical term with a very small active set.

Polynomial-tail regime.

For polynomially decaying coefficients, the retained depth grows as a power of nn. The balance in (59) chooses SS so that the statistical cost of adding atoms and the residual cost of truncating the tail are comparable. Width and time are then selected to keep the propagation and optimization components below that balanced scale. This regime is the most sensitive to the quotient dimension: replacing deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} by the ambient input dimension can change the exponent hidden in the practical sample size even when the asymptotic display has the same algebraic form. The architecture computations in Section 7 are included precisely to make this dimension visible for single-index and multi-index targets.

Ambient dimension versus effective dimension.

The rates displayed in the three regimes are intentionally written with deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} rather than dd. A single-index target in a high-dimensional input space should not pay the full ambient dimension after the active quotient has been identified. The input tail assumption is still ambient because it controls the random covariates, but the covering of the learned active dictionary is intrinsic to the target’s projection. This is the statistical counterpart of the identifiability theorem: once the function is known to live on a lower-dimensional active projection, the quotient chart should reflect that lower dimension.

Constants hidden in the rates.

The notation O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) hides constants depending on the activation envelope, the input-tail parameter, the regularization scale, and the propagated weighted moment radius. It does not hide additional powers of NN, nn, or SS beyond those displayed. This matters in the polynomial-tail regime, where the active depth itself grows with nn. The proof keeps the dependence on SS explicit through the statistical factor and the sparse residual. Any constant depending exponentially on SS would invalidate the displayed balance; the localized covering argument avoids this by treating the product chart dimension linearly in SS and by absorbing only polynomial radius factors into the logarithmic envelope.

How the three regimes share one theorem.

The finite-atom, exponential-tail, and polynomial-tail cases are not separate theorems because their proofs use the same four structural inputs. The existence theorem supplies the propagated moment ball and the particle approximation; the identifiability theorem supplies the active quotient; the sparse theorem supplies the thresholded support and the tail; the error theorem combines the four numerical components. What changes from regime to regime is only the rule that converts the coefficient tail of f∗f^{\ast} into a depth SS and a residual size. This organization is useful for later applications: a new activation or target class can be inserted by computing its coefficient tail and its quotient dimension, without reopening the mean-field or propagation proof.

What would need improvement for sharp constants.

A sharper version of the paper could optimize the empirical-process logarithms separately for bounded analytic activations, replace the conservative truncation radius by a refined Orlicz envelope, and use activation-specific curvature to improve the optimization constant. Those refinements would change constants and logarithms, not the four-component architecture of the theorem. The present manuscript keeps the common proof envelope because it is stable across ReLU, smooth bounded activations, polynomial activations, and multi-index targets. The displayed rates should therefore be read as structurally uniform rates. They identify which dimension, support depth, width, horizon, and residual tail control the error, while leaving activation-specific constant optimization to a separate analysis.

Reading the rates as diagnostics.

The same formulas also act as diagnostics for a concrete training run. If increasing NN does not change the error while increasing nn does, the propagation component is already below the statistical component. If increasing training time improves the error at fixed width and sample size, the optimization component is still visible. If neither width nor time helps and the error is stable under additional samples, the active dictionary or the sparse residual is the limiting factor. The theorem is not an algorithmic stopping rule, but it tells the reader which structural quantity each experimental or theoretical knob is meant to affect. This diagnostic interpretation is one reason the four components are kept separated rather than being hidden inside a single unspecified constant.

Consistency with the architecture table.

The examples in Section 7 should be read through the same diagnostic lens. ReLU changes the quotient dimension because of positive homogeneity; tanh changes the sparse depth because of analytic Hermite tails; polynomial activations change the realizable component because the feature map lives in a finite chaos span; multi-index targets change deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} without changing the ambient data law. Each row of the table therefore alters a different symbol in Theorem 6.1. This is the operational content of computing the invariants: the table is not an illustration appended after the proof, but the place where the abstract constants in the four-source bound become concrete quantities for standard architectures.

I.12 Final source-level consistency notes

The source-level checks are operational rather than mathematical, so they are not expanded as a further proof appendix. The manuscript uses a single convention for squared propagation-of-chaos rates, a target-dependent sparse residual, the active quotient dimension deff+2−Dorb∗d_{\mathrm{eff}}+2-D^{\ast}_{\mathrm{orb}}, and the weighted class ℳw∗\mathcal{M}_{w^{\ast}} generated by the reciprocal moment-growth boundary.
